Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 24, verses 1–2 (part 1 of 2):

Surat an-Nur has sixty-four verses and is Medinan.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿A surah which We have sent down and made obligatory, and in which We have sent down clear signs, that you may remember.﴾ ﴿The fornicatress and the fornicator—flog each of them with a hundred lashes. And let not pity for them overtake you in the religion of Allah, if you believe in Allah and the Last Day. And let a group of the believers witness their punishment.﴾ ﴿The fornicator does not marry except a fornicatress or an polytheist, and the fornicatress is not married except by a fornicator or a polytheist, and that has been forbidden to the believers.﴾ [An-Nur: 3] ﴿And those who accuse chaste women and then do not produce four witnesses—flog them with eighty lashes, and do not accept their testimony ever after. And those are the defiantly disobedient.﴾ [An-Nur: 4] ﴿Except those who repent after that and reform, for indeed Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.﴾ [An-Nur: 5] ﴿And those who accuse their wives and have no witnesses except themselves—then the testimony of one of them is four testimonies by Allah that he is indeed of the truthful.﴾ [An-Nur: 6] ﴿And the fifth [testimony] is that the curse of Allah be upon him if he is of the liars.﴾ [An-Nur: 7] ﴿But it will avert the punishment from her that she testify four testimonies by Allah that he is indeed of the liars.﴾ [An-Nur: 8] ﴿And the fifth [testimony] is that the wrath of Allah be upon her if he was of the truthful.﴾ [An-Nur: 9] ﴿And if not for the bounty of Allah upon you and His mercy, and that Allah is Accepting of repentance and Wise.﴾ [An-Nur: 10]

(p-426) This surah is Medinan without any disagreement. When the Exalted mentioned the polytheists of Quraysh and that they have deeds other than that—that is, evil deeds which they perform—and, after that, digressed to their conditions, their taking of offspring and partners, and their final destination in the Fire, among their evil deeds was that they had slave-girls who were prostitutes, from whom they earned money through fornication and ate of their earnings. So Allah sent down the beginning of this surah as a severe prohibition regarding the matter of fornication. It is related that some Muslims intended to marry them—and it seems improper that some Muslims intended to marry them.

The majority (al-Jumhur) read "surah" (سُورَةٌ) in the nominative, so they permitted it to be the predicate of an omitted subject, i.e., "this is a surah," or a subject with an omitted predicate, i.e., "in what We have revealed to you" or "in what is recited to you." Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "It may also be a subject whose predicate is ﴿the fornicatress and the fornicator﴾ and what follows it; the meaning being 'the surah which is sent down and made obligatory is such-and-such,' since a surah is an expression for a sequence of verses having a beginning and an end—unless the subject is not clearly the predicate, unless the predicate is assumed to be for the whole surah; and this is far-fetched in analogy." And ﴿We have sent it down﴾ in these readings is in the position of a qualifier. End of quote.

ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAziz, Mujahid, ʿIsa ibn ʿUmar al-Thaqafi al-Basri, ʿIsa ibn ʿUmar al-Hamdani al-Kufi, Ibn Abi ʿAbla, Abu Haywa, and Mahbub, from Abu ʿAmr and Umm al-Darda', read "surah" (سُورَةً) in the accusative. This is explained as an implied verb: "I recite a surah," and ﴿We have sent it down﴾ is a qualifier. Al-Zamakhshari said: "Or it is in the sense of 'take a surah' (دُونَكَ سُورَةً), so it is put in the accusative as an incitement (al-ighra'), and the particle of incitement may not be omitted." They also permitted that it be of the category of al-ishtighal (the verb's object being occupied by a pronoun): "We sent down a surah which We have sent down," so ﴿We have sent it down﴾ explains the hidden ﴿We sent down﴾; it has no place in grammar, except that it involves beginning with an indefinite noun without a justification—unless it is held that a qualifier is omitted, i.e., "a surah" that is "magnified" or "clarified," ﴿We have sent it down﴾, and then that is permissible.

Al-Farra' said: "(surah) is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun ha' and alif, and a circumstantial clause from a pronoun may precede it." End of quote. So the pronoun in ﴿We have sent it down﴾ in the accusative does not refer back to "surah." It seems the meaning is: "We sent down the rulings and made them obligatory, as a surah," i.e., in the state of being a surah from the surahs of the Qur'an. So these rulings are established not only by the Sunnah but by the Qur'an and the Sunnah together.

The majority read ﴿wa-faradnaha﴾ with a light ra' (فَرَضْناها), i.e., "We imposed its rulings and made them obligatory, and made them voluntary for those who undertake them." It was said: "We imposed the practice of what is in it." ʿAbdullah, ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAziz, Mujahid, Qatadah, Abu ʿAmr, and Ibn Kathir read it with a doubled ra' (فَرَّضْناها), either for emphasis in obligation, or because it contains various obligations, or because of the great number of things made obligatory upon them. It was said: every command and prohibition in this surah is an obligation.

﴿And We have sent down in it clear signs﴾: parables, admonitions, and rulings which contain no obscurity requiring interpretation. The majority read ﴿the fornicatress and the fornicator﴾ in the nominative, and ʿAbdullah read (wa-z-zani) without the yā'. The view of Sibawayh is that it is a subject whose predicate is omitted, i.e., "in what is recited to you is a ruling: ﴿the fornicatress and the fornicator﴾," and his saying ﴿flog﴾ is an explanation of that ruling. Al-Farra', al-Mubarrad, and al-Zajjaj held that the predicate is ﴿flog﴾. Al-Zamakhshari permitted this. The cause of the disagreement is that, according to Sibawayh, the subject whose predicate begins with the fa' must be a relative clause that can take a conditional particle, verbally or by implication, and the active participle and passive participle may not be preceded by a conditional particle. Those other than Sibawayh among those mentioned did not stipulate this. The presentation of both positions and the preference are mentioned in the science of grammar.

ʿIsa al-Thaqafi, Yahya ibn Yaʿmar, ʿAmr ibn Fa'id, Abu Jaʿfar, Shayba, Abu al-Sammal, and Ruways read ﴿the fornicatress and the fornicator﴾ in the accusative, both of them, as an occupied-object construction: "flog the fornicatress and the fornicator," as in your saying "Zayd, strike him," and the reason for the fa' has a explanation mentioned in the science of grammar. The accusative here is better than in ﴿a surah which We have sent down﴾ because of the imperative.

The surah contains many rulings concerning fornication, marrying fornicators, the accusation of chaste women, mutual cursing (li'an), the veil, and other matters. It began with fornication because of its ugliness and the corruptions and disgrace that arise from it. It had spread among the Arabs, and from their slave-women there arose owners of banners (ashab rayat). The fornicatress is mentioned before the fornicator because her inclination is stronger, due to the strength of her desire and the deficiency of her intellect, and because her fornication is more shameful and brings greater disgrace, and because of conception of an illegitimate child; and the state of women is one of veiling and protection.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "(If you ask): the fornicatress was mentioned before the fornicator first, then the fornicator was mentioned before her a second time. (I answer): That verse came for their punishment for what both of them committed, and the woman is mentioned first because she is the source from which the offense arose: if she did not entice the man, nor lie in wait for him, nor enable him, he would not have desired nor been able. Since she was the origin and first in that, she was mentioned first. As for the second, it is directed at the mention of marriage, and the man is the root in that, because he is the one desiring and proposing, and from him the seeking begins." End of quote. This answer is complete in the second case only if marriage is understood as the contract and not as sexual intercourse.

The "al" (ال) in ﴿the fornicatress and the fornicator﴾ is for generality, covering all fornicators.

Ibn Salam and others said: it is specific to the unmarried pair (al-bikrayn), and "jald" means striking the skin with the whip, as you say "his head, his belly, his back," meaning he struck his head, belly, and back. This pattern holds for three-letter names of bodily organs. The apparent meaning is that the disbeliever, the slave, and the married person are included in this generality, and it does not include the insane or the child, by consensus. Ibn Salam and others said: the jurists of the regions agree that the married person is stoned and not flogged. Al-Hasan, Ishaq, and Ahmad said: he is flogged and then stoned. "ʿAli, may Allah be pleased with him, flogged Shurahah al-Hamdaniyyah and then stoned her, and said: 'I flogged her by the Book of Allah and stoned her by the Sunnah of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ.'" There is no proof in the fact that the stoning of Unays's companion and of al-Ghamidiyyah was not reported with flogging, because that is known from the rulings of the Qur'an, so only what goes beyond the Qur'an is reported, and that is stoning; therefore stoning was mentioned and flogging was not.

Abu Hanifah's view is that Islam is a condition of ihsan (marriage-chastity), while al-Shafi'i's view is that it is not a condition. They agreed that the female slave is flogged fifty lashes, and likewise the male slave, according to the view of the majority. The people of the apparent meaning (Ahl al-Zahir) said: the male slave is flogged a hundred lashes, and some said: the female slave is flogged a hundred lashes unless she is married, then fifty. The apparent meaning includes the two dhimmis in the fornicatress and the fornicator, so they are flogged according to Abu Hanifah and al-Shafi'i, and if they are married they are stoned according to al-Shafi'i. Malik said: there is no punishment on them. The apparent meaning is that there is no punishment on the fornicatress and the fornicator other than flogging alone; this is the view of the Kharijites. Stoning, however, is established by widely transmitted Sunnah, and after the Messenger the caliphs of Islam acted upon it: Abu Bakr, ʿUmar, and ʿAli; and among the Companions: Jabir, Abu Hurayrah, Buraydah al-Aslami, and Zayd ibn Khalid. They differed regarding exile (taghrib) by banishing the unmarried after flogging. Al-Thawri, al-Awza'i, al-Hasan ibn Salih, and al-Shafi'i said: the fornicator is banished. Al-Awza'i and Malik said: the man is banished and the woman is not banished. Malik said: the slave is not banished for half a year. The apparent meaning is that this flogging applies only to the one upon whom fornication is established. If the two are found under one garment, Ishaq said: each of them is struck a hundred lashes, and this is narrated from ʿUmar and ʿAli. ʿAta', al-Thawri, Malik, and Ahmad said: they are disciplined according to their respective schools in discipline. As for coercion: the woman who is coerced has no punishment, and regarding the punishment of the coerced man there is disagreement and detail: whether a ruler coerces him, so he is not punished, or someone else, so he is punished. This is the view of Abu Hanifah; the view of Abu Yusuf, Muhammad, al-Hasan ibn Salih, and al-Shafi'i is that he is not punished in either case; and the view of Zufar is that he is punished in both cases. The apparent meaning is that the one who has intercourse with a woman via her anus, or with a male, or with an animal, is not included in fornication. It was said: he is included. Those commanded to flog are the leaders of the Muslims and their deputies. They differed regarding a rebellious Kharijite who has seized power establishing the hudud: it was said he may, and it was said he may not. And regarding a master establishing the hudud upon his slaves: Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn ʿUmar, ʿAra'ishah, Fatimah, and al-Shafi'i said he may. Abu Hanifah, Muhammad, and Zufar said he may not. Malik and al-Layth said he may, except for amputation for theft, which only the imam carries out. And flogging, as we have said, is striking the skin; the verse does not specify the posture of the one who flogs, nor the posture of the one flogged, nor the place of the flogging, nor the description of the instrument used for flogging; this is mentioned in the books of jurisprudence.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "(If you ask): is this ruling for all fornicators, male and female, or for some of them? (I answer): Rather, it is the ruling for the one among them who is not married, for the married person's ruling is stoning." (If you ask): the wording requires attaching the ruling to all fornicators, since His saying ﴿the fornicatress and the fornicator﴾ is general to all, encompassing both the married and the unmarried. (I answer): ﴿The fornicatress and the fornicator﴾ indicate the two genders opposed to the two genders of the chaste man and chaste woman by an absolute indication, and the genericness exists in all and in some together, so whichever the speaker intends, there is no fault, as is done with a homonym (al-ism al-mushtarak)." End of quote. The indication of the wording on the two genders is not, as he mentioned, an absolute indication, because the indication of general inclusion (istighraq) is distinct from the indication of general substitution (badal), which is absolute; and it is not like the indication of a homonym, because the indication of generality is each single individual in the manner of full inclusion, whereas the indication of a homonym indicates each single individual through inclusion in use—though there is disagreement about this in the principles of jurisprudence. But what I have mentioned is what is sound upon examination and in the usage of Arabic speech.

Ali ibn Abi Talib, al-Sulami, Ibn Miqsam and Dawud ibn Abi Hind, on the authority of Mujahid, read ﴿and let them not take you﴾ with a *ya'* (yā’) instead of a *ta'* (tā’). The reason is that the feminine gender of *ra'fah* (mercy, tenderness) is only figurative, and the separation between the verb and its subject made the *ya'* acceptable. The majority (al-Jumhur) read it with a *ta'* because *ra'fah* is grammatically feminine in form.

The majority read ﴿ra'fah﴾ with the hamzah silent (*sukun*). Ibn Kathir read it with a *fatḥah* on the hamzah, and Ibn Jurayj read it with an *alif* after the hamzah. This reading is also reported from Asim and Ibn Kathir. All of these are verbal nouns (*maṣādir*), and the most well-known is the first.

The *ra'fah* that is forbidden is that which would prevent those in charge from carrying out the *ḥadd* (the prescribed legal punishment). Abu Mijlaz, Mujahid, Ikrimah and Ata said: it refers to dropping the *ḥadd*, meaning: carry it out, and do not let this be averted. This is not the interpretation of Ibn Umar, Ibn Jubayr and others. Their position is that the *ḥadd* for fornication (*zina*), slander (*firyah*) and wine-drinking is of one and the same kind.

Qatadah, Ibn al-Musayyib and others said: the forbidden *ra'fah* concerns lightening the beating inflicted on fornicators. In their view, the beating for slander and wine-drinking should be lightened, while the beating for fornication should be made more severe.

Al-Zamakhshari said: the meaning is that it is obligatory for the believers to be firm in the religion of God, to exert zeal and resolve in it, and not to be swayed by leniency and indulgence in preserving its limits. End of quote. This is an embellishment of the view of Abu Mijlaz and those who agree with him.

Al-Zuhri said: it is made strict for fornication and slander, and lenient for the punishment for drinking.

Mujahid, al-Sha'bi and Ibn Zayd said: there is an omission in the speech, its implied meaning being: ﴿and let not pity for them take hold of you﴾ so that you suspend the limits and do not enforce them. The prohibition is apparently directed at *ra'fah*, but what is intended is what *ra'fah* leads to, namely the suspension or diminution of the *ḥudūd*. The meaning of ﴿in the religion of God﴾ is: in violating the religion of God, that is, His law. It has been said that *dīn* may here mean judgment (*ḥukm*).

﴿If you believe in God and the Last Day﴾ is a reinforcement, an exhortation and an incitement to anger for the sake of God and His religion, just as you say: "If you are a man, then do it." God, exalted is He, ordered that a group witness their flogging, as a means of severity against fornicators and of rebuke before the eyes of people. He called the flogging a *ʿadhāb* (punishment), since it involves pain and public disgrace, and it is a penalty for that act. The group (*ṭā'ifah*) commanded to witness it: the derivation of the word indicates something that goes around (*yaṭūfu*) a thing, and the least that can be conceived of in that is three; it is a generally prevailing description, because it is the group surrounding a thing. From Ibn Abbas and Ibn Zayd, in explaining it, comes "four to forty." From al-Hasan: ten. From Qatadah and al-Zuhri: three or more. From Ikrimah and Ata: two men or more, and this is the well-known view of Malik. From Mujahid: one or more. The use in Arabic speech of a plural pronoun referring back to *ṭā'ifah* is evidence that the plural is intended by it, and this is common in the Qur'an.

The apparent meaning includes the two dhimmis in the fornicatress and the fornicator, so they are flogged according to Abu Hanifah and al-Shafi'i, and if they are married they are stoned according to al-Shafi'i. Malik said: there is no punishment on them. The apparent meaning is that there is no punishment on the fornicatress and the fornicator other than flogging alone; this is the view of the Kharijites. Stoning, however, is established by widely transmitted Sunnah, and after the Messenger the caliphs of Islam acted upon it: Abu Bakr, ʿUmar, and ʿAli; and among the Companions: Jabir, Abu Hurayrah, Buraydah al-Aslami, and Zayd ibn Khalid. They differed regarding exile (taghrib) by banishing the unmarried after flogging. Al-Thawri, al-Awza'i, al-Hasan ibn Salih, and al-Shafi'i said: the fornicator is banished. Al-Awza'i and Malik said: the man is banished and the woman is not banished. Malik said: the slave is not banished for half a year. The apparent meaning is that this flogging applies only to the one upon whom fornication is established. If the two are found under one garment, Ishaq said: each of them is struck a hundred lashes, and this is narrated from ʿUmar and ʿAli. ʿAta', al-Thawri, Malik, and Ahmad said: they are disciplined according to their respective schools in discipline. As for coercion: the woman who is coerced has no punishment, and regarding the punishment of the coerced man there is disagreement and detail: whether a ruler coerces him, so he is not punished, or someone else, so he is punished. This is the view of Abu Hanifah; the view of Abu Yusuf, Muhammad, al-Hasan ibn Salih, and al-Shafi'i is that he is not punished in either case; and the view of Zufar is that he is punished in both cases. The apparent meaning is that the one who has intercourse with a woman via her anus, or with a male, or with an animal, is not included in fornication. It was said: he is included. Those commanded to flog are the leaders of the Muslims and their deputies. They differed regarding a rebellious Kharijite who has seized power establishing the hudud: it was said he may, and it was said he may not. And regarding a master establishing the hudud upon his slaves: Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn ʿUmar, ʿAra'ishah, Fatimah, and al-Shafi'i said he may. Abu Hanifah, Muhammad, and Zufar said he may not. Malik and al-Layth said he may, except for amputation for theft, which only the imam carries out. And flogging, as we have said, is striking the skin; the verse does not specify the posture of the one who flogs, nor the posture of the one flogged, nor the place of the flogging, nor the description of the instrument used for flogging; this is mentioned in the books of jurisprudence.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "(If you ask): is this ruling for all fornicators, male and female, or for some of them? (I answer): Rather, it is the ruling for the one among them who is not married, for the married person's ruling is stoning." (If you ask): the wording requires attaching the ruling to all fornicators, since His saying ﴿the fornicatress and the fornicator﴾ is general to all, encompassing both the married and the unmarried. (I answer): ﴿The fornicatress and the fornicator﴾ indicate the two genders opposed to the two genders of the chaste man and chaste woman by an absolute indication, and the genericness exists in all and in some together, so whichever the speaker intends, there is no fault, as is done with a homonym (al-ism al-mushtarak)." End of quote. The indication of the wording on the two genders is not, as he mentioned, an absolute indication, because the indication of general inclusion (istighraq) is distinct from the indication of general substitution (badal), which is absolute; and it is not like the indication of a homonym, because the indication of generality is each single individual in the manner of full inclusion, whereas the indication of a homonym indicates each single individual through inclusion in use—though there is disagreement about this in the principles of jurisprudence. But what I have mentioned is what is sound upon examination and in the usage of Arabic speech.

Ali ibn Abi Talib, al-Sulami, Ibn Miqsam and Dawud ibn Abi Hind, on the authority of Mujahid, read ﴿and let them not take you﴾ with a *ya'* (yā’) instead of a *ta'* (tā’). The reason is that the feminine gender of *ra'fah* (mercy, tenderness) is only figurative, and the separation between the verb and its subject made the *ya'* acceptable. The majority (al-Jumhur) read it with a *ta'* because *ra'fah* is grammatically feminine in form.

The majority read ﴿ra'fah﴾ with the hamzah silent (*sukun*). Ibn Kathir read it with a *fatḥah* on the hamzah, and Ibn Jurayj read it with an *alif* after the hamzah. This reading is also reported from Asim and Ibn Kathir. All of these are verbal nouns (*maṣādir*), and the most well-known is the first.

The *ra'fah* that is forbidden is that which would prevent those in charge from carrying out the *ḥadd* (the prescribed legal punishment). Abu Mijlaz, Mujahid, Ikrimah and Ata said: it refers to dropping the *ḥadd*, meaning: carry it out, and do not let this be averted. This is not the interpretation of Ibn Umar, Ibn Jubayr and others. Their position is that the *ḥadd* for fornication (*zina*), slander (*firyah*) and wine-drinking is of one and the same kind.

Qatadah, Ibn al-Musayyib and others said: the forbidden *ra'fah* concerns lightening the beating inflicted on fornicators. In their view, the beating for slander and wine-drinking should be lightened, while the beating for fornication should be made more severe.

Al-Zamakhshari said: the meaning is that it is obligatory for the believers to be firm in the religion of God, to exert zeal and resolve in it, and not to be swayed by leniency and indulgence in preserving its limits. End of quote. This is an embellishment of the view of Abu Mijlaz and those who agree with him.

Al-Zuhri said: it is made strict for fornication and slander, and lenient for the punishment for drinking.

Mujahid, al-Sha'bi and Ibn Zayd said: there is an omission in the speech, its implied meaning being: ﴿and let not pity for them take hold of you﴾ so that you suspend the limits and do not enforce them. The prohibition is apparently directed at *ra'fah*, but what is intended is what *ra'fah* leads to, namely the suspension or diminution of the *ḥudūd*. The meaning of ﴿in the religion of God﴾ is: in violating the religion of God, that is, His law. It has been said that *dīn* may here mean judgment (*ḥukm*).

﴿If you believe in God and the Last Day﴾ is a reinforcement, an exhortation and an incitement to anger for the sake of God and His religion, just as you say: "If you are a man, then do it." God, exalted is He, ordered that a group witness their flogging, as a means of severity against fornicators and of rebuke before the eyes of people. He called the flogging a *ʿadhāb* (punishment), since it involves pain and public disgrace, and it is a penalty for that act. The group (*ṭā'ifah*) commanded to witness it: the derivation of the word indicates something that goes around (*yaṭūfu*) a thing, and the least that can be conceived of in that is three; it is a generally prevailing description, because it is the group surrounding a thing. From Ibn Abbas and Ibn Zayd, in explaining it, comes "four to forty." From al-Hasan: ten. From Qatadah and al-Zuhri: three or more. From Ikrimah and Ata: two men or more, and this is the well-known view of Malik. From Mujahid: one or more. The use in Arabic speech of a plural pronoun referring back to *ṭā'ifah* is evidence that the plural is intended by it, and this is common in the Qur'an.

The apparent meaning is that it is a report (khabar) intended to denounce fornication (zina) and to emphasise its gravity. The meaning of ﴿lā yankiḥu﴾ ("does not marry") is: "does not have intercourse (waṭʾ)." The phrase "or a polytheist" (al-mushrikah) is added in the division, so the meaning is that the fornicator, during his fornication, does not have intercourse except with a fornicating woman from among the Muslims, or with one lower than her, namely a polytheist. The meaning of nikāḥ as intercourse is transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbās here. Al-Zamakhsharī said: "It has been said that by nikāḥ is meant waṭʾ (intercourse), but this is not a valid view, for two reasons. The first: this word, wherever it occurs in the Qur'an, is not intended except in the sense of the contract. The second: the meaning becomes corrupt, and it leads to your saying: 'The fornicator does not fornicate except with a fornicatress, and the fornicatress does not fornicate except with a fornicator.'" End of quotation. What he mentioned as the first point he took from al-Zajjāj, who said: "Nikāḥ is not known in the Book of God except in the sense of marriage (tazwīj)." But this is not as he said. In the Qur'an there is ﴿until she marries a husband other than him﴾ (Q 2:230), and the Messenger ﷺ explained that it means intercourse. As for the second point, what is intended by it is to denounce fornication and to denounce its matter, and that it is forbidden to the believers.

Al-Zamakhsharī said, taking it from al-Ḍaḥḥāk and approving it: the debauched, corrupt man whose nature is fornication and wickedness does not desire to marry the virtuous women who are contrary to his character; he desires only a debauched, corrupt woman of his kind (p. 430), or a polytheist. And the debauched, corrupt, fornicating woman likewise does not desire to marry the righteous men, and they shun her; she desires only one of her kind among the debauched and the polytheists. For a believer praised by God to marry a fornicatress, and to desire her, and to enter by that into the line of fornicators characterised by fornication, is forbidden and prohibited, because of what it contains of resemblance to the wicked, of being present at a place of suspicion, of causing bad talk about oneself, of backbiting, and of various kinds of corruption. Keeping company with sinners contains enough exposure to committing sins, so how much more so is the marrying of adulteresses and prostitutes, and his venturing into that. End of quotation.

It is related from Ibn ʿUmar, Ibn ʿAbbās and their companions that the verse concerns particular people who used to commit fornication in their pre-Islamic time with well-known prostitutes. When Islam came and they embraced it, they could not commit fornication, so, because of their poverty, they wanted to marry those women, since it was their custom to spend upon those who had registered to marry them. So the verse was revealed concerning them. The reference by "the fornicator" is to one of those men, and the name of fornication, which was (practised) in the pre-Islamic period, was applied to him. The phrase ﴿does not marry﴾ means "does not wed." On these two interpretations there is a sense of lamentation over them and a sense of rebuke, as if He were saying: "The fornicator does not wish to marry except a fornicatress or a polytheist," meaning that their souls incline towards these base things because of their lack of self-restraint. Against these two interpretations stands the consensus that a fornicatress may not be married by a polytheist of her people, and ﴿that is forbidden to the believers﴾ (Q 24:3). That is, the marriage of those prostitutes is forbidden. So the proponents of these two interpretations maintain that God forbade their marriage to the community of Muhammad.

Al-Ḥasan said: "What is meant is the fornicator who has been subjected to the hadd (prescribed punishment), and the fornicatress who has been subjected to the hadd." He said: "This is a ruling from God, so it is not permissible for a fornicator who has been punished to marry anyone except a fornicatress." It has been related that a man who had been punished married a woman who had not been punished, and ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib annulled her marriage.

﴿And that is forbidden to the believers﴾ refers to fornication. Al-Zahrānī transmitted in this regard a ḥadīth through the route of Abū Hurayrah that the Messenger of God ﷺ said: "The fornicator who has been punished may marry only one like himself." Ibn ʿAṭiyyah said: "This ḥadīth is not sound, and this view is open to question. The inclusion of the polytheist in the verse refutes it, and the wording of the verse rejects it. And if the polytheist woman is interpreted to mean the woman of the People of the Book, then there is no way around the word 'polytheist.'" End of quotation.

Ibn al-Musayyab said: "This ruling, which applied to fornicators, is general: that a fornicator may marry only a fornicatress. Then the concession came, and that was abrogated (nusikha) by God's words: ﴿And marry the single persons among you﴾ (Q 24:32), and His words: ﴿Marry what seems good to you of women﴾ (Q 4:3). The order of this abrogation is also related from Mujāhid, except that he said: 'He forbade the marriage of those prostitutes to those men.'" Ibn ʿAṭiyyah said: "The mention of polytheism in the verse weakens these approaches." End of quotation.

It is related from al-Jibāʾī that the verse is abrogated by consensus (ijmāʿ), and this is criticised on the grounds that it is established in the principles of jurisprudence (uṣūl al-fiqh) that consensus is neither abrogated nor abrogates. It is concluded from these statements that if nikāḥ is intended to mean intercourse, then the verse came as an exaggeration in denouncing fornication. If nikāḥ is intended to mean marriage, then either it is intended as a general statement about fornicators, which was then abrogated, or it is a general statement about wicked, corrupt debauchees who desire only those who are of their kind, and corrupt debauched women who desire only those who are of their kind. Marriage in this case is not permitted, according to what al-Zamakhsharī established. Or it is intended as a particular statement about a people who were fornicators with prostitutes in the pre-Islamic period, who wished to marry them because of their poverty and their wealth, while the women continued in prostitution, so that a chaste woman would not be married by them. If a man commits fornication with a woman and then wishes to marry her, Abū Bakr al-Ṣiddīq, Ibn ʿUmar, Ibn ʿAbbās, Jābir, Ṭāwūs, Ibn al-Musayyab, Jābir ibn Zayd, ʿAṭāʾ, al-Ḥasan, ʿIkrimah, Mālik, al-Thawrī and al-Shāfiʿī permitted that. Ibn Masʿūd, al-Barāʾ ibn ʿĀzib and ʿĀʾishah forbade it, and they said: "They will continue to be fornicators as long as they remain together." Among the rare reports is that if a man known for fornication, or for other immorality, marries, the option of remaining with him or separating from him is established, and this is a defect among the defects upon which the option of annulment is based.

Some people held that the verse is muḥkam (not abrogated), and in their view, if either spouse commits fornication, the marriage between them is invalidated. Others among them said: it is not annulled, but he is commanded to divorce her if she commits fornication; if he keeps her, he sins. They said: marrying a fornicatress is not permitted, nor is marrying from a fornicator, but if repentance is manifest, it becomes permitted.

Al-Zamakhsharī said: "(If) you say: 'What is the difference between the meaning of the first clause and the meaning of the second?' (I say): The meaning of the first is a description of the fornicator as not desiring chaste women but desiring the immoral ones. The meaning of the second is a description of her as not desired by the chaste, but desired by fornicators. These are two different meanings."

It is related from ʿAmr ibn ʿUbayd that ﴿lā yankiḥ﴾ is read with the jussive (jazm), as a prohibition (nahy). The indicative (marfūʿ) form carries the sense of a prohibition, but it is more emphatic and stronger, just as "may God have mercy on you" (raḥimaka Allāh) and "may God have mercy on you" (yarḥamuka Allāh) is more emphatic than "let him have mercy on you" (liyarḥamka). It is also possible that it is a plain report, in the sense that their custom runs in this way, and the believer should not place himself under this custom, and should guard himself from it. End of quotation.

Abū al-Barhasam read ﴿wa-ḥarrama﴾ in the active voice (mabnīy lil-fāʿil), meaning God. Zayd ibn ʿAlī read ﴿wa-ḥuruma﴾ with a ḍamma on the rāʾ and a fatḥa on the ḥāʾ. The majority read ﴿wa-ḥurrima﴾ with shadda, in the passive voice (mabnīy lil-mafʿūl).

Qadhf (slander, the accusation of fornication) is throwing an accusation of fornication or other things. What is meant here is fornication, because of its being juxtaposed with it, and because four witnesses are stipulated, which is specific to slander regarding fornication, since in other cases two witnesses suffice. Ibn Jubayr said: "It was revealed because of the incident of the slander (al-ifk)." It has been said: "It was revealed in general concerning slanderers." The verb "to throw" (ramā) is used figuratively for insulting, because it is harm by speech, as the poet said:

"The wound of the tongue is like the wound of the hand."

And he said:

"He accused me of a matter from which I and my father were innocent, and he accused me on account of al-Ṭawī."

The word al-muḥṣanāt ("the chaste women"): the apparent meaning is that what is intended is chaste women. Women were singled out for this, although men share in the ruling, because slander regarding them is more heinous and more repugnant to souls, and because they are, in terms of desire, the objects of men's desire, so there is harm in it to them, to their husbands, and to their relatives. It has been said: the meaning is "the chaste private parts," as He said: ﴿and she who guarded her chastity﴾ (Q 21:91). It has been said: the meaning is "the chaste persons," and this was said by Ibn Ḥazm and reported by al-Zahrāwī. On these two views the word encompasses both women and men. The second is indicated by His words: ﴿and chaste women from among the women﴾ (Q 4:24), and there is an omitted element there, i.e., "by fornication." And by "chaste" (al-muḥṣanāt) are excluded those whose fornication or whose being fornicated with has been established. The description of being "chaste" (iḥṣān) entails Islam, sanity, puberty and freedom. Abū Bakr al-Rāzī said: "We know of no disagreement among the jurists regarding this meaning." And what is meant by "chaste" is women who are not married to the accusers, or to whom a ruling applies that comes after this. Slander with fornication that makes the hadd (prescribed punishment) obligatory is an explicit statement, such as saying: "O fornicatress!", or "O fornicator!", or "O son of a fornicator!", "O son of a fornicatress!", "O child of fornication!", "You are not your father's son!", "You are not this woman's son!", and similar explicit expressions. If someone speaks allusively, such as saying: "I am not a fornicator, nor is my mother a fornicatress," he is not subjected to the hadd according to the school of Abū Ḥanīfah, Zufar, Abū Yūsuf, Muḥammad, Ibn Shubrumah, al-Thawrī, al-Ḥasan ibn Ṣāliḥ and al-Shāfiʿī. He is subjected to the hadd according to the school of Mālik, and the hadd was established in such a case from ʿUmar after consulting the people. Aḥmad and Isḥāq said: "It is slander only in a state of anger, not in a state of approval." If someone slanders a non-Muslim, if the one slandered has a Muslim child... It has been said: if he slanders a Christian woman who is under a Muslim husband, he is subjected to the hadd. They agreed that one who slanders a child is not subjected to the hadd, even if such a child is capable of intercourse, and they differed concerning one who slanders a girl-child. Mālik said: he is subjected to the hadd if she is of a kind that can be had sexually. Mālik and al-Layth said: he is subjected to the hadd if she is of a kind that can be had sexually. Mālik and al-Layth said: one who slanders a madman is subjected to the hadd. Others said: he is not subjected to the hadd.

﴿And those who accuse﴾: its apparent meaning is males, and the ruling for females is the same as theirs. If a child or a madman slanders his wife or a stranger, there is no hadd upon him. If a mute person has a well-known gesture or a understood sign, he is subjected to the hadd according to al-Shāfiʿī. Abū Ḥanīfah said: his slander is not valid, nor is his li'ān (mutual imprecation). Since the sin of fornication is a grave sin among the major sins, and its practitioner often conceals it, so that it is rarely discovered by anyone, God, exalted is He, was severe upon the slanderer by stipulating four witnesses for it, out of mercy to His servants and as a covering for them. The meaning of ﴿then they do not bring﴾ is: they do not bring the judges. The majority read ﴿arbaʿat﴾ in the construct form, idāfah, to ﴿shuhadāʾ﴾ (witnesses). Abū Zurʿah and ʿAbd Allāh ibn Muslim read ﴿bi-arbaʿah﴾ with tanwīn, and this is an eloquent reading, because when a numeral and an adjective come together, agreement (itbāʿ) is better than idāfah. For this reason Ibn Jinnī preferred this reading over the reading of the majority, since he took it as an absolute adjective, but this is not so. For when an adjective functions like a noun and is governed by operators, it functions in number and in other respects like a noun. Among these is shahīd (witness): do you not see His words: ﴿How then, when We bring from every nation a witness﴾ (Q 4:41), and His words ﴿and call upon two witnesses﴾ (Q 2:282)? Likewise, 'abd (p. 432) "three witnesses" with the idāfah is more eloquent than tanwīn and agreement, and likewise "three slaves."

Ibn ʿAṭiyyah said: "Sībawayh holds that tanwīn of the numeral and omission of its idāfah is permitted only in poetry." End of quotation. This is not as he stated. Sībawayh holds that only in the numeral that is followed by a noun, such as "three men," and as for the adjective, no. Rather the correct view is the distinction we have mentioned. If you put tanwīn on "four" (arbaʿatan), then "witnesses" (shuhadāʾ) is in apposition (badal), since it is a word that functions like a noun, or it is an adjective, since it is a true adjective. The view of one who says it is a ḥāl (circumstantial accusative) or a tamyīz (specificative) is weak. This testimony must be by clear eyewitness observation, like the kohl-stick in the kohl-pot. The apparent view is that it is not required that their testimony be given while they are together; rather, if they are brought separately, their testimony is valid. Abū Ḥanīfah said: the condition for this is that they testify together; if they come separately, they are slanderers. The apparent view is that one of the witnesses may be the husband of the slandered woman, since he falls within "four witnesses," and by His words: ﴿then call upon four of you to witness against them﴾ (Q 4:15), and He did not distinguish between the husband being among them and their being strangers. This is what Abū Ḥanīfah and his companions said, and the woman is subjected to the hadd. This was related from al-Ḥasan and al-Shaʿbī. Mālik and al-Shāfiʿī said: the husband performs li'ān, and the three are subjected to the hadd. The same was related from Ibn ʿAbbās.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 24, verse 3–4 (part 2 of 2):

﴿Then flog them﴾ is a command to the imam (ruler) and his deputies to administer the flogging. The apparent meaning is that flogging is obligatory even if the one slandered does not demand it; this is the view of Ibn Abi Layla. Abu Hanifa and his companions, al-Awza'i and al-Shafi'i said: he is not to be punished (hadd) except upon the demand of the one slandered. Malik said likewise, except that if the imam heard him slander someone, he punishes him when there are with the imam upright (ʿudul) witnesses, even if the one slandered does not demand it. The apparent meaning is that if a free slanderer does not produce four witnesses, he is punished with eighty lashes, because he falls under the general sense of: ﴿And those who accuse﴾; this is also the view of ʿAbdullah ibn Mas'ud and al-Awza'i. Abu Hanifa and his companions, Malik, al-Thawri, ʿUthman al-Batti and al-Shafi'i said: he is flogged forty times. This is the view of ʿAli, and the practice of Abu Bakr, ʿUmar and ʿAli, and of the caliphs after them; this was stated by ʿAbdullah ibn Rabi'a. If one person slanders a group with a single expression, or addresses each one separately, he receives one punishment (hadd). This is the view of Abu Hanifa and his companions, Malik, al-Thawri and al-Layth. ʿUthman al-Batti and al-Shafi'i said: each one has his own punishment. Al-Sha'bi and Ibn Abi Layla said: if it is with a single expression, such as "O adulterers," then there is one punishment; or if he says to each one, "O adulterer," then each person has a punishment. The apparent meaning of the verse is that only the slanderer is flogged, and there is no report of flogging a witness whose testimony did not complete the required number of witnesses. The one who comes to testify for the accuser is not a slanderer, though ʿUmar treated him as a slanderer. ʿUmar flogged Abu Bakra, his brother Nafi' and Shibl ibn Ma'bad al-Bajali, because the fourth had hesitated, and that is an addition to the testimony, so he did not render it complete. Had four corrupt (fasiq) witnesses been brought, Zufar said: the punishment is averted from the slanderer and the witnesses. It is reported from Abu Yusuf that the slanderer is punished and the witnesses are spared. Malik and ʿUbayd Allah ibn al-Hasan said: the witnesses and the slanderer are both punished.

﴿And do not accept their testimony ever﴾. The apparent meaning is that his testimony is not accepted ever, even if he retracts his lie and repents. This is a prohibition that comes after a command, so just as his ruling is flogging, his ruling is also the rejection of his testimony. This is the view of Shurayh the judge, al-Nakha'i, Ibn al-Musayyib, Ibn Jubayr, al-Hasan, al-Thawri, Abu Hanifa and his companions, and al-Hasan ibn Salih: the testimony of one who has been punished for slander is not accepted, even if he repents, while his testimony in matters other than slander is accepted if he repents. Malik said: his testimony is accepted in slander concerning adultery and other matters if he repents. This is also the view of ʿAta', Tawus, Mujahid, al-Sha'bi, al-Qasim ibn Muhammad, Salim and al-Zuhri. And he said: the testimony of one who has been punished under hadd is not accepted in Islam, meaning absolutely; and his repentance is by what is accepted: by retracting his slander. This is the view of al-Shafi'i. ʿUmar acted likewise with Nafi' and Shibl, who retracted their statements, and he accepted their testimony, but Abu Bakra persisted, so his testimony was not accepted until he died.

﴿And those are the corrupt (fasiqun)﴾. The apparent meaning is that this is a new, independent statement, not included within the scope of ﴿Those who accuse﴾ [al-Nur: 23], as if it is an informing about the state of the accusers after the relative clause, which contains the sense of a conditional, is complete, and what follows in its predicate of flogging and the non-acceptance of testimony forever.

The apparent meaning is that it is a report (khabar) intended to denounce fornication (zina) and to emphasise its gravity. The meaning of ﴿lā yankiḥu﴾ ("does not marry") is: "does not have intercourse (waṭʾ)." The phrase "or a polytheist" (al-mushrikah) is added in the division, so the meaning is that the fornicator, during his fornication, does not have intercourse except with a fornicating woman from among the Muslims, or with one lower than her, namely a polytheist. The meaning of nikāḥ as intercourse is transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbās here. Al-Zamakhsharī said: "It has been said that by nikāḥ is meant waṭʾ (intercourse), but this is not a valid view, for two reasons. The first: this word, wherever it occurs in the Qur'an, is not intended except in the sense of the contract. The second: the meaning becomes corrupt, and it leads to your saying: 'The fornicator does not fornicate except with a fornicatress, and the fornicatress does not fornicate except with a fornicator.'" End of quotation. What he mentioned as the first point he took from al-Zajjāj, who said: "Nikāḥ is not known in the Book of God except in the sense of marriage (tazwīj)." But this is not as he said. In the Qur'an there is ﴿until she marries a husband other than him﴾ (Q 2:230), and the Messenger ﷺ explained that it means intercourse. As for the second point, what is intended by it is to denounce fornication and to denounce its matter, and that it is forbidden to the believers.

Al-Zamakhsharī said, taking it from al-Ḍaḥḥāk and approving it: the debauched, corrupt man whose nature is fornication and wickedness does not desire to marry the virtuous women who are contrary to his character; he desires only a debauched, corrupt woman of his kind (p. 430), or a polytheist. And the debauched, corrupt, fornicating woman likewise does not desire to marry the righteous men, and they shun her; she desires only one of her kind among the debauched and the polytheists. For a believer praised by God to marry a fornicatress, and to desire her, and to enter by that into the line of fornicators characterised by fornication, is forbidden and prohibited, because of what it contains of resemblance to the wicked, of being present at a place of suspicion, of causing bad talk about oneself, of backbiting, and of various kinds of corruption. Keeping company with sinners contains enough exposure to committing sins, so how much more so is the marrying of adulteresses and prostitutes, and his venturing into that. End of quotation.

It is related from Ibn ʿUmar, Ibn ʿAbbās and their companions that the verse concerns particular people who used to commit fornication in their pre-Islamic time with well-known prostitutes. When Islam came and they embraced it, they could not commit fornication, so, because of their poverty, they wanted to marry those women, since it was their custom to spend upon those who had registered to marry them. So the verse was revealed concerning them. The reference by "the fornicator" is to one of those men, and the name of fornication, which was (practised) in the pre-Islamic period, was applied to him. The phrase ﴿does not marry﴾ means "does not wed." On these two interpretations there is a sense of lamentation over them and a sense of rebuke, as if He were saying: "The fornicator does not wish to marry except a fornicatress or a polytheist," meaning that their souls incline towards these base things because of their lack of self-restraint. Against these two interpretations stands the consensus that a fornicatress may not be married by a polytheist of her people, and ﴿that is forbidden to the believers﴾ (Q 24:3). That is, the marriage of those prostitutes is forbidden. So the proponents of these two interpretations maintain that God forbade their marriage to the community of Muhammad.

Al-Ḥasan said: "What is meant is the fornicator who has been subjected to the hadd (prescribed punishment), and the fornicatress who has been subjected to the hadd." He said: "This is a ruling from God, so it is not permissible for a fornicator who has been punished to marry anyone except a fornicatress." It has been related that a man who had been punished married a woman who had not been punished, and ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib annulled her marriage.

﴿And that is forbidden to the believers﴾ refers to fornication. Al-Zahrānī transmitted in this regard a ḥadīth through the route of Abū Hurayrah that the Messenger of God ﷺ said: "The fornicator who has been punished may marry only one like himself." Ibn ʿAṭiyyah said: "This ḥadīth is not sound, and this view is open to question. The inclusion of the polytheist in the verse refutes it, and the wording of the verse rejects it. And if the polytheist woman is interpreted to mean the woman of the People of the Book, then there is no way around the word 'polytheist.'" End of quotation.

Ibn al-Musayyab said: "This ruling, which applied to fornicators, is general: that a fornicator may marry only a fornicatress. Then the concession came, and that was abrogated (nusikha) by God's words: ﴿And marry the single persons among you﴾ (Q 24:32), and His words: ﴿Marry what seems good to you of women﴾ (Q 4:3). The order of this abrogation is also related from Mujāhid, except that he said: 'He forbade the marriage of those prostitutes to those men.'" Ibn ʿAṭiyyah said: "The mention of polytheism in the verse weakens these approaches." End of quotation.

It is related from al-Jibāʾī that the verse is abrogated by consensus (ijmāʿ), and this is criticised on the grounds that it is established in the principles of jurisprudence (uṣūl al-fiqh) that consensus is neither abrogated nor abrogates. It is concluded from these statements that if nikāḥ is intended to mean intercourse, then the verse came as an exaggeration in denouncing fornication. If nikāḥ is intended to mean marriage, then either it is intended as a general statement about fornicators, which was then abrogated, or it is a general statement about wicked, corrupt debauchees who desire only those who are of their kind, and corrupt debauched women who desire only those who are of their kind. Marriage in this case is not permitted, according to what al-Zamakhsharī established. Or it is intended as a particular statement about a people who were fornicators with prostitutes in the pre-Islamic period, who wished to marry them because of their poverty and their wealth, while the women continued in prostitution, so that a chaste woman would not be married by them. If a man commits fornication with a woman and then wishes to marry her, Abū Bakr al-Ṣiddīq, Ibn ʿUmar, Ibn ʿAbbās, Jābir, Ṭāwūs, Ibn al-Musayyab, Jābir ibn Zayd, ʿAṭāʾ, al-Ḥasan, ʿIkrimah, Mālik, al-Thawrī and al-Shāfiʿī permitted that. Ibn Masʿūd, al-Barāʾ ibn ʿĀzib and ʿĀʾishah forbade it, and they said: "They will continue to be fornicators as long as they remain together." Among the rare reports is that if a man known for fornication, or for other immorality, marries, the option of remaining with him or separating from him is established, and this is a defect among the defects upon which the option of annulment is based.

Some people held that the verse is muḥkam (not abrogated), and in their view, if either spouse commits fornication, the marriage between them is invalidated. Others among them said: it is not annulled, but he is commanded to divorce her if she commits fornication; if he keeps her, he sins. They said: marrying a fornicatress is not permitted, nor is marrying from a fornicator, but if repentance is manifest, it becomes permitted.

Al-Zamakhsharī said: "(If) you say: 'What is the difference between the meaning of the first clause and the meaning of the second?' (I say): The meaning of the first is a description of the fornicator as not desiring chaste women but desiring the immoral ones. The meaning of the second is a description of her as not desired by the chaste, but desired by fornicators. These are two different meanings."

It is related from ʿAmr ibn ʿUbayd that ﴿lā yankiḥ﴾ is read with the jussive (jazm), as a prohibition (nahy). The indicative (marfūʿ) form carries the sense of a prohibition, but it is more emphatic and stronger, just as "may God have mercy on you" (raḥimaka Allāh) and "may God have mercy on you" (yarḥamuka Allāh) is more emphatic than "let him have mercy on you" (liyarḥamka). It is also possible that it is a plain report, in the sense that their custom runs in this way, and the believer should not place himself under this custom, and should guard himself from it. End of quotation.

Abū al-Barhasam read ﴿wa-ḥarrama﴾ in the active voice (mabnīy lil-fāʿil), meaning God. Zayd ibn ʿAlī read ﴿wa-ḥuruma﴾ with a ḍamma on the rāʾ and a fatḥa on the ḥāʾ. The majority read ﴿wa-ḥurrima﴾ with shadda, in the passive voice (mabnīy lil-mafʿūl).

Qadhf (slander, the accusation of fornication) is throwing an accusation of fornication or other things. What is meant here is fornication, because of its being juxtaposed with it, and because four witnesses are stipulated, which is specific to slander regarding fornication, since in other cases two witnesses suffice. Ibn Jubayr said: "It was revealed because of the incident of the slander (al-ifk)." It has been said: "It was revealed in general concerning slanderers." The verb "to throw" (ramā) is used figuratively for insulting, because it is harm by speech, as the poet said:

"The wound of the tongue is like the wound of the hand."

And he said:

"He accused me of a matter from which I and my father were innocent, and he accused me on account of al-Ṭawī."

The word al-muḥṣanāt ("the chaste women"): the apparent meaning is that what is intended is chaste women. Women were singled out for this, although men share in the ruling, because slander regarding them is more heinous and more repugnant to souls, and because they are, in terms of desire, the objects of men's desire, so there is harm in it to them, to their husbands, and to their relatives. It has been said: the meaning is "the chaste private parts," as He said: ﴿and she who guarded her chastity﴾ (Q 21:91). It has been said: the meaning is "the chaste persons," and this was said by Ibn Ḥazm and reported by al-Zahrāwī. On these two views the word encompasses both women and men. The second is indicated by His words: ﴿and chaste women from among the women﴾ (Q 4:24), and there is an omitted element there, i.e., "by fornication." And by "chaste" (al-muḥṣanāt) are excluded those whose fornication or whose being fornicated with has been established. The description of being "chaste" (iḥṣān) entails Islam, sanity, puberty and freedom. Abū Bakr al-Rāzī said: "We know of no disagreement among the jurists regarding this meaning." And what is meant by "chaste" is women who are not married to the accusers, or to whom a ruling applies that comes after this. Slander with fornication that makes the hadd (prescribed punishment) obligatory is an explicit statement, such as saying: "O fornicatress!", or "O fornicator!", or "O son of a fornicator!", "O son of a fornicatress!", "O child of fornication!", "You are not your father's son!", "You are not this woman's son!", and similar explicit expressions. If someone speaks allusively, such as saying: "I am not a fornicator, nor is my mother a fornicatress," he is not subjected to the hadd according to the school of Abū Ḥanīfah, Zufar, Abū Yūsuf, Muḥammad, Ibn Shubrumah, al-Thawrī, al-Ḥasan ibn Ṣāliḥ and al-Shāfiʿī. He is subjected to the hadd according to the school of Mālik, and the hadd was established in such a case from ʿUmar after consulting the people. Aḥmad and Isḥāq said: "It is slander only in a state of anger, not in a state of approval." If someone slanders a non-Muslim, if the one slandered has a Muslim child... It has been said: if he slanders a Christian woman who is under a Muslim husband, he is subjected to the hadd. They agreed that one who slanders a child is not subjected to the hadd, even if such a child is capable of intercourse, and they differed concerning one who slanders a girl-child. Mālik said: he is subjected to the hadd if she is of a kind that can be had sexually. Mālik and al-Layth said: he is subjected to the hadd if she is of a kind that can be had sexually. Mālik and al-Layth said: one who slanders a madman is subjected to the hadd. Others said: he is not subjected to the hadd.

﴿And those who accuse﴾: its apparent meaning is males, and the ruling for females is the same as theirs. If a child or a madman slanders his wife or a stranger, there is no hadd upon him. If a mute person has a well-known gesture or a understood sign, he is subjected to the hadd according to al-Shāfiʿī. Abū Ḥanīfah said: his slander is not valid, nor is his li'ān (mutual imprecation). Since the sin of fornication is a grave sin among the major sins, and its practitioner often conceals it, so that it is rarely discovered by anyone, God, exalted is He, was severe upon the slanderer by stipulating four witnesses for it, out of mercy to His servants and as a covering for them. The meaning of ﴿then they do not bring﴾ is: they do not bring the judges. The majority read ﴿arbaʿat﴾ in the construct form, idāfah, to ﴿shuhadāʾ﴾ (witnesses). Abū Zurʿah and ʿAbd Allāh ibn Muslim read ﴿bi-arbaʿah﴾ with tanwīn, and this is an eloquent reading, because when a numeral and an adjective come together, agreement (itbāʿ) is better than idāfah. For this reason Ibn Jinnī preferred this reading over the reading of the majority, since he took it as an absolute adjective, but this is not so. For when an adjective functions like a noun and is governed by operators, it functions in number and in other respects like a noun. Among these is shahīd (witness): do you not see His words: ﴿How then, when We bring from every nation a witness﴾ (Q 4:41), and His words ﴿and call upon two witnesses﴾ (Q 2:282)? Likewise, 'abd (p. 432) "three witnesses" with the idāfah is more eloquent than tanwīn and agreement, and likewise "three slaves."

Ibn ʿAṭiyyah said: "Sībawayh holds that tanwīn of the numeral and omission of its idāfah is permitted only in poetry." End of quotation. This is not as he stated. Sībawayh holds that only in the numeral that is followed by a noun, such as "three men," and as for the adjective, no. Rather the correct view is the distinction we have mentioned. If you put tanwīn on "four" (arbaʿatan), then "witnesses" (shuhadāʾ) is in apposition (badal), since it is a word that functions like a noun, or it is an adjective, since it is a true adjective. The view of one who says it is a ḥāl (circumstantial accusative) or a tamyīz (specificative) is weak. This testimony must be by clear eyewitness observation, like the kohl-stick in the kohl-pot. The apparent view is that it is not required that their testimony be given while they are together; rather, if they are brought separately, their testimony is valid. Abū Ḥanīfah said: the condition for this is that they testify together; if they come separately, they are slanderers. The apparent view is that one of the witnesses may be the husband of the slandered woman, since he falls within "four witnesses," and by His words: ﴿then call upon four of you to witness against them﴾ (Q 4:15), and He did not distinguish between the husband being among them and their being strangers. This is what Abū Ḥanīfah and his companions said, and the woman is subjected to the hadd. This was related from al-Ḥasan and al-Shaʿbī. Mālik and al-Shāfiʿī said: the husband performs li'ān, and the three are subjected to the hadd. The same was related from Ibn ʿAbbās.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 24, verse 3–4 (part 2 of 2):

﴿Then flog them﴾ is a command to the imam (ruler) and his deputies to administer the flogging. The apparent meaning is that flogging is obligatory even if the one slandered does not demand it; this is the view of Ibn Abi Layla. Abu Hanifa and his companions, al-Awza'i and al-Shafi'i said: he is not to be punished (hadd) except upon the demand of the one slandered. Malik said likewise, except that if the imam heard him slander someone, he punishes him when there are with the imam upright (ʿudul) witnesses, even if the one slandered does not demand it. The apparent meaning is that if a free slanderer does not produce four witnesses, he is punished with eighty lashes, because he falls under the general sense of: ﴿And those who accuse﴾; this is also the view of ʿAbdullah ibn Mas'ud and al-Awza'i. Abu Hanifa and his companions, Malik, al-Thawri, ʿUthman al-Batti and al-Shafi'i said: he is flogged forty times. This is the view of ʿAli, and the practice of Abu Bakr, ʿUmar and ʿAli, and of the caliphs after them; this was stated by ʿAbdullah ibn Rabi'a. If one person slanders a group with a single expression, or addresses each one separately, he receives one punishment (hadd). This is the view of Abu Hanifa and his companions, Malik, al-Thawri and al-Layth. ʿUthman al-Batti and al-Shafi'i said: each one has his own punishment. Al-Sha'bi and Ibn Abi Layla said: if it is with a single expression, such as "O adulterers," then there is one punishment; or if he says to each one, "O adulterer," then each person has a punishment. The apparent meaning of the verse is that only the slanderer is flogged, and there is no report of flogging a witness whose testimony did not complete the required number of witnesses. The one who comes to testify for the accuser is not a slanderer, though ʿUmar treated him as a slanderer. ʿUmar flogged Abu Bakra, his brother Nafi' and Shibl ibn Ma'bad al-Bajali, because the fourth had hesitated, and that is an addition to the testimony, so he did not render it complete. Had four corrupt (fasiq) witnesses been brought, Zufar said: the punishment is averted from the slanderer and the witnesses. It is reported from Abu Yusuf that the slanderer is punished and the witnesses are spared. Malik and ʿUbayd Allah ibn al-Hasan said: the witnesses and the slanderer are both punished.

﴿And do not accept their testimony ever﴾. The apparent meaning is that his testimony is not accepted ever, even if he retracts his lie and repents. This is a prohibition that comes after a command, so just as his ruling is flogging, his ruling is also the rejection of his testimony. This is the view of Shurayh the judge, al-Nakha'i, Ibn al-Musayyib, Ibn Jubayr, al-Hasan, al-Thawri, Abu Hanifa and his companions, and al-Hasan ibn Salih: the testimony of one who has been punished for slander is not accepted, even if he repents, while his testimony in matters other than slander is accepted if he repents. Malik said: his testimony is accepted in slander concerning adultery and other matters if he repents. This is also the view of ʿAta', Tawus, Mujahid, al-Sha'bi, al-Qasim ibn Muhammad, Salim and al-Zuhri. And he said: the testimony of one who has been punished under hadd is not accepted in Islam, meaning absolutely; and his repentance is by what is accepted: by retracting his slander. This is the view of al-Shafi'i. ʿUmar acted likewise with Nafi' and Shibl, who retracted their statements, and he accepted their testimony, but Abu Bakra persisted, so his testimony was not accepted until he died.

﴿And those are the corrupt (fasiqun)﴾. The apparent meaning is that this is a new, independent statement, not included within the scope of ﴿Those who accuse﴾ [al-Nur: 23], as if it is an informing about the state of the accusers after the relative clause, which contains the sense of a conditional, is complete, and what follows in its predicate of flogging and the non-acceptance of testimony forever.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 24, verse 5–10 (part 1 of 2):

﴿Except those who repent﴾. This exception (istithna') follows three sentences: the command to flog, which holds that even if he repents and retracts his accusation, the penalty for slander (hadd al-qadhf) does not fall from him; the prohibition of accepting their testimony ever; and the ruling that they are defiant sinners (fasiq). There is disagreement over whether the acceptance of their testimony is restored upon repentance, based on whether this exception returns to the prohibition sentence, or to the sentence declaring them sinners, or whether it returns to the last sentence, which is the third, namely the ruling of their defiance. What analysis requires is that when an exception follows a series of sentences, it can be specified to apply to each one of them, or it can be made to specify the last sentence. This question has been discussed in usul al-fiqh (principles of jurisprudence), where there is disagreement and detail. I have not seen anyone among the grammarians (nuhat) discuss it except al-Mahadhabi and Ibn Malik. Ibn Malik chose that it returns to all the sentences, like the conditional, while al-Mahadhabi chose that it returns to the last sentence. This is what we choose, and we have argued for the soundness of this in the book al-Tadhyil wa'l-Takmil fi Sharh al-Tashil. Al-Zamakhshari said: He (meaning al-Shafi'i) made the exception attached to the second sentence. The excepted noun (al-mustathna) in his view should be in the genitive, as a substitute (badal) for the (hum) in (lahum). In the view of Abu Hanifa it should be in the accusative, because it is a non-obligatory (ghayr muwajjab) exception. What the apparent meaning and structure of the verse require is that the three sentences together constitute the response (jaza') of the condition, meaning the relative pronoun that carries the sense of a condition, as if it were said: "And those who accuse chaste women, flog them, reject their testimony, and declare them sinners," that is, combine for him the penalty, the rejection, and the defiance.
﴿Except those who repent﴾ from the accusation, ﴿and reform, then indeed Allah is Forgiving, Merciful﴾, so they return neither flogged, nor rejected, nor declared defiant. End of quotation. The apparent meaning of the verse does not require that the exception returns to all three sentences. Rather, the apparent meaning is what the usage of the Arabs supports, namely that it returns to the sentence immediately following it. To say that it is a disjunctive exception (istithna' munqati') despite its evident connection is weak and is not to be adopted except out of necessity.
When Allah mentioned the accusation of chaste women, and it was apparent that it includes wives and others, Sa'd ibn 'Ubadah said for this reason: "O Messenger of Allah, if I find a man with my wife, shall I give him time until I bring four witnesses? By Allah, I will strike him with the sword, without turning the blade aside." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) had decided to apply the hadd punishment on Hilal ibn Umayya when he accused his wife of adultery with Shurayk ibn Sahma. Then the verse was revealed: ﴿And those who accuse their wives﴾. It became clear that what is meant by ﴿And those who accuse chaste women﴾ [al-Nur: 4] is other than wives. The well-known view is that the incident of Hilal came before the incident of 'Uwaymir. It is said that the incident of 'Uwaymir came first. The meaning is adultery, and they did not have witnesses. The number was not specified, being satisfied with the specification in the accusation of non-wives. The meaning of (shuhada') is witnesses to the truth of their statement. It was read "wa-lam takun" with the feminine ta'. The majority read it with the masculine ya', and this is the eloquent (fasih) reading, because when the verb governs what follows illa (except) and the subject is feminine, the eloquent form is to say: "ma qama illa Hindun" (no one stood except Hind). As for "ma qamat illa Hindun," most of our companions restrict it to necessity (darura), while some grammarians permit it in speech though rarely.
And ﴿their wives﴾ (azwajahum) includes all wives, from believing women, disbelieving women, and slave women, so all of them may invoke li'an against the husband to deny the offspring. Abu Hanifa and his companions said, in one of two senses: the first is that the wife is one for whom the hadd is not obligatory on her accuser even if he is a stranger, such as when the wife is a slave or a dhimmi and has been had sexually in unlawful intercourse without ownership. The second is that one of them is not of those eligible to testify, such as being subject to hadd for slander, or being a disbeliever, or a slave. But if he is blind or defiant, he may invoke li'an. Al-Thawri and al-Hasan ibn Salih said: there is no li'an if one of the spouses is a slave or a disbeliever, and the one who was subject to hadd for slander may invoke li'an. Al-Awza'i said: there is no li'an between People of the Book (ahl al-kitab), nor between one subject to hadd for slander and his wife. Al-Layth said: a slave may invoke li'an against his free wife, and one subject to hadd for slander may do so. From Malik: a Muslim slave woman and a free Christian woman may invoke li'an against a free Muslim man, and a slave may invoke li'an against his Christian wife. Also from him: there is no li'an between a Muslim and a disbelieving woman except for one who says, "I saw her committing adultery," and he invokes li'an whether the pregnancy has become apparent or not. A Muslim does not invoke li'an against a disbelieving woman or against his slave wife except to deny pregnancy, and two Muslim slaves invoke li'an, but not two disbelieving ones. Al-Shafi'i said: every husband whose divorce is valid and who is obligated to maintenance (al-fard) invokes li'an. The apparent meaning is generality in regard to those who accuse and their wives who are accused of adultery. The apparent meaning is the accusation of adultery, whether he says, "I witnessed her committing adultery," or says, "You committed adultery." This is the view of Abu Hanifa and his companions. Malik would not invoke li'an unless he said, "I saw you committing adultery," or denied a pregnancy by her or a child from her. The blind man may invoke li'an. Al-Layth said: he does not invoke li'an unless he says, "I saw a man upon her," or he had tested her (istibra'a), and says, "This pregnancy is not from me." The verse does not address li'an except for its manner between the two spouses. The exegetes, such as al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya and others, have expanded upon the mention of many rulings of li'an that the verse does not address, and these may be found in the books of jurisprudence.
The majority read (arba'a shahadat) with the accusative as a verbal noun (masdar). ﴿Then the testimony﴾ (fa-shahadatu) is nominative as a predicate (khabar) with an omitted subject, meaning: "then the ruling or what is obligatory is...", or as a subject (mubtada') with an omitted predicate placed before it, meaning: "then upon him is that he testify", or placed after it, meaning: "what suffices for him or his obligation is...". (bi-Allah) is connected to (shahadat), and it is permissible that it be connected to ﴿fa-shahadatu﴾; so said Ibn 'Atiyya. Al-Hawfi derived this from the rule of government (a'mal): according to the view and choice of the Basrans, it is connected to (shahadat), and according to the choice of the Kufans, it is connected to the statement ﴿fa-shahadatu﴾. Al-Akhawan, Hafs, al-Hasan, Qatada, al-Za'farani, Ibn Miqsam, Abu Haywa, Ibn Abi 'Abla, Abu Bahriyya, Aban, and Ibn Sa'dan read (arba'u) with the nominative as the predicate of the subject, which is ﴿fa-shahadatu﴾. (bi-Allah) is connected to (shahadat) in this reading, and it is not permissible for it to be connected to ﴿fa-shahadatu﴾ because of the separation between the verbal noun and its genitive complement, and this is not permissible.
The majority read (wal-khamisatu) with the nominative in both places. Talha, al-Sulami, al-Hasan, al-A'mash, and Khalid ibn Iyas (also called Ibn Iliyas) read it with the accusative in both places. Hafs and al-Za'farani read the second with the accusative and not the first. So the nominative is by way of the subject, and what follows is the predicate. Whoever read the first with the accusative does so by coordination (ataf) with (arba'a) in the reading of those who read (arba'a) with the accusative, and by an omitted verb indicated by the meaning in the reading of those who read (arba'u) with the nominative, meaning: "and she testifies the fifth." Whoever read the second with the accusative coordinated it with (arba'a). In the accusative reading of (al-khamisata), (anna) after it would be on the omission of the preposition, meaning bi-anna (that), and it is permitted that (anna) and what follows be a substitute (badal) for (al-khamisata).
Nafi' read (an la'natu) with a light (an) and nominative (la'natu), and (an ghadiba) with a light (an) and (ghadiba) as a past verb, and the word Allah following it is nominative. This is because the light (an) is from the heavy (anna), and when it was lightened, its noun, which is the pronoun of the matter (dhamir al-sha'n), was omitted. What analysis requires is that when an exception follows a series of sentences, it can be specified to apply to each one of them, or it can be made to specify the last sentence. This question has been discussed in usul al-fiqh (principles of jurisprudence), where there is disagreement and detail. I have not seen anyone among the grammarians (nuhat) discuss it except al-Mahadhabi and Ibn Malik. Ibn Malik chose that it returns to all the sentences, like the conditional, while al-Mahadhabi chose that it returns to the last sentence. When Allah mentioned the accusation of chaste women, and it was apparent that it includes wives and others, Sa'd ibn 'Ubadah said for this reason: "O Messenger of Allah, if I find a man with my wife, shall I give him time until I bring four witnesses? By Allah, I will strike him with the sword, without turning the blade aside." Al-Layth said: a slave may invoke li'an against his free wife, and one subject to hadd for slander may do so. Al-Shafi'i said: every husband whose divorce is valid and who is obligated to maintenance (al-fard) invokes li'an. The apparent meaning is generality in regard to those who accuse and their wives who are accused of adultery. The apparent meaning is the accusation of adultery, whether he says, "I witnessed her committing adultery," or says, "You committed adultery." This is the view of Abu Hanifa and his companions. Al-Hawfi derived this from the rule of government (a'mal): according to the view and choice of the Basrans, it is connected to (shahadat), and according to the choice of the Kufans, it is connected to the statement ﴿fa-shahadatu﴾. Al-Akhawan, Hafs, al-Hasan, Qatada, al-Za'farani, Ibn Miqsam, Abu Haywa, Ibn Abi 'Abla, Abu Bahriyya, Aban, and Ibn Sa'dan read (arba'u) with the nominative as the predicate of the subject, which is ﴿fa-shahadatu﴾. The majority read (wal-khamisatu) with the nominative in both places. Talha, al-Sulami, al-Hasan, al-A'mash, and Khalid ibn Iyas (also called Ibn Iliyas) read it with the accusative in both places. Hafs and al-Za'farani read the second with the accusative and not the first. So the nominative is by way of the subject, and what follows is the predicate. Whoever read the first with the accusative does so by coordination (ataf) with (arba'a) in the reading of those who read (arba'a) with the accusative, and by an omitted verb indicated by the meaning in the reading of those who read (arba'u) with the nominative, meaning: "and she testifies the fifth." Whoever read the second with the accusative coordinated it with (arba'a). In the accusative reading of (al-khamisata), (anna) after it would be on the omission of the preposition, meaning bi-anna (that), and it is permitted that (anna) and what follows be a substitute (badal) for (al-khamisata).

The rest of the seven read (anna la'nata Allah) and (anna ghadaba Allah) with a heavy (anna) and accusative of what follows them as its noun, and its predicate is what follows. Ibn 'Atiyya said: the light (an) in Nafi's reading in His saying (an ghadiba) has been followed directly by the verb.
Abu 'Ali said: The people of Arabic consider it abhorrent for the verb to directly follow it, unless a separation is made between them by something, such as His saying: ﴿He knows that there will be﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 20], and His saying: (Do they not see that it does not return). As for His saying ﴿And that man has nothing but what he strives for﴾ [al-Najm: 39], that is because of the rank of laysa among verbs. As for His saying ﴿Blessed is whoever is in the fire﴾ [al-Naml: 8], then (buriku) is in the sense of supplication, so the insertion of separators did not occur, lest the meaning be corrupted. End of quotation. There is no difference between ﴿an ghadiba Allahu﴾ and ﴿an buriku﴾ [al-Naml: 8] in the verb after (an) being a supplication. Ibn 'Atiyya did not explain this, nor did al-Farisi. And (ghadiba) would be a supplication, which the grammarians have illustrated: when the verb is a supplication, no separator is placed between it and (an). Ibn 'Atiyya presented the reading of Nafi' with (an ghadiba) as something strange.

The people of opinion (ashab al-ra'y) said: there is no hadd upon her if he does not invoke li'an, and the husband's statement alone does not make it obligatory upon her. Al-Tabari related from others that "the punishment" is imprisonment. The apparent view is that li'an is satisfied with this described manner mentioned in the verse, and al-Layth said so. Al-Zamakhshari said: (If you say): why was the woman who invokes li'an specified to be sworn with the wrath of Allah? (I say): as an intensification against her, because she is the origin of wickedness and is followed in her enticement. For this reason she was mentioned first in the verse of flogging. What supports this is the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ) to Khuwaylah: "Stoning is easier for you than the wrath of Allah."

﴿Had it not been for the grace of Allah﴾ to the end of the verse. Al-Suddi said: His grace (fadl) is His favour (minnah), His mercy (rahmah) is His blessing (ni'mah). Ibn Salam said: His grace is Islam, and His mercy is the concealment (of sins).

When the Exalted explained the ruling on one who accuses chaste women and wives, it was part of His grace and mercy that He made li'an (the oath of mutual imprecation) a means to concealment and to averting the hadd (the prescribed punishment). The answer to *law-la* (لَوْلا, "were it not for") is omitted. Al-Tabrizi said: Its estimated answer is "you would have been destroyed," or "He would have exposed you," or "He would have hastened punishment upon you," or "the liar would have been made manifest" (لَتَبَيَّنَ الكاذِبُ). Ibn Atiyya said: "He would have exposed the fornicators by an easier means than this," or "He would have seized them with a punishment from Him," and other meanings of this kind, which the omission of the answer necessarily requires one to estimate, because the answer is left ambiguous.
