For entering in a manner other than this leads to the occurrence of accusation, and there is in that a harm that is not hidden.

The apparent meaning is that a person may enter his own house without seeking permission or greeting, because of His saying: ﴿other than your own houses﴾. It is also narrated that a man said to the Prophet (ﷺ): "Should I seek permission to enter upon my mother?" He said: "Yes." The man said: "She has no servant other than me; should I seek permission to enter upon her every time I go in?" He said: "Would you like to see her naked?" The man said: "No." [The narrator] said: The prohibition on entering is limited by "until you have sought companionship (istinas) and greeting" upon the people of those houses.

The apparent meaning of istinas is the opposite of istiwhash (feeling of strangeness or unease). The one who knocks on another's door does not know whether he will be permitted or not, so he is like one who feels estranged from the awkwardness of the situation; when he is given permission, he feels at ease (istanas). So the meaning is "until you are given permission," like His saying: ﴿Do not enter the houses of the Prophet unless permission is given to you﴾ [al-Ahzab: 53]. This is of the category of kinayat (metonymy) and irdaf (implication), because this kind of ease follows (yurdafu) the permission, so it is placed in the position of the permission.

It is narrated from Ibn Abbas that he said: "(tasta'nisu) means (tasta'dhinu), to seek permission." Whoever narrates from Ibn Abbas that his saying "tasta'nisu" is an error or a mistake of the copyist, and that he read "hatta tasta'dhinu," then he has attacked Islam and deviated in the religion; and Ibn Abbas is innocent of this statement. And (tasta'nisu) is firmly established in meaning and clear in form in the language of the Arabs.

"Umar said to the Prophet (ﷺ): 'Shall I seek companionship, O Messenger of Allah?' while Umar was standing at the door of the upper room," the well-known hadith. This indicates that he sought ease through it. It has also been said that it is of the istinas that means seeking information and discovering, the form istif'al from anisa al-shay' when he saw it clearly and openly. The meaning would be "until you seek information and discover the situation: whether your entry is wanted or not." From this comes the phrase "Istanis, do you see anyone?" and "I sought information (istanastu) and did not see anyone," meaning I sought to know and inquired. From this is the verse of al-Nabigha:

*"As if my saddle, when the day declined with us on the day of al-Jalil, were upon a lone traveler seeking information."*

It may also be that it comes from al-uns (companionship), meaning to find out whether there is a human being there.

It is narrated from Abu Ayyub, who said: "We said: 'O Messenger of Allah, what is istinas?' He said: 'A man speaks with a tasbih (saying Subhan Allah) and a takbir (saying Allahu akbar), clears his throat, and informs the people of the house. As for the greeting, it is that he says: "As-salamu alaykum."'"

The people of the Jahiliyyah used to say, when a man of them entered a house other than his own: "Good morning to you, good evening to you," then he would enter. Often a man would end up with his wife under one blanket. So Allah forbade that and taught the better and more complete way.

Al-Tabari, regarding "tasta'nisu," held that it means "until you make the people of the house feel at ease about you by clearing the throat, seeking permission, and the like, and make yourselves feel at ease by knowing that you have been noticed." Ibn Atiyyah said: "The morphology of the verb rules out that it is from anasa (to make at ease)," end of quote.

Ata' said: "Seeking permission is obligatory upon every one who has reached puberty, and the apparent meaning is the absolute seeking of permission, so one time suffices for it." And in a hadith: "Seeking permission is three times," meaning its completeness. "If permission is granted to him, [he enters]; otherwise let him go back. He should not repeat more than three times unless he is certain that the one in the house has not heard." The apparent meaning is that seeking permission precedes the greeting. In the hadith of Abu Dawud: "Say: 'As-salamu alaykum, may I enter?'"

The waw in ﴿and greet﴾ does not necessarily imply sequence, so the greeting was legislated at the beginning of the call, before permission, because of what the greeting contains of optimism for safety.

(dhalikum) refers to the verbal noun implied by ﴿tasta'nisu﴾. And ﴿tusallimu﴾ means that "that" — the seeking of ease and the greeting — is ﴿better for you﴾ than the greeting of the Jahiliyyah.

﴿That you may remember﴾: that is, We have legislated that and alerted you to what contains your benefit, namely concealment and not being exposed to what you dislike being exposed to.

﴿That you may remember﴾: out of care for your interests.

﴿But if you find no one in them﴾: that is, no one who gives you permission. ﴿Do not enter until you are given permission﴾, because the owner of the house may have in it what he does not want to be seen. ﴿And if you are told, "Go back," then go back﴾: this refers to the one who asked permission to enter another's house and was not granted it, whether or not there is someone in it who could grant permission. That is: do not insist in seeking permission, nor in standing at the door waiting.

﴿It is purer﴾: that is, returning is purer for you and more productive of good, because of what it contains of peace of heart and distance from suspicion. Then He informed that He, exalted is He, is ﴿Knowing of what you do﴾: that is, of what you commit and what you leave of what you were addressed with, and He will reward you for it. In this is a warning to those who spy on houses, seek to enter upon others, and look at what is not lawful.

﴿There is no blame upon you﴾: al-Zamakhshari said: "He made an exception from the houses in which seeking permission is required for their occupants those that are not inhabited, such as the funduq (inns), which are the khanat, the ribat (hostels), and the shops of merchants. And mata' (benefit) is the utility, such as sheltering from heat and cold, lodging travelers and goods, and buying and selling," end of quote. What al-Zamakhshari mentioned, that it is an exception from the houses as he stated, is narrated from Ibn Abbas, Ikrimah, and al-Hasan. But it does not appear to be an exception, because the first verse concerns inhabited and owned houses; that is why He said ﴿houses other than your own﴾, while this second verse concerns houses open to the public. Scholars have given examples of these houses. Muhammad ibn al-Hanafiyyah, Qatadah, and Mujahid said: they are the inns along the roads of travelers. Mujahid said: "No one resides in them; rather they are endowed, and every wayfarer takes refuge in them." And ﴿in which there is benefit for you﴾ means enjoyment of their utility. Ata' gave the example of ruins that are entered for relieving oneself. Ibn Zayd and al-Sha'bi said: they are the shops of (p-447) the qaysariyyah and the market. Ibn al-Hanafiyyah also said: they are the houses of Makkah, and this is only tenable on the view that the houses of Makkah are not owned, that people share them, and that Makkah was conquered by force ('anwatan).

﴿And Allah knows what you reveal and what you conceal﴾: a warning to those who enter uninhabited houses among the people of suspicion.

The (min) in ﴿from their gaze﴾ is, according to al-Akhfash, superfluous, meaning "lower their gaze from what is forbidden." According to others it is partitive (lil-tab'id), because the first glance is not within a person's control, and he only lowers his gaze after that. This is supported by the saying of Ali, may Allah ennoble his face: "Do not follow a glance with another glance; the first is yours, but the second is not yours." Ibn Atiyyah said: "It is valid for (min) to be explanatory of the kind (li-bayan al-jins), and it is valid for it to indicate the starting point (li-ibtida' al-ghayah)," end of quote. But there is no preceding indefinite term for it to be explanatory of the kind, and in any case the correct view is that "min" is not among its established functions of explaining the kind.

﴿And guard their private parts﴾: that is, from fornication and from exposure. The (min) appears in ﴿from their gaze﴾ but not before the private parts, indicating that the matter of gaze is broader. Do you not see that a husband may look at the beauties of his wife, her hair, chest, arm, shin, and foot, and likewise a female slave offered for sale; and from a non-related woman he may look at her face and her palms? But the matter of the private parts is restricted. Abu al-Aliyah and Ibn Zayd said: "Everything in the Qur'an about guarding the private parts refers to fornication, except this one, which refers to concealment." But what they said is not necessarily fixed; rather, guarding the private parts includes both kinds.

﴿That﴾ — that is, lowering the gaze and guarding the private parts — is purer for them.

﴿Indeed, Allah is Aware of what they do﴾: of diverting the gaze and exposing the private parts, and He will reward them for it. He placed lowering the gaze before guarding the private parts, because the gaze is the messenger of adultery and the forerunner of immorality; the trial in it is greater and more frequent, and one can hardly be safeguarded from it. It is the greatest gateway to the heart and the most populated of the senses' routes to it, and falls often occur through it. Some of the men of letters said:

*"Love is nothing but one glance after another glance, which grows and increases in intensity if you keep pursuing it with obstinacy."*

Then He mentioned the ruling for believing women, [namely] their equality with men in lowering the gaze and in guarding their private parts. Then He said: ﴿And not to display their adornment﴾, and He made an exception for what is apparent of the adornment. Adornment (zinah) is that with which a woman adorns herself, such as jewelry, kohl, or dye. So what is apparent of it, such as the ring, the fatkhah (a ring with a wide setting), kohl and dye, there is no harm in displaying it to non-mahram men. And what is hidden of it, such as the bracelet, the anklet, the armlet, the necklace, the diadem, the sash, and the earring, you must not display it except to those who are excepted. He mentioned the adornment rather than its locations as an intensification in the command to guard and conceal, because these adornments are placed upon parts of the body which it is not permissible to look at for anyone other than these [excepted persons]: namely the shin, the upper arm, the neck, the head, the chest and the ears. So He forbade displaying the adornments themselves, so that it would be known that looking at them is not permissible because they are in contact with those places, as evidenced by the permissibility of looking at them when they are not in contact with them. The apparent adornment was given leeway, because concealing it entails hardship: a woman cannot avoid handling things with her hands, and from the need to uncover her face, especially in testimony, litigation and marriage, and she is compelled to walk in the streets, with her feet exposed, particularly poor women. This is the meaning of His words: ﴿except what appears thereof﴾, meaning: except what custom and natural disposition have made apparent, and the basic principle regarding it is that it is apparent; leeway was granted for light adornment.

Those mentioned [in the exceptions] are those with whom she has a specific need for close contact and association, and because the likelihood of temptation from them is small; and because human nature is averse to intimacy with close relatives. A woman needs their company during journeys, for mounting and dismounting and other matters.

Ibn Mas'ud said: ﴿what appears thereof﴾ is the garments. Ahmad explicitly stated this, saying: "The apparent adornment is the garments." Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Take your adornment at every place of worship﴾ [al-A'raf: 31], and adornment was interpreted as garments.

Ibn 'Abbas said: kohl and the ring. Al-Hasan, together with a group, said: the face and the palms. Ibn Jurayj said: the face, kohl, the ring, dye and the bracelet. Al-Hasan also said: the ring and the bracelet. Ibn 'Abbas [also] said: only kohl and the ring. Al-Miswar ibn Makhramah said: these and the bracelet. Al-Hasan also said: the ring and the bracelet. Ibn Bahr said: adornment applies to the beautiful features of creation that Allah made, and to what is adorned with, of excellent clothing. So Allah forbade them from displaying that to one who is not a mahram, and He excepted what cannot be concealed at certain times, such as the face and the extremities, [provided it is] not for the purpose of enjoyment. Some denied the application of the term "adornment" to natural form, but the closer view is that it is included in adornment, for what adornment is finer than the limb's creation in utmost proportion and beauty?

In His words: ﴿and to draw their head-coverings over their bosoms﴾ there is evidence that adornment encompasses both natural form and other things; He forbade them from displaying the beauties of their natural form and so made it obligatory to cover them with the khimar. It may be said that, since the face and the two palms are usually apparent in custom and in worship such as prayer and Hajj, it is fitting that the exception refers to them. In the Sunan of Abu Dawud, it is related that he (ﷺ) said: "O Asma', when a woman reaches menstruation, it is not fitting that anything of her be seen except this," and he pointed to his face and his two palms. Ibn Khuwayz Mandad said: if she is beautiful and temptation is feared from her face and palms, then she must cover them. Women used to cover their heads with khimars and let them hang behind the back, leaving the chest, neck and ears uncovered.

The verb ﴿wal-yadribna﴾ was made to carry the sense of "wal-yulqina" and "wal-yada'na" (and let them cast/place), hence it takes 'ala, as you say "I struck my hand on the wall" when you place it upon it.

'Ayyash, from Abu 'Amr, read ﴿wali-yadribna﴾ with a kasrah on the lam; Talhah read ﴿bi-khumrihinna﴾ with a sukun on the mim; Abu 'Amr, Nafi', 'Asim and Hisham read ﴿juyubihinna﴾ with a damma on the jim; the rest of the seven read it with a kasrah on the jim.

He began with the husbands, because their observation falls upon the greater part of adornment; then He followed with the mahrams and equated them in the display of adornment, though their ranks differ in sanctity according to what is in human souls: the father and brother are not like the husband's son, for something may be displayed to the father that is not displayed to the husband's son. Here Allah did not mention the paternal uncle or the maternal uncle. Al-Hasan said: they are like the other mahrams in permissibility of looking, saying: because the verse does not mention fosterage, and it is like lineage. And in Surat al-Ahzab He said: ﴿There is no blame upon them regarding their fathers﴾ [al-Ahzab: 55], and it did not mention husbands there, but it mentioned them here. The attribution in "their women" to the believing women requires generality of what is attributed to them of women, Muslim and non-Muslim, People of the Book and polytheists, from among those who are in the company and service of the believing women. Most of the early scholars held that His words ﴿or their women﴾ are restricted to those of their own religion.

Ibn 'Abbas said: a Muslim woman may not undress among the women of the dhimmis, nor display to a non-Muslim woman anything except what she displays to non-mahram men, unless she is a slave-woman, based on His words: ﴿or those their right hands possess﴾. 'Umar wrote to Abu 'Ubaydah to forbid the women of the dhimmis from entering the bath-house with Muslim women. The apparent generality in His words ﴿or those their right hands possess﴾ includes male and female [slaves], so it is permissible for a male slave to look at his mistress what those excepted persons may look at; this is the view of 'A'ishah and Umm Salamah. It is related from Mujahid: the mothers of the believers did not veil from their mukatab slaves so long as a single dirham remained owed on them. It is narrated that 'A'ishah used to comb her hair while her slave was looking at her. Similarly from Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, who later retracted it. Ibn Mas'ud, al-Hasan, Ibn al-Musayyab and Ibn Sirin said: a slave may not look at the hair of his mistress; this is the view of Abu Hanifah. In a hadith: "It is not permissible for a woman who believes in Allah and the Last Day to travel a journey of more than three [days] except with a mahram," and a slave is not a mahram. Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab said: let not the verse of al-Nur deceive you, for its intent is the slave-women. Al-Zamakhshari said: this is the correct view, for a woman's slave is in the position of a non-mahram stranger to her, whether he is a eunuch or a full man. It is related from Maysun bint Bahdal al-Kalbiyyah that Mu'awiyah entered upon her with a eunuch, and she covered herself from him. He said: "He is a eunuch." She said: "O Mu'awiyah, do you think mutilation makes lawful what Allah has made unlawful?" According to Abu Hanifah, it is not permissible to keep eunuchs, employ them, sell them or buy them; no one from the early generation is reported to have kept them. End of quotation. Al-Irbah means need for sexual intercourse; they are the simple-minded who know nothing of women's affairs, and they follow [the household] because they get some of the surplus food.

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: included in this description are the insane, the mentally deficient, the effeminate, the decrepit old man, and the one disabled by his incapacity.

Ibn 'Amir and Abu Bakr read ﴿ghayri ulil-irbati﴾ in the accusative, as a circumstantial accusative (hal) or an exception; the rest of the seven read it in the genitive, as an adjective. He conjoined ﴿awi't-tifli﴾ to ﴿min al-rijal﴾. He divided the male attendants who have no need for intercourse into two categories: men and children. The singular noun introduced by the definite article (al) is for the genus and so is general, which is why it is described with the plural in His words ﴿alladhina lam yazharu﴾. From this is the Arab saying: "The yellow dinar and the white dirham have ruined people," meaning the dinars and dirhams; it is as if he said: "or the children." "Tifl" is one who has not reached puberty. In the Mushaf of Hafsah it reads ﴿aw al-atfal﴾ in the plural.

Al-Zamakhshari said: he placed the singular in the position of the plural, since it conveys the genus, and what follows it shows that the plural is intended, similar to ﴿yukhrijukum tiflan﴾ [Ghafir: 67]. End of quotation. Placing the singular in the position of the plural is not analogous according to Sibawayh; rather, His words "al-tifl" belong to the category of the singular defined by the article of genus, which generalizes, like His words ﴿Indeed, mankind is in loss﴾ [al-'Asr: 2], and for this reason exception from it is valid and the recitation ﴿thumma yukhrijukum﴾ [Ghafir: 67] with thumma, not with waw, is correct. His words "and similar" are not truly similar, because that is defined by the article of genus while "tiflan" is indefinite; and "tiflan" here need not be taken as the plural which Sibawayh does not analogize, since it may mean "then He brings forth each one of you," as was said about His words ﴿and she prepared for them a couch﴾ [Yusuf: 31], i.e., for each one of them. Like when you say: "The family of so-and-so, a loaf feeds them," meaning a loaf feeds each one of them. His words ﴿lam yazharu﴾ are either from the expression "zahara 'ala al-shay'" meaning he became aware of it, i.e., they do not know what 'awrah is nor distinguish it from other things; or from "zahara 'ala fulan" meaning he prevailed over him and overcame his opponent. From this is ﴿fa-asbahu zahirin﴾ [al-Saff: 14], meaning victorious and capable over it. So the meaning is: they have not reached the age of capability for intercourse.

The majority read ﴿'awrat﴾ with a sukun on the waw; this is the dialect of most Arabs, who do not vowel the waw and ya in such plurals. It is related from Ibn 'Abbas that the waw of ﴿'awarat﴾ is vowelled with a fatha. The well-known position in grammar books is that vowelling the waw and ya in such plurals is the dialect of Hudhayl ibn Mudrikah. Ibn Khalawayh, in his book "Shawadhdh al-Qira'at," reports that Ibn Abi Ishaq and al-A'mash read ﴿'awarat﴾ with a fatha. He said: we heard Ibn Mujahid say: it is a solecism; but he considered it a solecism and an error on the part of transmission, otherwise it has a standing in Arabic: the Banu Tamim say "rawadat," "judarat," and "'awarat," while the rest of the Arabs use the sukun. Al-Farra' said: the Arabs lighten this, except Hudhayl, who make heavy such plurals of the ya and waw type. One of them recited to me:

Abu bayadat ra'ihun mut'awwib
rafiqun bi-mashi al-mankibayni sabuh

﴿And let them not stamp their feet so that what they conceal of their adornment may be known.﴾ A woman used to strike the ground with her foot so that her anklet would jingle and it would be known that she wore an anklet. Ibn 'Abbas said: it is the striking of the anklet while walking and the moving of the anklets in front of men. A man from Hadramawt claimed that a woman made an anklet of silver, and made a bead of agate and placed it on her shin; she passed by a group of people and struck the ground with her foot, the anklet fell upon the agate, and it made a sound; so this verse was revealed. Al-Zajjaj said: the hearing of the sound of one who wears adornment stirs desire more strongly than displaying it. End of quotation. Abu Muhammad ibn Hazm said, in substance, that He forbade them from this because when a woman passes by men they may not turn to her or notice her, while she dislikes not being looked at; so when she does that she draws attention to herself, and this is due to her love for men being attached to her; and this is one of the hidden indications of their condition. Makki said: there is no verse in the Book of Allah with more pronouns than this one: it gathers twenty-five pronouns referring to the believing women, both in the genitive and the nominative.

Al-Zamakhshari said: He forbade the display of the sound of the jewelry after forbidding the display of the jewelry itself; from this it is known that the prohibition on displaying the places of the jewelry is more emphatic.

﴿And turn to Allah in repentance together, O believers, that you may succeed.﴾ Since commands and prohibitions from Him, the Exalted, have preceded, and a person can hardly always be able to observe them, even if he restrains himself and strives, there must be some shortcoming; so He commanded repentance and held out the hope of success if they repent. It is related from Ibn 'Abbas: "Turn [in repentance] from what you used to do in the Jahiliyyah, that you may be felicitous in this world and the Hereafter." Ibn 'Amir read ﴿ayyuhu al-mu'minun﴾, and ﴿ya ayyuhu al-sahir﴾ and ﴿ya ayyuhu al-thaqalan﴾ with a damma on the ha'; its basis is that it was fatha because it occurs before the alif; when the alif fell by the meeting of two sukuns, its vowel followed the vowel of what preceded it. The damma of the ha', which is for alerting, after ayy is a dialect of the Banu Malik, the kin of Shaqiq ibn Salamah. Some stopped with a sukun on the ha', since it is written in the Mushaf without an alif after it; and some stopped with the alif.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 24, verses 32–34 (part 1 of 2):

﴿And marry off the single among you, and the righteous among your male slaves and female slaves. If they are poor, Allah will enrich them from His bounty, and Allah is All-Encompassing, All-Knowing.﴾ ﴿Let those who cannot find a marriage (nikah) keep chaste until Allah enriches them from His bounty. And those of your slaves who seek a deed of manumission, write it for them if you know any good in them, and give them from the wealth of Allah which He has given you. And do not compel your slave girls to prostitution if they desire chastity, seeking the goods of this worldly life. And whoever compels them, then indeed Allah, after their compulsion, is Forgiving and Merciful.﴾ ﴿And We have certainly sent down to you clear verses, and an example from those who passed away before you, and an admonition for the God-fearing.﴾

When commands and prohibitions preceded, regarding lowering the gaze, guarding the private parts, concealing adornment, and other matters, and what usually drives men toward women and women toward men is not marrying, because the burdens of marriage and what is owed by each of the two spouses occupy one, Allah the Exalted commanded the marrying off of the single (al-ayama), who are those of both categories who have no spouses, so that each of them is occupied with what is incumbent upon him and does not turn to anyone else. The apparent meaning of the command in His words ﴿And marry off﴾ is obligation (wujub), and this is the view of the Zahiriyya (the literalist school), but most scholars hold that it here denotes recommendation (nadb). No era has been free of the existence of ﴿al-ayama﴾ [p. 451] and no one has objected to this, nor have guardians been commanded to arrange marriages.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "﴿al-ayama﴾ and al-yatama (orphans): their origin is aya'im and yata'im, then they were transposed," end quote. In al-Tahrir, Abu 'Umar said: "Ayama is the transposed form of aya'im, and other grammarians mentioned that ayyim (a single person) and yatim (orphan) were pluralized as ayama and yatama anomalously (shudhudh), which is to be memorized, and its pattern is fa'ala, and this is the apparent meaning of Sibawayh's speech." Sibawayh said at the end of this chapter: "This is the chapter of breaking (taksir) what is among the adjectives." And they said: "wajj and wajya, just as they said zamin and zamna," so they treated it according to meaning, just as they said yatim and yatama, and ayyim and ayama, and they treated it in the manner of raja'a, end quote. Earlier, in al-Mufradat, it was said that al-ayyim is one who has no spouse, male or female. In Abu Bakr al-Khaffaf's commentary on Sibawayh's book: "The ayyim is the one who has no spouse. Originally it applied to a woman who had been married and then lost her husband through a calamity that befell her, so it is one of the afflictions. Then it was said, metaphorically, of a virgin, because she has no spouse," end quote.

(﴿minkum﴾, "from among you") is an address to the believers. He commanded the marrying off of those among the free men and women who are single, and those among the slaves and slave girls who are righteous. The feminine is included in the masculine in His words ﴿and the righteous﴾. He specified the righteous so that their religion would be protected and their righteousness preserved for them, and because the righteous among the slaves are those whom their masters are compassionate toward and treat in the manner of children in favor and affection, so they are likely to receive attention regarding their affairs and acceptance of advice concerning them, whereas the corrupt among them are in the opposite condition with their masters. It was said: the meaning of ﴿and the righteous﴾ is: fit for marriage and capable of fulfilling its rights. Mujahid and al-Hasan read ﴿min 'ibadikum﴾ with a yaʼ in place of the alif and a fatha on the ʻayn, and its most common usage is for slaves (mamalik).

﴿If they are poor, Allah will enrich them from His bounty﴾: this is conditional upon the will mentioned in His words: ﴿And if you fear poverty, Allah will soon enrich you from His bounty, if He wills﴾ [al-Tawbah: 28].

﴿And Allah is All-Encompassing﴾: that is, possessor of wealth and abundance; Allah extends provision to whomever He wills. ("Upon them" refers to) the needs of people, so what has been decreed of provision flows to them.

﴿Let those who cannot find keep chaste﴾: that is, let them strive for chastity and the guarding of the self. The form is istaf'ala, meaning seeking chastity from one's self and compelling it to that. The unassimilated form (fakk) came according to the dialect of the Hijaz, and no one is known to have read (li-yasta'iffa) with idgham (assimilation of the doubled consonant).

﴿Who do not find marriage (nikah)﴾: it was said that nikah here is the name of what is given as a dowry and spent on marriage, like al-lihaf (blanket) and al-libas (clothing), for what one is covered with and wears. The following supports this: ﴿until Allah enriches them from His bounty﴾. So the one commanded to keep chaste is the one who lacks the wealth with which he marries and manages the affairs of marriage. The apparent meaning is that this is a command of recommendation, because of His earlier words: ﴿If they are poor, Allah will enrich them from His bounty﴾.

The meaning of ﴿do not find marriage﴾ is: they are not able to reach it. The sense is that He commanded keeping chaste to everyone for whom marriage is impossible and who cannot find it by any means of impossibility. Then the most prevalent obstacle to marriage is lack of wealth. ﴿Until He enriches them﴾ is a postponement for those who keep chaste and an advance promise of His bounty toward them, so the meaning is that waiting for that and hoping for it is a kindness to their chastity and a strengthening of their hearts. How excellently these commands are ordered: He first commanded what protects from temptation and keeps away from committing sin, which is lowering the gaze; then marriage, by which religion is guarded and by which self-sufficiency through the lawful is achieved over the unlawful; then restraining the self that commands evil and turning it away from aspiring to desire when unable to marry, until it is granted the ability to do so. End quote. This is from al-Zamakhshari's speech, and it is good. When He motivated the master to marry off the righteous among the male and female slaves, He encouraged them to grant them manumission contracts if they request that, so that they would become free and manage their own affairs.

﴿And those who seek the deed (al-kitab)﴾: that is, the contract of manumission (mukatabah), like al-'itab and al-mu'atabah (reproach and reconciliation).

﴿Of what your right hands possess﴾ includes male and female slaves. The ﴿alladhina﴾ ("those who") may be a subject (mubtada') whose predicate is the clause, and the fa' entered the predicate because the relative pronoun contains the meaning of a conditional particle. It may also be in the accusative case, as when you say: "Zayd, so strike him," because you may say "Zayd, strike," and "Zayd, strike him." When the fa' enters, the implied meaning is "strike Zayd" with the intention of ("fa-idrib"), so the fa' is in response to an omitted command. This is clarified in grammar at greater length than this. Al-Azhari said: "This contract was named mukatabah because a document (kitab) is written for the slave against the master concerning manumission when he pays what they agreed upon in wealth, and a document is written for the master against the slave concerning the installments (nujum) which he pays." [p. 452]

The apparent meaning is that mukatabah is obligatory, because of His words: ﴿so write it for them﴾. This is the view of 'Ata', 'Amr ibn Dinar, al-Dahhak, Ibn Sirin, Dawud, and the apparent view of 'Umar, because when Sirin asked Anas for a contract and Anas hesitated, he said to him: "Either I will write it for you or I will strike you with the whip (durra)." Malik and a group went to the view that it is a command of recommendation, and its wording is: "I have made a contract with you for such and such," specifying what he contracted for. The apparent meaning of the command requires that no staggered payment (tanjim) or immediate due date (hulul) be stipulated; rather it may be immediate, deferred, staggered, or unstaggered. This is the view of Abu Hanifa.

Al-Shafi'i said: it is not permitted for fewer than three installments. Most scholars said: it is permitted for one installment. Ibn Khuwayz Mandad said: if one contracts for a prompt payment, it is manumission for a sum and not a mukatabah. Some Malikis permitted immediate mukatabah and called it qita'ah.

"The good" (al-khayr) means wealth, said by Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, 'Ata', and al-Dahhak; or the skill that entails earning, said by Ibn 'Abbas also; or religion, said by al-Hasan; or establishing prayer, said by 'Ubaydah al-Salmani; or truthfulness, trustworthiness and honesty, said by al-Hasan and Ibrahim; or the intention of good in the contract, said by Sa'id ibn Jubayr. Al-Shafi'i said: trustworthiness and capacity for earning. What appears from usage is that it is religion: one says "so-and-so has good in him," and nothing comes to mind except righteousness. The command to write the contract is restricted by this condition, so if one does not know any good in him, writing the contract is not required by His words ﴿so write it for them﴾.

Regarding ﴿and give them﴾, the apparent meaning is that it is a command to the contract-makers (al-mukatibin), and so the exegetes and the majority of scholars said, and they differed over whether it is obligatory or recommended. Ibn Mas'ud and al-Hasan considered it proper that it be one-third of the contract, 'Ali one-quarter, and Qatadah one-tenth. 'Umar said: from the first of its installments, as a hastening toward good. Malik said: from the last installment. Buraydah, al-Hasan, al-Nakha'i, 'Ikrimah, al-Kalbi, and the two Muqatils said: He commanded all people to assist and support the mukatab. Zayd ibn Aslam said: the address is to the rulers of affairs, that they give the mukatabs their due from the zakat funds, and this is what His words contain: ﴿and for the slaves﴾ [al-Tawbah: 60].

The author of al-Nazm said: "If the intended meaning of giving were remission (hatt), then the Arabic expression would have had to be: 'Put it down from them' (da'uhu 'anhum) or 'Offset it against them' (qassuhum). When He said ﴿and give them﴾, it indicates that it is from zakat, since it is a handing over and giving; and this is confirmed by it being a command to give, and whatever is called giving is in the category of charity. His words ﴿from the wealth of Allah which He has given you﴾ refer to what the owner's ownership is established in, and He commanded the removal of part of it. The mukatab's debt is not a valid debt, because it is owed by his slave, and a master cannot establish a valid debt against his own slave. Also, what Allah has given is what comes into his hand and he owns, and what is dropped immediately after the contract does not become his ownership, so it does not deserve the description 'from the wealth of Allah which He has given him.'"

﴿And do not compel your slave girls to prostitution﴾: In Sahih Muslim, on the authority of Jabir: "A slave girl belonging to 'Abd Allah ibn Ubayy, called Musaykah, and another called Umaymah, he used to compel them to fornication, so they complained of that to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)" — and it was revealed. It was also said: "He had six: Mu'adhah, Musaykah, Umaymah, 'Amrah, Arwa, and Qutaylah. One of them came to him one day with a dinar and another with a cloak, and he said to them: 'Go back and commit fornication.' They said: 'By Allah, we will not do that, for Allah has brought us Islam and forbidden fornication.' So they went to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and complained," and it was revealed. The slave girl is one who is owned. This is an address to all, and it confirms that ﴿and give them﴾ is an address to all. The prohibition against compelling fornication is conditional upon their desire for chastity, because compulsion is only possible when they desire chastity; if they desire fornication, compulsion is not conceivable. The word ﴿in (in)﴾ and its preference over ﴿idha (when)﴾ is an indication that the prostitutes did this with their own desire and willingness, and that what occurred from Mu'adhah and Musaykah is a rare anomaly. This view was not clear to many exegetes. Some said: ﴿in aradna (if they desire)﴾ refers back to His words ﴿And marry off the single among you﴾. This has a great distance and separation, and also al-ayama includes males and females, so if this meaning were intended the structure would have been: "in aradu tahassunan" (if they desire chastity), with the masculine taking precedence over the feminine. Some said: this conditional is void (mulgha). Al-Karmani said: this is a condition in appearance but not a real condition, like His words ﴿if you know any good in them﴾, and although the contract is valid even if one does not know any good in him.

Ibn 'Isa said: it came in the form of a conditional to make the compulsion to that abhorrent, and he said: because it was revealed on a specific occasion, so the prohibition fell on that attribute, end quote. ﴿The goods of the worldly life﴾ refers to what they earn through fornication. His words ﴿then indeed Allah﴾ are the response of the conditional. The correct view is that the estimated completion is ﴿Forgiving, Merciful﴾ toward them, so that the response of the conditional contains a pronoun referring back to ﴿those who (alladhina)﴾, which is the conditional particle, and that this is conditional upon repentance. Because al-Zamakhshari, Ibn 'Atiyyah, and Abu al-Baqa' overlooked this ruling, they estimated ﴿then indeed Allah﴾ ﴿Forgiving, Merciful﴾ toward them, meaning toward the compelled women, so the response clause lacked a pronoun referring back to the conditional particle. Abu 'Abd Allah al-Razi weakened what we have said, and he said: "There are two aspects: the first is that indeed Allah is Forgiving and Merciful toward them, because compulsion removes sin and punishment from the one compelled regarding what he did; the second is that indeed Allah is Forgiving and Merciful toward the one compelled, on condition of repentance. This is weak, because on the first explanation there is no need for this implied pronoun, while on the second it is needed," end quote. Their speech is the speech of one who has not examined the language of the Arabs deeply.

(If you say): "His words ﴿their compulsion﴾ are a verbal noun (masdar, the noun of action) that has been put in construct with its object, and the agent together with the verbal noun is omitted. What is omitted is treated as if it were pronounced, so the meaning is 'after their compelling them,' and the connecting element (al-rabt, the pronoun or noun linking the clause back to its subject) is achieved through this omitted, implied agent. So let the issue be permitted." (I say): They did not count the omitted agent among the connecting elements. You say: "Hind, I am amazed at her striking Zayd," and the construction is permitted. But if you say, "Hind, I am amazed at a striking of Zayd," it is not permitted. When al-Zamakhshari, in one of his interpretations of ﴿for them﴾, raised an objection, he said: (If you say): there is no need to make the forgiveness dependent on them, because a woman compelled to fornication is different from a man compelled to it, in that she is not sinful. (I say): Perhaps the compulsion was less than what the Shariah takes into account, namely compulsion by killing, or by something that threatens destruction or the loss of a limb, such as severe beating or otherwise, so that she is free from sin. Perhaps she fell short of the limit at which she is excused, and so she would be sinful. End of quotation. This objection and answer are both built on the assumption that ﴿for them﴾ is the reading.

The two Harameen (the Meccan and Medinan readers), Abu 'Amr, and Abu Bakr read ﴿mubayyanat﴾ with a fatha on the ya', meaning: God has made clear and explained in this surah verses that contain rulings, limits and obligations, so those verses are the ones that are made clear. It is also possible that the meaning is that they are making clear within themselves, and then it was extended so that the one making clear is in reality other than them. The word is an adverbial complement (zarf) of the one making clear. The rest of the Seven, al-Hasan, Talha, and al-A'mash read it with a kasra on the ya'. Then either it is transitive, meaning ﴿mubayyinat﴾ makes clear other rulings and limits, and that action is attributed to the verses metaphorically; or it is intransitive, meaning they are clear in themselves, needing no one to clarify them, but are evident. This is based on the proverb: "The morning has made itself clear to one who has two eyes," meaning it has appeared and become plain.

His words ﴿and an example﴾ are conjoined to ﴿verses﴾. It is possible that the meaning is ﴿and an example﴾ from the examples of those before you, that is, a remarkable story from their stories, like the story of Joseph and Mary in their innocence, for the innocence of the one against whom the slander was spoken, so that they might look at God's power in His creation and His making in it, and thus take warning. Al-Dahhak said: the meaning of the example is what is in the Torah and the Gospel concerning establishing the limits, so He sent down in the Qur'an the like of it. Muqatil said: that is, a likeness of their state in denying the messengers, that is, We have made clear to you what punishment We inflicted upon them because of their rebellion, and We made that an example for you so that you would know that if you share with them in disobedience, you will be like them in deserving punishment.

﴿And an admonition for the God-fearing﴾: that is, what He admonished in the verses and the example, such as His saying: ﴿And let not pity for them take hold of you﴾ (al-Nur: 2), ﴿Why, when you heard it﴾ (al-Nur: 12), ﴿God admonishes you never to return to the like of it ever﴾ (al-Nur: 17). He specified the God-fearing because they are the ones who benefit from admonition.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 24, verses 32–34 (part 1 of 2):

﴿And marry off the single among you, and the righteous among your male slaves and female slaves. If they are poor, Allah will enrich them from His bounty, and Allah is All-Encompassing, All-Knowing.﴾ ﴿Let those who cannot find a marriage (nikah) keep chaste until Allah enriches them from His bounty. And those of your slaves who seek a deed of manumission, write it for them if you know any good in them, and give them from the wealth of Allah which He has given you. And do not compel your slave girls to prostitution if they desire chastity, seeking the goods of this worldly life. And whoever compels them, then indeed Allah, after their compulsion, is Forgiving and Merciful.﴾ ﴿And We have certainly sent down to you clear verses, and an example from those who passed away before you, and an admonition for the God-fearing.﴾

Originally it applied to a woman who had been married and then lost her husband through a calamity that befell her, so it is one of the afflictions. Then it was said, metaphorically, of a virgin, because she has no spouse," end quote.

(﴿minkum﴾, "from among you") is an address to the believers. He commanded the marrying off of those among the free men and women who are single, and those among the slaves and slave girls who are righteous. The feminine is included in the masculine in His words ﴿and the righteous﴾. ﴿If they are poor, Allah will enrich them from His bounty﴾: this is conditional upon the will mentioned in His words: ﴿And if you fear poverty, Allah will soon enrich you from His bounty, if He wills﴾ [al-Tawbah: 28].

﴿And Allah is All-Encompassing﴾: that is, possessor of wealth and abundance; Allah extends provision to whomever He wills. ("Upon them" refers to) the needs of people, so what has been decreed of provision flows to them.

﴿Let those who cannot find keep chaste﴾: that is, let them strive for chastity and the guarding of the self. The form is istaf'ala, meaning seeking chastity from one's self and compelling it to that. The unassimilated form (fakk) came according to the dialect of the Hijaz, and no one is known to have read (li-yasta'iffa) with idgham (assimilation of the doubled consonant).

﴿Who do not find marriage (nikah)﴾: it was said that nikah here is the name of what is given as a dowry and spent on marriage, like al-lihaf (blanket) and al-libas (clothing), for what one is covered with and wears. The following supports this: ﴿until Allah enriches them from His bounty﴾. So the one commanded to keep chaste is the one who lacks the wealth with which he marries and manages the affairs of marriage. The apparent meaning is that this is a command of recommendation, because of His earlier words: ﴿If they are poor, Allah will enrich them from His bounty﴾.

The meaning of ﴿do not find marriage﴾ is: they are not able to reach it. The sense is that He commanded keeping chaste to everyone for whom marriage is impossible and who cannot find it by any means of impossibility. Then the most prevalent obstacle to marriage is lack of wealth. ﴿Until He enriches them﴾ is a postponement for those who keep chaste and an advance promise of His bounty toward them, so the meaning is that waiting for that and hoping for it is a kindness to their chastity and a strengthening of their hearts. How excellently these commands are ordered: He first commanded what protects from temptation and keeps away from committing sin, which is lowering the gaze; then marriage, by which religion is guarded and by which self-sufficiency through the lawful is achieved over the unlawful; then restraining the self that commands evil and turning it away from aspiring to desire when unable to marry, until it is granted the ability to do so. End quote. This is from al-Zamakhshari's speech, and it is good. When He motivated the master to marry off the righteous among the male and female slaves, He encouraged them to grant them manumission contracts if they request that, so that they would become free and manage their own affairs.

﴿And those who seek the deed (al-kitab)﴾: that is, the contract of manumission (mukatabah), like al-'itab and al-mu'atabah (reproach and reconciliation).

﴿Of what your right hands possess﴾ includes male and female slaves. The ﴿alladhina﴾ ("those who") may be a subject (mubtada') whose predicate is the clause, and the fa' entered the predicate because the relative pronoun contains the meaning of a conditional particle. It may also be in the accusative case, as when you say: "Zayd, so strike him," because you may say "Zayd, strike," and "Zayd, strike him." When the fa' enters, the implied meaning is "strike Zayd" with the intention of ("fa-idrib"), so the fa' is in response to an omitted command. This is clarified in grammar at greater length than this. [p. 452]

The apparent meaning is that mukatabah is obligatory, because of His words: ﴿so write it for them﴾. This is the view of 'Ata', 'Amr ibn Dinar, al-Dahhak, Ibn Sirin, Dawud, and the apparent view of 'Umar, because when Sirin asked Anas for a contract and Anas hesitated, he said to him: "Either I will write it for you or I will strike you with the whip (durra)." Malik and a group went to the view that it is a command of recommendation, and its wording is: "I have made a contract with you for such and such," specifying what he contracted for. The apparent meaning of the command requires that no staggered payment (tanjim) or immediate due date (hulul) be stipulated; rather it may be immediate, deferred, staggered, or unstaggered. This is the view of Abu Hanifa.

Al-Shafi'i said: it is not permitted for fewer than three installments. Most scholars said: it is permitted for one installment. "The good" (al-khayr) means wealth, said by Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, 'Ata', and al-Dahhak; or the skill that entails earning, said by Ibn 'Abbas also; or religion, said by al-Hasan; or establishing prayer, said by 'Ubaydah al-Salmani; or truthfulness, trustworthiness and honesty, said by al-Hasan and Ibrahim; or the intention of good in the contract, said by Sa'id ibn Jubayr. Al-Shafi'i said: trustworthiness and capacity for earning. What appears from usage is that it is religion: one says "so-and-so has good in him," and nothing comes to mind except righteousness. The command to write the contract is restricted by this condition, so if one does not know any good in him, writing the contract is not required by His words ﴿so write it for them﴾.

Regarding ﴿and give them﴾, the apparent meaning is that it is a command to the contract-makers (al-mukatibin), and so the exegetes and the majority of scholars said, and they differed over whether it is obligatory or recommended. Ibn Mas'ud and al-Hasan considered it proper that it be one-third of the contract, 'Ali one-quarter, and Qatadah one-tenth. 'Umar said: from the first of its installments, as a hastening toward good. Malik said: from the last installment. Buraydah, al-Hasan, al-Nakha'i, 'Ikrimah, al-Kalbi, and the two Muqatils said: He commanded all people to assist and support the mukatab. Zayd ibn Aslam said: the address is to the rulers of affairs, that they give the mukatabs their due from the zakat funds, and this is what His words contain: ﴿and for the slaves﴾ [al-Tawbah: 60].

When He said ﴿and give them﴾, it indicates that it is from zakat, since it is a handing over and giving; and this is confirmed by it being a command to give, and whatever is called giving is in the category of charity. His words ﴿from the wealth of Allah which He has given you﴾ refer to what the owner's ownership is established in, and He commanded the removal of part of it. The mukatab's debt is not a valid debt, because it is owed by his slave, and a master cannot establish a valid debt against his own slave. Also, what Allah has given is what comes into his hand and he owns, and what is dropped immediately after the contract does not become his ownership, so it does not deserve the description 'from the wealth of Allah which He has given him.'"

﴿And do not compel your slave girls to prostitution﴾: In Sahih Muslim, on the authority of Jabir: "A slave girl belonging to 'Abd Allah ibn Ubayy, called Musaykah, and another called Umaymah, he used to compel them to fornication, so they complained of that to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)" — and it was revealed. It was also said: "He had six: Mu'adhah, Musaykah, Umaymah, 'Amrah, Arwa, and Qutaylah. One of them came to him one day with a dinar and another with a cloak, and he said to them: 'Go back and commit fornication.' They said: 'By Allah, we will not do that, for Allah has brought us Islam and forbidden fornication.' So they went to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and complained," and it was revealed. The slave girl is one who is owned. This is an address to all, and it confirms that ﴿and give them﴾ is an address to all. The prohibition against compelling fornication is conditional upon their desire for chastity, because compulsion is only possible when they desire chastity; if they desire fornication, compulsion is not conceivable. The word ﴿in (in)﴾ and its preference over ﴿idha (when)﴾ is an indication that the prostitutes did this with their own desire and willingness, and that what occurred from Mu'adhah and Musaykah is a rare anomaly. This view was not clear to many exegetes. Some said: ﴿in aradna (if they desire)﴾ refers back to His words ﴿And marry off the single among you﴾. This has a great distance and separation, and also al-ayama includes males and females, so if this meaning were intended the structure would have been: "in aradu tahassunan" (if they desire chastity), with the masculine taking precedence over the feminine. Some said: this conditional is void (mulgha). Al-Karmani said: this is a condition in appearance but not a real condition, like His words ﴿if you know any good in them﴾, and although the contract is valid even if one does not know any good in him.

Ibn 'Isa said: it came in the form of a conditional to make the compulsion to that abhorrent, and he said: because it was revealed on a specific occasion, so the prohibition fell on that attribute, end quote. ﴿The goods of the worldly life﴾ refers to what they earn through fornication. His words ﴿then indeed Allah﴾ are the response of the conditional. The correct view is that the estimated completion is ﴿Forgiving, Merciful﴾ toward them, so that the response of the conditional contains a pronoun referring back to ﴿those who (alladhina)﴾, which is the conditional particle, and that this is conditional upon repentance. Because al-Zamakhshari, Ibn 'Atiyyah, and Abu al-Baqa' overlooked this ruling, they estimated ﴿then indeed Allah﴾ ﴿Forgiving, Merciful﴾ toward them, meaning toward the compelled women, so the response clause lacked a pronoun referring back to the conditional particle. Abu 'Abd Allah al-Razi weakened what we have said, and he said: "There are two aspects: the first is that indeed Allah is Forgiving and Merciful toward them, because compulsion removes sin and punishment from the one compelled regarding what he did; the second is that indeed Allah is Forgiving and Merciful toward the one compelled, on condition of repentance. This is weak, because on the first explanation there is no need for this implied pronoun, while on the second it is needed," end quote. Their speech is the speech of one who has not examined the language of the Arabs deeply.

(If you say): "His words ﴿their compulsion﴾ are a verbal noun (masdar, the noun of action) that has been put in construct with its object, and the agent together with the verbal noun is omitted. What is omitted is treated as if it were pronounced, so the meaning is 'after their compelling them,' and the connecting element (al-rabt, the pronoun or noun linking the clause back to its subject) is achieved through this omitted, implied agent. So let the issue be permitted." (I say): They did not count the omitted agent among the connecting elements. You say: "Hind, I am amazed at her striking Zayd," and the construction is permitted. But if you say, "Hind, I am amazed at a striking of Zayd," it is not permitted. When al-Zamakhshari, in one of his interpretations of ﴿for them﴾, raised an objection, he said: (If you say): there is no need to make the forgiveness dependent on them, because a woman compelled to fornication is different from a man compelled to it, in that she is not sinful. (I say): Perhaps the compulsion was less than what the Shariah takes into account, namely compulsion by killing, or by something that threatens destruction or the loss of a limb, such as severe beating or otherwise, so that she is free from sin. Perhaps she fell short of the limit at which she is excused, and so she would be sinful. End of quotation. This objection and answer are both built on the assumption that ﴿for them﴾ is the reading.

The two Harameen (the Meccan and Medinan readers), Abu 'Amr, and Abu Bakr read ﴿mubayyanat﴾ with a fatha on the ya', meaning: God has made clear and explained in this surah verses that contain rulings, limits and obligations, so those verses are the ones that are made clear. It is also possible that the meaning is that they are making clear within themselves, and then it was extended so that the one making clear is in reality other than them. The word is an adverbial complement (zarf) of the one making clear. The rest of the Seven, al-Hasan, Talha, and al-A'mash read it with a kasra on the ya'. Then either it is transitive, meaning ﴿mubayyinat﴾ makes clear other rulings and limits, and that action is attributed to the verses metaphorically; or it is intransitive, meaning they are clear in themselves, needing no one to clarify them, but are evident. This is based on the proverb: "The morning has made itself clear to one who has two eyes," meaning it has appeared and become plain.

His words ﴿and an example﴾ are conjoined to ﴿verses﴾. It is possible that the meaning is ﴿and an example﴾ from the examples of those before you, that is, a remarkable story from their stories, like the story of Joseph and Mary in their innocence, for the innocence of the one against whom the slander was spoken, so that they might look at God's power in His creation and His making in it, and thus take warning. Al-Dahhak said: the meaning of the example is what is in the Torah and the Gospel concerning establishing the limits, so He sent down in the Qur'an the like of it. Muqatil said: that is, a likeness of their state in denying the messengers, that is, We have made clear to you what punishment We inflicted upon them because of their rebellion, and We made that an example for you so that you would know that if you share with them in disobedience, you will be like them in deserving punishment.

﴿And an admonition for the God-fearing﴾: that is, what He admonished in the verses and the example, such as His saying: ﴿And let not pity for them take hold of you﴾ (al-Nur: 2), ﴿Why, when you heard it﴾ (al-Nur: 12), ﴿God admonishes you never to return to the like of it ever﴾ (al-Nur: 17). He specified the God-fearing because they are the ones who benefit from admonition.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 24, verses 32–34 (part 1 of 2):

﴿And marry off the single among you, and the righteous among your male slaves and female slaves. If they are poor, Allah will enrich them from His bounty, and Allah is All-Encompassing, All-Knowing.﴾ ﴿Let those who cannot find a marriage (nikah) keep chaste until Allah enriches them from His bounty. And those of your slaves who seek a deed of manumission, write it for them if you know any good in them, and give them from the wealth of Allah which He has given you. And do not compel your slave girls to prostitution if they desire chastity, seeking the goods of this worldly life. And whoever compels them, then indeed Allah, after their compulsion, is Forgiving and Merciful.﴾ ﴿And We have certainly sent down to you clear verses, and an example from those who passed away before you, and an admonition for the God-fearing.﴾

When commands and prohibitions preceded, regarding lowering the gaze, guarding the private parts, concealing adornment, and other matters, and what usually drives men toward women and women toward men is not marrying, because the burdens of marriage and what is owed by each of the two spouses occupy one, Allah the Exalted commanded the marrying off of the single (al-ayama), who are those of both categories who have no spouses, so that each of them is occupied with what is incumbent upon him and does not turn to anyone else. The apparent meaning of the command in His words ﴿And marry off﴾ is obligation (wujub), and this is the view of the Zahiriyya (the literalist school), but most scholars hold that it here denotes recommendation (nadb). No era has been free of the existence of ﴿al-ayama﴾ [p. 451] and no one has objected to this, nor have guardians been commanded to arrange marriages.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "﴿al-ayama﴾ and al-yatama (orphans): their origin is aya'im and yata'im, then they were transposed," end quote. In al-Tahrir, Abu 'Umar said: "Ayama is the transposed form of aya'im, and other grammarians mentioned that ayyim (a single person) and yatim (orphan) were pluralized as ayama and yatama anomalously (shudhudh), which is to be memorized, and its pattern is fa'ala, and this is the apparent meaning of Sibawayh's speech." Sibawayh said at the end of this chapter: "This is the chapter of breaking (taksir) what is among the adjectives." And they said: "wajj and wajya, just as they said zamin and zamna," so they treated it according to meaning, just as they said yatim and yatama, and ayyim and ayama, and they treated it in the manner of raja'a, end quote. Earlier, in al-Mufradat, it was said that al-ayyim is one who has no spouse, male or female. In Abu Bakr al-Khaffaf's commentary on Sibawayh's book: "The ayyim is the one who has no spouse. Originally it applied to a woman who had been married and then lost her husband through a calamity that befell her, so it is one of the afflictions. Then it was said, metaphorically, of a virgin, because she has no spouse," end quote.

(﴿minkum﴾, "from among you") is an address to the believers. He commanded the marrying off of those among the free men and women who are single, and those among the slaves and slave girls who are righteous. The feminine is included in the masculine in His words ﴿and the righteous﴾. He specified the righteous so that their religion would be protected and their righteousness preserved for them, and because the righteous among the slaves are those whom their masters are compassionate toward and treat in the manner of children in favor and affection, so they are likely to receive attention regarding their affairs and acceptance of advice concerning them, whereas the corrupt among them are in the opposite condition with their masters. It was said: the meaning of ﴿and the righteous﴾ is: fit for marriage and capable of fulfilling its rights. Mujahid and al-Hasan read ﴿min 'ibadikum﴾ with a yaʼ in place of the alif and a fatha on the ʻayn, and its most common usage is for slaves (mamalik).

﴿If they are poor, Allah will enrich them from His bounty﴾: this is conditional upon the will mentioned in His words: ﴿And if you fear poverty, Allah will soon enrich you from His bounty, if He wills﴾ [al-Tawbah: 28].

﴿And Allah is All-Encompassing﴾: that is, possessor of wealth and abundance; Allah extends provision to whomever He wills. ("Upon them" refers to) the needs of people, so what has been decreed of provision flows to them.

﴿Let those who cannot find keep chaste﴾: that is, let them strive for chastity and the guarding of the self. The form is istaf'ala, meaning seeking chastity from one's self and compelling it to that. The unassimilated form (fakk) came according to the dialect of the Hijaz, and no one is known to have read (li-yasta'iffa) with idgham (assimilation of the doubled consonant).

﴿Who do not find marriage (nikah)﴾: it was said that nikah here is the name of what is given as a dowry and spent on marriage, like al-lihaf (blanket) and al-libas (clothing), for what one is covered with and wears. The following supports this: ﴿until Allah enriches them from His bounty﴾. So the one commanded to keep chaste is the one who lacks the wealth with which he marries and manages the affairs of marriage. The apparent meaning is that this is a command of recommendation, because of His earlier words: ﴿If they are poor, Allah will enrich them from His bounty﴾.

The meaning of ﴿do not find marriage﴾ is: they are not able to reach it. The sense is that He commanded keeping chaste to everyone for whom marriage is impossible and who cannot find it by any means of impossibility. Then the most prevalent obstacle to marriage is lack of wealth. ﴿Until He enriches them﴾ is a postponement for those who keep chaste and an advance promise of His bounty toward them, so the meaning is that waiting for that and hoping for it is a kindness to their chastity and a strengthening of their hearts. How excellently these commands are ordered: He first commanded what protects from temptation and keeps away from committing sin, which is lowering the gaze; then marriage, by which religion is guarded and by which self-sufficiency through the lawful is achieved over the unlawful; then restraining the self that commands evil and turning it away from aspiring to desire when unable to marry, until it is granted the ability to do so. End quote. This is from al-Zamakhshari's speech, and it is good. When He motivated the master to marry off the righteous among the male and female slaves, He encouraged them to grant them manumission contracts if they request that, so that they would become free and manage their own affairs.

﴿And those who seek the deed (al-kitab)﴾: that is, the contract of manumission (mukatabah), like al-'itab and al-mu'atabah (reproach and reconciliation).

﴿Of what your right hands possess﴾ includes male and female slaves. The ﴿alladhina﴾ ("those who") may be a subject (mubtada') whose predicate is the clause, and the fa' entered the predicate because the relative pronoun contains the meaning of a conditional particle. It may also be in the accusative case, as when you say: "Zayd, so strike him," because you may say "Zayd, strike," and "Zayd, strike him." When the fa' enters, the implied meaning is "strike Zayd" with the intention of ("fa-idrib"), so the fa' is in response to an omitted command. This is clarified in grammar at greater length than this. Al-Azhari said: "This contract was named mukatabah because a document (kitab) is written for the slave against the master concerning manumission when he pays what they agreed upon in wealth, and a document is written for the master against the slave concerning the installments (nujum) which he pays." [p. 452]

The apparent meaning is that mukatabah is obligatory, because of His words: ﴿so write it for them﴾. This is the view of 'Ata', 'Amr ibn Dinar, al-Dahhak, Ibn Sirin, Dawud, and the apparent view of 'Umar, because when Sirin asked Anas for a contract and Anas hesitated, he said to him: "Either I will write it for you or I will strike you with the whip (durra)." Malik and a group went to the view that it is a command of recommendation, and its wording is: "I have made a contract with you for such and such," specifying what he contracted for. The apparent meaning of the command requires that no staggered payment (tanjim) or immediate due date (hulul) be stipulated; rather it may be immediate, deferred, staggered, or unstaggered. This is the view of Abu Hanifa.

Al-Shafi'i said: it is not permitted for fewer than three installments. Most scholars said: it is permitted for one installment. Ibn Khuwayz Mandad said: if one contracts for a prompt payment, it is manumission for a sum and not a mukatabah. Some Malikis permitted immediate mukatabah and called it qita'ah.

"The good" (al-khayr) means wealth, said by Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, 'Ata', and al-Dahhak; or the skill that entails earning, said by Ibn 'Abbas also; or religion, said by al-Hasan; or establishing prayer, said by 'Ubaydah al-Salmani; or truthfulness, trustworthiness and honesty, said by al-Hasan and Ibrahim; or the intention of good in the contract, said by Sa'id ibn Jubayr. Al-Shafi'i said: trustworthiness and capacity for earning. What appears from usage is that it is religion: one says "so-and-so has good in him," and nothing comes to mind except righteousness. The command to write the contract is restricted by this condition, so if one does not know any good in him, writing the contract is not required by His words ﴿so write it for them﴾.

Regarding ﴿and give them﴾, the apparent meaning is that it is a command to the contract-makers (al-mukatibin), and so the exegetes and the majority of scholars said, and they differed over whether it is obligatory or recommended. Ibn Mas'ud and al-Hasan considered it proper that it be one-third of the contract, 'Ali one-quarter, and Qatadah one-tenth. 'Umar said: from the first of its installments, as a hastening toward good. Malik said: from the last installment. Buraydah, al-Hasan, al-Nakha'i, 'Ikrimah, al-Kalbi, and the two Muqatils said: He commanded all people to assist and support the mukatab. Zayd ibn Aslam said: the address is to the rulers of affairs, that they give the mukatabs their due from the zakat funds, and this is what His words contain: ﴿and for the slaves﴾ [al-Tawbah: 60].

The author of al-Nazm said: "If the intended meaning of giving were remission (hatt), then the Arabic expression would have had to be: 'Put it down from them' (da'uhu 'anhum) or 'Offset it against them' (qassuhum). When He said ﴿and give them﴾, it indicates that it is from zakat, since it is a handing over and giving; and this is confirmed by it being a command to give, and whatever is called giving is in the category of charity. His words ﴿from the wealth of Allah which He has given you﴾ refer to what the owner's ownership is established in, and He commanded the removal of part of it. The mukatab's debt is not a valid debt, because it is owed by his slave, and a master cannot establish a valid debt against his own slave. Also, what Allah has given is what comes into his hand and he owns, and what is dropped immediately after the contract does not become his ownership, so it does not deserve the description 'from the wealth of Allah which He has given him.'"

﴿And do not compel your slave girls to prostitution﴾: In Sahih Muslim, on the authority of Jabir: "A slave girl belonging to 'Abd Allah ibn Ubayy, called Musaykah, and another called Umaymah, he used to compel them to fornication, so they complained of that to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)" — and it was revealed. It was also said: "He had six: Mu'adhah, Musaykah, Umaymah, 'Amrah, Arwa, and Qutaylah. One of them came to him one day with a dinar and another with a cloak, and he said to them: 'Go back and commit fornication.' They said: 'By Allah, we will not do that, for Allah has brought us Islam and forbidden fornication.' So they went to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and complained," and it was revealed. The slave girl is one who is owned. This is an address to all, and it confirms that ﴿and give them﴾ is an address to all. The prohibition against compelling fornication is conditional upon their desire for chastity, because compulsion is only possible when they desire chastity; if they desire fornication, compulsion is not conceivable. The word ﴿in (in)﴾ and its preference over ﴿idha (when)﴾ is an indication that the prostitutes did this with their own desire and willingness, and that what occurred from Mu'adhah and Musaykah is a rare anomaly. This view was not clear to many exegetes. Some said: ﴿in aradna (if they desire)﴾ refers back to His words ﴿And marry off the single among you﴾. This has a great distance and separation, and also al-ayama includes males and females, so if this meaning were intended the structure would have been: "in aradu tahassunan" (if they desire chastity), with the masculine taking precedence over the feminine. Some said: this conditional is void (mulgha). Al-Karmani said: this is a condition in appearance but not a real condition, like His words ﴿if you know any good in them﴾, and although the contract is valid even if one does not know any good in him.

Ibn 'Isa said: it came in the form of a conditional to make the compulsion to that abhorrent, and he said: because it was revealed on a specific occasion, so the prohibition fell on that attribute, end quote. ﴿The goods of the worldly life﴾ refers to what they earn through fornication. His words ﴿then indeed Allah﴾ are the response of the conditional. The correct view is that the estimated completion is ﴿Forgiving, Merciful﴾ toward them, so that the response of the conditional contains a pronoun referring back to ﴿those who (alladhina)﴾, which is the conditional particle, and that this is conditional upon repentance. Because al-Zamakhshari, Ibn 'Atiyyah, and Abu al-Baqa' overlooked this ruling, they estimated ﴿then indeed Allah﴾ ﴿Forgiving, Merciful﴾ toward them, meaning toward the compelled women, so the response clause lacked a pronoun referring back to the conditional particle. Abu 'Abd Allah al-Razi weakened what we have said, and he said: "There are two aspects: the first is that indeed Allah is Forgiving and Merciful toward them, because compulsion removes sin and punishment from the one compelled regarding what he did; the second is that indeed Allah is Forgiving and Merciful toward the one compelled, on condition of repentance. This is weak, because on the first explanation there is no need for this implied pronoun, while on the second it is needed," end quote. Their speech is the speech of one who has not examined the language of the Arabs deeply.

(If you say): "His words ﴿their compulsion﴾ are a verbal noun (masdar, the noun of action) that has been put in construct with its object, and the agent together with the verbal noun is omitted. What is omitted is treated as if it were pronounced, so the meaning is 'after their compelling them,' and the connecting element (al-rabt, the pronoun or noun linking the clause back to its subject) is achieved through this omitted, implied agent. So let the issue be permitted." (I say): They did not count the omitted agent among the connecting elements. You say: "Hind, I am amazed at her striking Zayd," and the construction is permitted. But if you say, "Hind, I am amazed at a striking of Zayd," it is not permitted. When al-Zamakhshari, in one of his interpretations of ﴿for them﴾, raised an objection, he said: (If you say): there is no need to make the forgiveness dependent on them, because a woman compelled to fornication is different from a man compelled to it, in that she is not sinful. (I say): Perhaps the compulsion was less than what the Shariah takes into account, namely compulsion by killing, or by something that threatens destruction or the loss of a limb, such as severe beating or otherwise, so that she is free from sin. Perhaps she fell short of the limit at which she is excused, and so she would be sinful. End of quotation. This objection and answer are both built on the assumption that ﴿for them﴾ is the reading.

The two Harameen (the Meccan and Medinan readers), Abu 'Amr, and Abu Bakr read ﴿mubayyanat﴾ with a fatha on the ya', meaning: God has made clear and explained in this surah verses that contain rulings, limits and obligations, so those verses are the ones that are made clear. It is also possible that the meaning is that they are making clear within themselves, and then it was extended so that the one making clear is in reality other than them. The word is an adverbial complement (zarf) of the one making clear. The rest of the Seven, al-Hasan, Talha, and al-A'mash read it with a kasra on the ya'. Then either it is transitive, meaning ﴿mubayyinat﴾ makes clear other rulings and limits, and that action is attributed to the verses metaphorically; or it is intransitive, meaning they are clear in themselves, needing no one to clarify them, but are evident. This is based on the proverb: "The morning has made itself clear to one who has two eyes," meaning it has appeared and become plain.

His words ﴿and an example﴾ are conjoined to ﴿verses﴾. It is possible that the meaning is ﴿and an example﴾ from the examples of those before you, that is, a remarkable story from their stories, like the story of Joseph and Mary in their innocence, for the innocence of the one against whom the slander was spoken, so that they might look at God's power in His creation and His making in it, and thus take warning. Al-Dahhak said: the meaning of the example is what is in the Torah and the Gospel concerning establishing the limits, so He sent down in the Qur'an the like of it. Muqatil said: that is, a likeness of their state in denying the messengers, that is, We have made clear to you what punishment We inflicted upon them because of their rebellion, and We made that an example for you so that you would know that if you share with them in disobedience, you will be like them in deserving punishment.

﴿And an admonition for the God-fearing﴾: that is, what He admonished in the verses and the example, such as His saying: ﴿And let not pity for them take hold of you﴾ (al-Nur: 2), ﴿Why, when you heard it﴾ (al-Nur: 12), ﴿God admonishes you never to return to the like of it ever﴾ (al-Nur: 17). He specified the God-fearing because they are the ones who benefit from admonition.

(p. 454) ﴿Allah is the Light of the heavens and the earth. The likeness of His light is like a niche in which is a lamp, the lamp is in a glass, the glass is as if it were a brilliant star, lit from a blessed olive tree, neither of the east nor of the west, whose oil would almost glow even if no fire touched it. Light upon light. Allah guides to His light whom He wills. And Allah sets forth parables for mankind, and Allah is Knowing of all things.﴾ ﴿In houses which Allah has permitted to be raised and His name mentioned therein; glorifying Him therein morning and evening.﴾ ﴿Men whom neither trade nor sale distracts from the remembrance of Allah, the establishment of prayer, and the giving of zakah. They fear a Day when hearts and eyes will be turned about.﴾ ﴿That Allah may reward them with the best of what they did and increase them from His bounty. And Allah provides for whom He wills without account.﴾

In the language of the Arabs, *al-nur* (light) is the illumination perceived by the eye. Its attribution to Allah the Exalted is therefore a figurative usage (*majaz*), just as you say "Zayd is generosity and bounty." This attribution may be understood in two ways. The first is that the word carries the meaning of an active participle (*ism al-fa'il*), i.e. "the Illuminator of the heavens and the earth." This interpretation is supported by the reading of ʿAli ibn Abi Talib, Abu Jaʿfar, ʿAbd al-ʿAziz al-Makki, Zayd ibn ʿAli, Thabit ibn Abi Hafsa, al-Qawrasi, Maslama ibn ʿAbd al-Malik, Abu ʿAbd al-Rahman al-Sulami, and ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿAyyash ibn Abi Rabiʿa, who read *nawwara* as a past-tense verb, with *al-ard* (the earth) in the accusative. The second is that it is elliptical, meaning "Possessor of light," and this is supported by His words ﴿the likeness of His light﴾. It is also possible that He is described as light by way of praise, as they say: "So-and-so is the sun of the lands, the light and moon of the tribes." This is widespread in Arabic speech and poetry. A poet said:

*You are as if you were the sun, and the kings are stars.*

And he said:

*The moon of the tribes is Khalid ibn Yazid.*

And he said:

*When ʿAbd Allah travels from Marw for a night, its full moon and its beauty have departed with him.*

It is also narrated as "its light." The light is attributed to "the heavens and the earth" to indicate the breadth of its radiance and the pervasiveness of its illumination, so that the heavens and the earth are lit by it. Or it may mean the inhabitants of the heavens and the earth, who are illuminated by it. Ibn ʿAbbas said: ﴿the light of the heavens﴾ means the guide of the people of the heavens. Mujahid said: the one who manages the affairs of the heavens. al-Hasan said: the one who illuminates the heavens. Ubayy said: Allah is by Him the light of the heavens, or from Him is the light of the heavens, meaning their brightness. Abu al-ʿAliya said: the One who adorns the heavens with the sun, moon and stars, and adorns the earth with the prophets and scholars. It has also been said: the One who is free of every defect, like the woman Nawwar, who was innocent of suspicion and immorality. al-Karmani said: He is the One by whom one sees and is seen, a figurative description applied to Allah, because He sees and is seen through His creatures by causing them to exist and bringing them into being.

The apparent meaning is that the pronoun in ﴿the likeness of His light﴾ refers to Allah the Exalted. The scholars differed over this statement: what is meant by the light attributed to Him? It was said: the clear signs in His words ﴿Certainly We have sent down to you clear signs﴾ [al-Nur: 34]. It was said: faith cast into the hearts of believers. It was said: the light here is the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). It was said: the light here is the believer. Kaʿb and Ibn Jubayr said: the pronoun in *nurihi* (His light) refers to Muhammad (ﷺ), meaning the likeness of the light of Muhammad. Ubayy said: it refers to the believers, and in his reading it is "the likeness of the light of the believer."
