As for reward, it has good deeds for those who have it, because it is according to what is deserved. He finished. In his saying "according to what is deserved" there is a Muʿtazilite insinuation.

(p. 454) ﴿Allah is the Light of the heavens and the earth. The likeness of His light is like a niche in which is a lamp, the lamp is in a glass, the glass is as if it were a brilliant star, lit from a blessed olive tree, neither of the east nor of the west, whose oil would almost glow even if no fire touched it. Light upon light. Allah guides to His light whom He wills. And Allah sets forth parables for mankind, and Allah is Knowing of all things.﴾ ﴿In houses which Allah has permitted to be raised and His name mentioned therein; glorifying Him therein morning and evening.﴾ ﴿Men whom neither trade nor sale distracts from the remembrance of Allah, the establishment of prayer, and the giving of zakah. They fear a Day when hearts and eyes will be turned about.﴾ ﴿That Allah may reward them with the best of what they did and increase them from His bounty. And Allah provides for whom He wills without account.﴾

In the language of the Arabs, *al-nur* (light) is the illumination perceived by the eye. Its attribution to Allah the Exalted is therefore a figurative usage (*majaz*), just as you say "Zayd is generosity and bounty." This attribution may be understood in two ways. The first is that the word carries the meaning of an active participle (*ism al-fa'il*), i.e. "the Illuminator of the heavens and the earth." This interpretation is supported by the reading of ʿAli ibn Abi Talib, Abu Jaʿfar, ʿAbd al-ʿAziz al-Makki, Zayd ibn ʿAli, Thabit ibn Abi Hafsa, al-Qawrasi, Maslama ibn ʿAbd al-Malik, Abu ʿAbd al-Rahman al-Sulami, and ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿAyyash ibn Abi Rabiʿa, who read *nawwara* as a past-tense verb, with *al-ard* (the earth) in the accusative. The second is that it is elliptical, meaning "Possessor of light," and this is supported by His words ﴿the likeness of His light﴾. It is also possible that He is described as light by way of praise, as they say: "So-and-so is the sun of the lands, the light and moon of the tribes." This is widespread in Arabic speech and poetry. A poet said:

*You are as if you were the sun, and the kings are stars.*

And he said:

*The moon of the tribes is Khalid ibn Yazid.*

And he said:

*When ʿAbd Allah travels from Marw for a night, its full moon and its beauty have departed with him.*

It is also narrated as "its light." The light is attributed to "the heavens and the earth" to indicate the breadth of its radiance and the pervasiveness of its illumination, so that the heavens and the earth are lit by it. Or it may mean the inhabitants of the heavens and the earth, who are illuminated by it. Ibn ʿAbbas said: ﴿the light of the heavens﴾ means the guide of the people of the heavens. Mujahid said: the one who manages the affairs of the heavens. al-Hasan said: the one who illuminates the heavens. Ubayy said: Allah is by Him the light of the heavens, or from Him is the light of the heavens, meaning their brightness. Abu al-ʿAliya said: the One who adorns the heavens with the sun, moon and stars, and adorns the earth with the prophets and scholars. It has also been said: the One who is free of every defect, like the woman Nawwar, who was innocent of suspicion and immorality. al-Karmani said: He is the One by whom one sees and is seen, a figurative description applied to Allah, because He sees and is seen through His creatures by causing them to exist and bringing them into being.

The apparent meaning is that the pronoun in ﴿the likeness of His light﴾ refers to Allah the Exalted. The scholars differed over this statement: what is meant by the light attributed to Him? It was said: the clear signs in His words ﴿Certainly We have sent down to you clear signs﴾ [al-Nur: 34]. It was said: faith cast into the hearts of believers. It was said: the light here is the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). It was said: the light here is the believer. Kaʿb and Ibn Jubayr said: the pronoun in *nurihi* (His light) refers to Muhammad (ﷺ), meaning the likeness of the light of Muhammad. Ubayy said: it refers to the believers, and in his reading it is "the likeness of the light of the believer." It is also narrated that it reads "the likeness of the light of one who believes in Him." al-Hasan said: it refers to the Qur'an and faith. These three views have the pronoun referring to something not previously mentioned, whereas referring it to Allah the Exalted conveys the intended meaning of the verse. For this reason Makki said: one should pause at *wa-l-ard* (and the earth) in those three views.

The scholars also differed over this comparison: is it a comparison of one whole sentence with another, in which no part is intended to correspond to a part and no thing to a thing, or is it one in which this correspondence is intended? That is: the likeness of the light of Allah, which is His guidance, His perfect craftsmanship of every creature, and His shining proofs in general, is like this whole sentence of light which you yourselves make, in this quality which is the most eloquent description of light among people; i.e. the likeness of Allah's light in clarity is like this which is the limit of your reach, O mankind. It was also said that it is a detailed comparison in which each part corresponds to a part. They formulated it according to those three views: ﴿the likeness of His light﴾ in Muhammad, or in the believer, or in the Qur'an and faith, ﴿as a niche﴾. So the niche is the Messenger or his breast; the ﴿lamp﴾ is prophethood and what is connected with it of his knowledge and guidance; the ﴿glass﴾ is his heart. The ﴿blessed tree﴾ is revelation, and the angels are the messengers of Allah to him. He likened the distinction it provides to oil, which is the proofs, arguments and signs contained in the revelation. According to the view of the believer, the niche is his breast, the lamp is faith and knowledge, the glass is his heart, and the tree is the Qur'an, whose oil is the proofs and wisdom it contains. Ubayy said: so he is in the best condition, walking among people like a living man walking among the graves of the dead. According to the view of faith and the Qur'an, the likeness of faith and the Qur'an in the believer's breast, in his heart, is ﴿as a niche﴾. This view is not a comparison of parts like the first two, because the niche does not correspond to faith.

Al-Zamakhshari said: the description of "His light" is wondrous in its illumination ﴿as a niche﴾, i.e. as the description of a niche, end of quote. It appears to me that His words ﴿as a niche﴾ involve an omitted noun, meaning: ﴿the likeness of His light﴾ is the likeness of the light of a niche. It was mentioned earlier in *al-Mufradat* that the *mishkah* (niche) is the non-penetrating recess in a wall, which is the view of Ibn Jubayr, Saʿid ibn ʿIyad and the majority. Abu Musa said: the *mishkah* is the iron and lead piece in which the wick is set inside the glass. Mujahid said: the *mishkah* is the pillar on whose top the lamp stands, and he also said: the iron rings from which the lamps are hung.

﴿In it is a lamp﴾, i.e. a large lantern. The apparent meaning is that the glass is a container for the lamp, based on His words ﴿the lamp is in a glass﴾. al-Zamakhshari supposed it to be "in Syrian glass," since in his view the purest glass is Syrian, but the verse does not specify this. Abu Rajaʾ and Nasr ibn ʿAsim read *fi zijajatin al-zijajatu* with a kasra on the zay in both words, while Ibn Abi ʿAbla and Nasr ibn ʿAsim in the narration of Ibn Mujahid read them with a fatha. ﴿As if it were﴾, i.e. as if the glass were, because of the purity of its substance and essence, and this is more eloquent in illumination and in what it contains of the lamp's light.

﴿a brilliant star (kawkab durri)﴾. al-Dahhak said: it is Venus (*al-Zuhra*). It likened the glass in its brightness to one of the bright stars among the famous planets, namely Jupiter, Venus, Mars, Canopus and the like. Among the seven readers, Nafiʿ, Ibn ʿAmir, Hafs and Ibn Kathir read *durriyyun* with a damma on the dal and a shadda on the ra and the ya. The apparent meaning is that the star is attributed to *durr* (pearl) because of its whiteness and clarity, though it is possible that its original form had a hamza which was replaced and assimilated. Qatada, Zayd ibn ʿAli and al-Dahhak read it likewise except that they put a fatha on the dal. This is also narrated from Nasr ibn ʿAsim, Abu Rajaʾ and Ibn al-Musayyab. al-Zuhri read it likewise except that he put a kasra on the dal. Hamza read it likewise except that he read it with a hamza, from *al-dar'* (to repel), meaning that some of it repels others, or its light repels its obscurity; its pattern is *fu'ayyil*. It was said: *fu'ayyil* is not found except in the words *murrayq* (for safflower) and *durrī'* in this reading. It was said: also *surriyya*, if it is said to derive from *surur* (joy), where one of the doubled letters was replaced by ya and assimilated into the ya of *fu'ayyil*. The form *murrayk* has also been heard for the thing inside a dry horn, with a damma or kasra on the mim. It was said: from it is *ullayya*. It was said: *durri* originally had the pattern *fu'ul* like *subbuh*; the damma was felt to be heavy so it was reduced to a kasra, and the same was said of *surratihi* and *durratihi*. Abu ʿAmr and al-Kisai read it likewise except that they put a kasra on the dal, which is a common pattern in nouns like *sikkin* (knife), and in adjectives like *sikkir*. Qatada also read it, along with Aban ibn ʿUthman, Ibn al-Musayyab, Abu Rajaʾ, ʿAmr ibn Faʾid, al-Aʿmash and Nasr ibn ʿAsim, likewise, except with a fatha on the dal. Ibn Jinni said: this is rare, and nothing has been preserved of it except *al-sakkina* with a fatha on the sin and a shadda on the kaf, end of quote. Among the patterns, al-Akhfash transmitted *kawkab darri'* (from *daraʾtuhu*) and *darriyya*; and "ʿalayka bi-l-sakina wa-l-waqar" (keep to tranquillity and dignity), from Abu Zayd. al-Farra' transmitted it with a kasra on the sin.

The two Akhawan (Ibn ʿAmir and ʿAsim, via Hafs?) — the readers Hamza, al-Kisai, Abu Bakr, al-Hasan, Zayd ibn ʿAli, Qatada, Ibn Thabbat, Talha, ʿIsa and al-Aʿmash read ﴿is kindled (tūqadu)﴾ with a damma on the ta, meaning ﴿the glass﴾, the present tense of *uqidat*, in the passive voice. Nafiʿ, Ibn ʿAmir and Hafs read it likewise except with a ya, meaning ﴿the lamp﴾. Ibn Kathir and Abu ʿAmr read *tawaqqada* with a fatha on all four letters as a past-tense verb, meaning ﴿the lamp﴾. al-Hasan, al-Sulami, Qatada, Ibn Muhaysin, Salam, Mujahid, Ibn Abi Ishaq, and al-Mufaddal from ʿAsim read it likewise except with a damma on the dal, as the present tense of *tawaqqada*, originally *tatawaqqadu*, meaning ﴿the glass﴾. ʿAbd Allah read *wuqqida* without a ta, with the qaf doubled, as a past-tense passive verb: "the lamp was kindled." al-Sulami, Qatada and Salam likewise read it except with a ya from below. This is also transmitted from al-Hasan and Ibn Muhaysin, and the original is *yatawaqqadu*, meaning ﴿the lamp﴾. The deletion of the ya in *yatawaqqadu* is analogous, since what remains indicates what was deleted. The reading *yuqadu* is very rare, because the remaining ya does not indicate the deleted ta. It has a basis in analogy, namely treating it like *yaʿidu* (he promises), since *yaʿidu*, *taʿidu* and *aʿidu* drop the waw in the same way; and when they deleted one ta from *tatawaqqadu* with its two tas, they deleted the ta together with the ya, even though the combination of ta and ya is not considered heavy.

﴿from a tree﴾, i.e. from the oil of a tree, which is the olive tree.

﴿blessed﴾, abundant in benefits, or because it grows in the land which He blessed for the worlds. It was said: He blessed it for the worlds. It was said: seventy prophets were blessed by it, among them Ibrahim (peace be upon him). The olive is among the greatest trees in fruit, growth, abundant branches and freshness of boughs. Abu Talib said:

*The stranger, the dead, is blessed as the pomegranate's freshness and the olive are blessed.*

﴿neither of the east nor of the west﴾. Ibn Zayd said: it is from the trees of Syria, so it is neither from the eastern part of the earth nor from its western part, since the trees of Syria are the best of trees. Ibn ʿAbbas, ʿIkrima, Qatada and others said: it is in an open place of the earth, which the sun touches all day as it turns over it, so it is not exclusively of the east to be called eastern, nor of the west to be called western. al-Hasan said: this is a parable, and it is not from the trees of this world, for if it were in this world it would be either eastern or western. It is narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas that it is in a place surrounded by something so that it is not exposed either from the east or from the west; but this is not authentic from Ibn ʿAbbas, because if it were in this state its fruit would be spoiled. Ibn ʿAtiyya said: it is in the middle of the trees, where the sun does not touch it at rising or setting, but only in the morning and evening. ʿIkrima said: it is from the trees of Paradise. Ibn ʿUmar said: the tree is a parable, meaning that it is the religion of Ibrahim, which is neither Jewish nor Christian. It was said: it is the religion of Islam, which is neither harsh nor soft. It was said: it is neither exposed to the midday sun nor in constant shade, but the sun and shade alternate over it, which is best for its fruit and purest for its oil.

﴿olive﴾ is an apposition (*badal*) to ﴿tree﴾. Some allowed that it could be an explanatory apposition (*ʿatf bayan*), but this is not permitted according to the Basran school, since explanatory apposition for them occurs only with definite nouns; the Kufans, and al-Farisi after them, permitted it with indefinite nouns. ﴿Neither eastern﴾ (*la*) and ﴿nor western﴾ are, according to the reading of the majority with a kasra, adjectives of ﴿olive﴾. al-Dahhak read it with a damma, meaning: it is neither eastern nor western, and the sentence is in the position of an adjective.

﴿يَكادُ زَيْتُها يُضِيءُ ولَوْ لَمْ تَمْسَسْهُ نارٌ﴾ This is hyperbole about the purity of the oil, and about its brightness and quality: its oil nearly gives light even without fire touching it. The clause ﴿ولَوْ لَمْ تَمْسَسْهُ نارٌ﴾ ("even if no fire touched it") is a circumstantial clause (ḥāliyyah) conjoined to an omitted circumstance. The sense is: ﴿its oil nearly gives light﴾ in every state, even in this state, which would require that it not give light because no fire touches it. It was mentioned earlier that this kind of conjunction (ʿaṭf) comes in a set order for something that should not normally occur, because the ordering is impossible in ordinary usage, and it serves to exhaust all possibilities so that what cannot be imagined to be included is included in what precedes it. An example is: "Give to the beggar even if he comes on a horse; turn away the beggar even with a burnt hoof." The majority of readers recite ﴿تَمْسَسْهُ﴾ with a *tā'*, while Ibn ʿAbbās and al-Ḥasan recite it with a *yā'* below. The separation (faṣl) between the verb and its subject makes the *yā'* reading acceptable, and the feminine gender of "fire" is metaphorical (majāzī), since it is feminine without a feminine marker.

﴿نُورٌ عَلى نُورٍ﴾ means light upon light, multiplied, with the niche (mishkāh), the glass, the lamp and the oil all cooperating on it. Nothing remains that could strengthen the light and increase its brilliance. A lamp in a narrow place gathers its light more completely than in a wide place, where the light spreads out. A lantern is the thing most helpful for increasing light, and so is the oil and its purity. Here the example is complete.

Then He said: ﴿يَهْدِي اللَّهُ لِنُورِهِ مَن يَشاءُ﴾ ("God guides to His light whom He wills"), meaning to His guidance and to faith, whomever He wills to guide and chooses for it. Whoever interprets "light" in ﴿مَثَلُ نُورِهِ﴾ as prophethood supposes that the sense is "God guides to His prophethood." It has also been said: "to reasoning from the signs." Then He mentioned that He strikes examples for people so that they may draw a lesson and reflect in a way that leads to faith. Then He mentioned the comprehensiveness of His knowledge of things, so He places His guidance with whomever He wills.

﴿فِي بُيُوتٍ﴾ ("in houses") is connected to *yūqadu* (is kindled), as al-Rummānī said. Or it is in the position of a qualifier (ṣifah) to ﴿كَمِشْكاةٍ﴾ ("like a niche"), meaning: like a niche in houses, as al-Ḥawfī said, and al-Zamakhsharī followed him, saying: "﴿كَمِشْكاةٍ﴾ is in some of God's houses, which are the mosques." He said: "﴿مَثَلُ نُورِهِ﴾: as you see in the mosque the light of the niche, whose description is such-and-such." His saying "as though" to the end is an explanation of meaning, not a grammatical (iʿrāb) explanation. Or it is in the position of a qualifier to *miṣbāḥ* (lamp), meaning: a lamp ﴿in houses﴾, as some said; or in the position of a qualifier to *zujājah* (glass), as some said. According to these four views, one does not stop at His saying ("Knowing"). It has also been said that ﴿فِي بُيُوتٍ﴾ is a new (resumptive) clause whose governing element is *yusabbiḥu* (glorifies). Abū Ḥātim related this, and al-Zamakhsharī permitted it. He said: its connection to ﴿كَمِشْكاةٍ﴾ has been mentioned, and he said: or it is connected to what follows it, which is *yusabbiḥu*, meaning: men glorify Him in houses, and there is a repetition in it, like your saying "Zayd is in the house sitting in it." Or it is connected to an omitted element, like His saying ﴿فِي تِسْعِ آياتٍ﴾ [An-Naml 27:12], meaning: they glorified Him in houses. According to these three views one stops at His saying ("Knowing"). What I choose is that ﴿فِي بُيُوتٍ﴾ is connected to His saying *yusabbiḥu* (glorifies). The link of this to what precedes it is that, when He mentioned that He guides whom He wills to His light, He mentioned the state of those who were granted guidance to that light, namely the believers. Then He mentioned the most noble of their inward worship, which is their declaring God free of deficiencies, and manifesting that by pronouncing it in the mosques of congregation. Then He mentioned the rest of their attributes: committing to the remembrance of God, establishing prayer, paying zakat, and their fear of what will happen at the Resurrection. For this reason the opposite of the believers, the unbelievers, comes in His saying "and those who disbelieved." It seems that when guidance to the light was mentioned, the division came concerning the one who accepts guidance and the one who does not, so it began with the believer and what he was affected by of the kinds of guidance, then it mentioned the unbeliever. The apparent meaning is that His saying ﴿فِي بُيُوتٍ﴾ is intended in its plural meaning.

Al-Ḥasan said: what is intended is the House of the Holy Place (Bayt al-Maqdis, Jerusalem), and it was called "houses" because within it there are places that are separated from one another. It is related that the custom of the Children of Israel in its lighting was in the utmost care, and the oil was sealed on its vessels, and it was made and consecrated so that the lighting would not be done with anything else, so it was the brightest of the houses on earth. The apparent meaning is that ﴿فِي بُيُوتٍ﴾ is unrestricted, so it applies to the mosques and to the houses in which prayer and knowledge take place. Mujāhid said: the houses of the Messenger (ﷺ). Ibn ʿAbbās, al-Ḥasan also, and Mujāhid said: they are the mosques which customarily are illuminated with that kind of lamp. It has been said: the Kaʿbah, the House of the Holy Place, the Mosque of the Messenger (peace and blessings be upon him), and the Mosque of Quba. It has been said: the houses of the prophets. What strengthens that they are mosques is His saying ﴿يُسَبِّحُ لَهُ فِيها بِالغُدُوِّ والآصالِ﴾ ("He is glorified in them morning and evening") and His permission and command that they be ﴿raised﴾, meaning that their status be magnified, as al-Ḥasan and al-Ḍaḥḥāk said. Ibn ʿAbbās and Mujāhid said: they are built and elevated, from His saying ﴿وإذْ يَرْفَعُ إبْراهِيمُ القَواعِدَ مِنَ البَيْتِ وإسْماعِيلُ﴾ [Al-Baqarah 2:127] ("when Abraham and Ishmael raised the foundations of the House"). It has been said: ﴿raised﴾ means purified from impurities and sins. It has been said: ﴿raised﴾ means that needs are raised in them to God. It has been said: ﴿raised﴾ means that voices are raised with the remembrance of God and the recitation of the Qur'an.

﴿ويُذْكَرَ فِيها اسْمُهُ﴾ ("and His name is mentioned in them"): its apparent meaning is unrestricted mention, so it includes every kind of remembrance by way of general substitution. From Ibn ʿAbbās: His oneness, which is "there is no god but God." From him also: His Book is recited in them. It has been said: His beautiful names. It has been said: prayer is performed in them. The majority recite *yusabbiḥu* with a *kasrah* on the *bāʾ* and with a *yā'* below. Ibn Wathhāb and Abū Ḥaywah recite it likewise, except that they have a *tā'* above. Ibn ʿĀmir, Abū Bakr, al-Buḥturī from Ḥafṣ, Maḥbūb from Abū ʿAmr, al-Minhāl from Yaʿqūb, al-Mufaḍḍal and Abān recite it with a *fatḥah* on it and a *yā'* below, and one of the prepositional phrases stands in the position of the object of the passive verb (the unnamed agent), and the first in position is the one next to the verb, because the demand of the verb for the nominative is stronger than its demand for the accusative complement.

Abū Jaʿfar recites *tusabbaḥu* with a *tā'* above and a *fatḥah* on the *bāʾ*. Al-Zamakhsharī said: its explanation is that it is attributed to the times of morning and evening, with the *bāʾ* being added, and the times are made the ones glorified, while the intended meaning is their Lord, like "two days were hunted, and the intended meaning is their wild animals." He finished. It is also possible that the unnamed passive subject is a pronoun referring to the glorification that is indicated by ﴿تُسَبَّحُ﴾ [Al-Isrāʾ 17:44], meaning: it is glorified for Him, i.e., the glorification itself, just as they said *liyujzā qawman* in the reading of the one who made it passive, meaning: that it be recompensed, i.e., the recompense itself.

Abū Mijlaz recites *wal-īṣāl* and its parallel has been mentioned. On these two readings ﴿رِجالٌ﴾ ("men") is nominative as the agent, with a verb omitted, meaning: *yusabbiḥu* (He is glorified), or: men glorify Him. There is disagreement about the analogy of this construction: on its analogy one would say *ḍaraba Hind Zayd* ("Zayd struck Hind") meaning: Zayd struck her. It is also possible that it is the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: those who glorify are men. The discussion of the explanation of the morning and evening and what is meant by them has already been mentioned.

Then He mentioned the description of those who glorify: that, because they are mindful of God's command and seek His pleasure, they are not distracted from the remembrance of God. His saying ﴿لا تُلْهِيهِمْ تِجارَةٌ ولا بَيْعٌ﴾ ("trade or commerce does not distract them") admits two possibilities. The first: they have no trade and no sale, so that it would distract them from the remembrance of God, like the line: "on a faint road whose landmark cannot be followed," meaning it has no landmark by which one could be guided. The second: they are people of trade and sale, but that does not occupy them from the remembrance of God and from what is obligatory upon them. The apparent meaning is that *tijārah* (trade) and *bayʿ* (sale) are different, and for this reason they are conjoined. It is possible that *tijārah* is a general term used to mean a specific one, so that by *tijārah* he means purchasing, and for this reason he paired it with sale; or it means trade in importing goods, and it is said: "so-and-so traded in such-and-such" when he imported it; and by sale is meant selling in the markets. It is also possible that ﴿ولا بَيْعٌ﴾ is a specific mention after a general one, because trade is buying and selling for the sake of profit. He drew attention to this specific item because it is more likely to distract, since a merchant, when a profitable deal comes to him, which is his whole aim from his craft, distracts him from anything whose profit is merely expected, because this is certain and that is conjectural.

Al-Zamakhsharī said: the *tā'* in *iqāmah* (establishing) is a substitute for the dropped middle radical due to the process of *iʿlāl* (weak-letter alteration). The original was *iqwām*. When it was made the first term of an annexation (iḍāfah), the annexation took the place of the letter of substitution and it was dropped. Similar to it is: "they broke their promise to you concerning the matter which they promised" (*ʿidā*). He finished. What he mentioned, that the *tā'* was dropped because of the annexation, is the position of al-Farrāʾ. The position of the Basrans is that the *tā'* in such a construction is not dropped because of the annexation. The discussion of ﴿وإقامَ الصَّلاةِ﴾ ("and establishing prayer") [Al-Anbiyāʾ 21:73] was mentioned earlier in Al-Anbiyāʾ. The first half of the line of which he quoted the second half is: "Indeed the companions resolved on parting and set off." Khālid ibn Kulthūm interpreted the phrase *ʿidā al-amr* as the plural of *ʿudwah*, which means a side, as though the poet meant the sides and the edges of the matter.

﴿يَخافُونَ يَوْمًا﴾ ("they fear a day") is the Day of Resurrection. The apparent meaning of *tatakallabu* ("will turn about") is that they are agitated by the terror of that day, as He said: ﴿وإذْ زاغَتِ الأبْصارُ وبَلَغَتِ القُلُوبُ الحَناجِرَ﴾ [Al-Aḥzāb 33:10] ("when the eyes swerved and the hearts reached the throats"). So their turning about is their unease and agitation; they turn from hope of salvation to another hope, and from fear of destruction to another destruction. The Arabs use this meaning in wars, as in the line: "Rather your heart was between the wings of a bird." The view of one who said ﴿tatakallabu﴾ means "on the embers of Hell" is far-fetched, because that is not on the Day of Resurrection but after it. The view of one who said that their turning about is the manifestation of truth to them, meaning that they turn from beliefs of error to belief in the truth as it is, so that hearts understand after having been sealed, and eyes see after having been blind, is less forceful; the first view is more emphatic in its awe-inspiring effect. Ibn Muḥaysin recited *tataqallabu* with the *tā'* assimilated into the *tā'*.

The *lām* in ﴿لِيَجْزِيَهم﴾ ("that He may recompense them") is connected to an omitted element, meaning: they did that ﴿so that He may recompense them﴾. It is also possible that it is connected to *yusabbiḥu*, and this is the apparent meaning. Al-Zamakhsharī said: the meaning is: they glorify and fear ﴿so that He may recompense them﴾. The apparent meaning is that His saying "they fear" is a qualifier of *rijāl* (men), just as ﴿لا تُلْهِيهِمْ﴾ is. *Aḥsana* ("the best") is with an omitted annexed noun, meaning: the reward of the best of what they did; or *aḥsana* is the recompense of what they did.

﴿ويَزِيدَهم مِن فَضْلِهِ﴾ ("and increase them of His bounty") beyond what their deeds require, so the people of Paradise are always in increase. Al-Zamakhsharī said: ﴿لِيَجْزِيَهم﴾ means their reward multiplied, and ﴿ويَزِيدَهم﴾ means an additional favour above the reward. Likewise is the meaning of His saying ﴿الحُسْنى وزِيادَةٌ﴾ [Yūnus 10:26] ("the best and an increase"): the good reward, and an addition to it of bounty and the gift of God, the Mighty and Majestic, either as favour, or as reward, or as compensation.

﴿واللَّهُ يَرْزُقُ مَن يَشاءُ﴾ ("God provides for whom He wills") that which He bestows as favour ﴿without reckoning﴾. As for reward, it has good deeds for those who have it, because it is according to what is deserved. He finished. In his saying "according to what is deserved" there is a Muʿtazilite insinuation.

(p-460) ﴿And those who disbelieve, their deeds are like a mirage in a level plain, which the thirsty one thinks is water, until, when he comes to it, he finds it to be nothing; and he finds Allah with him, and He pays him his account in full. And Allah is swift in reckoning.﴾ ﴿Or [their deeds are] like darknesses in a deep sea, covered by waves, above which are waves, above which are clouds — darknesses, some above others. When he extends his hand, he can hardly see it. And whomever Allah does not give light, for him there is no light.﴾

When He, exalted is He, mentioned the state of faith and of the believers, and their illumination of hearts, and the description of them with the beneficial deeds in the Hereafter that He attributed to them, He followed that by mentioning their counterparts, the disbelievers, and their deeds. So He gave them and their deeds two similitudes. One of them requires the nullification of their deeds in the Hereafter and that they do not benefit from them. The second requires their state in this world, of being bewildered in misguidance and darkness. He first likened their deeds, in their dissipation and the loss of their fruit, to a mirage in a low-lying place, which the thirsty one thinks is water, so he goes toward it and exhausts himself in reaching it.

﴿Until, when he comes to it﴾, that is, comes to the place he imagined it to be in, ﴿he finds it to be nothing﴾, that is, he finds it absent, because even on approaching he sees nothing. Likewise the disbeliever thinks that his deed will benefit him in this world, until, when he arrives at the Hereafter, his deed does not benefit him, but rather becomes a burden upon him.

Maslamah ibn Muharib recited: ﴿بِقِيعاتٍ﴾ (biqī'ātin) with an elongated tā' (تاء ممطوطة), the plural of qī'ah, like dīmāt and qīmāt from dīmah and qīmah. Also from him, with a tā' shaped like a hā', and he pauses on it with a hā'; this may be the plural of qī'ah, and he paused with a hā' according to the dialect of Ṭayyi', as they say al-banāhu and al-akhawhu in pausing on al-banāt and al-akhawāt. The author of al-Lawāmiḥ said: It is also permissible that he intended qī'ah, as the common reading, but he prolonged the fatḥah so that an alif was produced from it, like mukhrinbiq and linbā'. Al-Zamakhsharī said: Some have made it biqī'ātin with an extended tā', like rajulun 'izhāh. The author of al-Lawāmiḥ said: It is also permissible that he treated it like saʿlah and saʿlāh, and laylah and laylāh. And qī'ah is a singular synonymous with qā', or a plural of qā' like nār and nīrah; in that case the reading qī'ātin is a sound plural that encompasses a broken plural, like rijālāt Quraysh and jimālāt ṣufr.

Shaybah, Abu Ja'far and Nafi', with a variant from them both, recited (al-ẓamʾān) with the hamzah dropped and its vowel transferred to the mīm. The apparent meaning is that the phrase ﴿يَحْسَبُهُ الظَّمْآنُ﴾ describes the mirage, and it means only the thirsty one in general, not the thirsty disbeliever. Al-Zamakhsharī said: He likened what one who does not believe in faith and does not follow the truth does of righteous deeds, which he thinks will benefit him with Allah and save him from His punishment on the Day of Resurrection, and then his hope fails in the end and he meets the opposite of what he had estimated, to a mirage that the disbeliever sees in the desert, and whom the thirst of the Day of Resurrection has overcome, so he thinks it is water, comes to it and does not find what he hoped for, and finds the angels of Allah with him, who seize him, drag him, and give him to drink of boiling water and of the intensely cold liquid. These are the ones about whom Allah said: ﴿Labouring, weary﴾ [al-Ghashiyah: 3], ﴿and they think they are doing good work﴾ [al-Kahf: 104], ﴿And We will turn to what they did of deeds and make them scattered dust﴾ [al-Furqan: 23]. It was said: It was revealed concerning 'Utbah ibn Rabi'ah ibn Umayyah, who had devoted himself to worship, wore woollen garments, and sought religion in the Jahiliyyah, then disbelieved in Islam. End of quotation. So he made the thirsty one the disbeliever himself, so that the pronouns in (jā'ahu), ﴿لَمْ يَجِدْهُ﴾, (wajada), (ʿindahu) and ﴿فَوَفّاهُ﴾ all refer to one person. Others differentiated between the pronouns: the pronoun in (jā'ahu) and ﴿لَمْ يَجِدْهُ﴾ refers to the thirsty one. In (wajada) it refers to the disbeliever for whom the thirsty one was given as a parable, that is, this disbeliever found Allah's promise of recompense for his deed ready for him, ﴿and He paid him his account﴾, his deed for which He recompensed him. This is the meaning of the statement of Ubayy, Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, al-Hasan and Qatadah. The pronoun in (wajada) was made singular after the plural had preceded, taking into account each one of the disbelievers.

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: It is possible that the pronoun in (jā'ahu) returns to the mirage. Then there is much omitted in the speech that the apparent meaning indicates, its estimate being: and likewise the disbeliever on the Day of Resurrection thinks his deed beneficial, ﴿until, when he comes to it, he finds it to be nothing﴾. The pronoun may also return to the deed indicated by His saying (a'māluhum), and the completion of the parable is at His saying (māʾan). On this interpretation the speech needs no omission, but there is in the parable concision and brevity, because the intended meaning is clear.

﴿And he finds Allah with him﴾, that is, with recompense. The pronoun in (ʿindahu) returns to the deed. End of quotation. What appears to me is that He, exalted is He, likened their deeds, in their not benefiting them, to a mirage with such-and-such a description, and that the pronouns after ﴿الظَّمْآنُ﴾ refer to it. The meaning of ﴿وَجَدَ اللَّهَ عِنْدَهُ﴾ is: (wajada) the decree of Allah concerning him of destruction by thirst; (ʿindahu), that is, at the place of the mirage; ﴿فَوَفّاهُ﴾ what was written for him of that, which is what was reckoned for him; and Allah hastens his reckoning and does not delay it from him. Thus the speech is coherent, each part holding the next, through the connection of the pronouns to one thing. This similitude corresponds to their deeds in that they believed them beneficial, but they did not benefit them, and destruction befell them immediately after they were reckoned. As for al-Zamakhsharī's view, although he made the pronouns refer to the thirsty one, he made the thirsty one the disbeliever himself, which is likening a thing to itself, as he said. And he likened the water after the exertion to the water. As for the view of others, it involves disjointing the speech, since they differentiated between the pronouns, and the arrangement of the speech was broken by making some of it slip away from the rest.

﴿Or like darknesses﴾: this is the second similitude for their deeds. The first concerns what their deeds lead to in the Hereafter, and this second concerns their state in the present world. He began with the first similitude because it is more emphatic in the report, for it mentions what their affair leads to of everlasting punishment and eternal torment. Then He followed it with this parable, which alerts them to what their deeds are like, that perhaps they will return to faith and reflect upon the light of Allah which the Messenger ﷺ brought. The apparent meaning is that it is a likening of their deeds and their misguidance to dense darknesses.

Abu 'Ali al-Farisi said: The estimate is: "or like one of darknesses" (aw ka-dhī ẓulumāt). He said: What indicates this omitted modifier is His saying: ﴿when he extends his hand﴾; so the pronoun returns to the omitted modifier. Thus the comparison, according to Abu 'Ali, falls on the disbeliever and not on the deeds, which is contrary to the apparent meaning. It may be imagined in explaining his speech that the estimate is "or like those who are as those in darknesses," so the first similitude is for their deeds and the second for them in their state of misguidance. Abu al-Baqa' said: There are two possibilities for the estimate. One: "or like the deeds of one of darknesses," so "one of darknesses" is estimated so that the pronoun in His saying ﴿when he extends his hand﴾ returns to it, and "deeds" is estimated so that the likening of the deeds of the disbelievers to the deeds of the owner of darkness is sound, since there is no sense in likening a deed to the owner of darkness. The second: there is no omission in it; the meaning is that He likened the deeds of the disbelievers to darkness in its obstructing between the heart and what it is guided to. As for the pronoun in His saying ﴿when he extends his hand﴾, it returns to an unmentioned referent that was omitted relying on the meaning; its estimate is "when he extends his hand, one who is in them."

Al-Jurjani said: The first verse is about the deeds of the disbelievers, and the second is about their disbelief. He coordinated disbelief with their deeds, because disbelief is also among their deeds. And He, exalted is He, has said: ﴿He brings them out of the darknesses into the light﴾ [al-Baqarah: 257], from disbelief to faith. So the parable falls on their deeds through the disbelief of the disbeliever, and (their deeds) includes their disbelief; thus He likened their deeds to darknesses. The coordinating particle ("aw") here is for variety and detail, not that "aw" indicates doubt. Al-Kirmani said: ("aw") is for choice, on the estimate: liken the deeds of the disbelievers to whichever of the two you wish.

Sufyan ibn Husayn recited ﴿أوَ كَظُلُماتٍ﴾ with a fatḥah on the waw, making it a coordinating waw preceded by the hamzah which serves to establish the comparison, free of pure interrogation. The apparent meaning is that the pronoun in ﴿يَغْشاهُ﴾ returns to ﴿بَحْرٍ لُجِّيٍّ﴾, that is, it covers that sea, meaning some of it covers others, in the sense that one wave comes followed by another, so it is turbulent and does not calm, and it is most frightening when its waves follow one another. Above this wave is (clouds), which is greater for fear, because it hides the stars by which one is guided, and because of the wind and rain that arise together with the clouds. Whoever estimated "or like one of darknesses" returns the pronoun in ﴿يَغْشاهُ﴾ to the omitted "one of", that is, it covers the owner of the darknesses.

The majority read (sahābun) with tanwīn and (ẓulumātun) in the nominative, on the estimate of a predicate for an omitted subject, that is: these or those are (ẓulumātun). Al-Hawfi permitted that it be a subject, and ﴿بَعْضُها فَوْقَ بَعْضٍ﴾ is a subject whose predicate is in the position of the predicate of (ẓulumātun). The apparent meaning is that this is not permissible, for lack of a justification for beginning with an indefinite noun, unless an omitted qualifier is estimated: "darknesses, many or great, ﴿some above others﴾."

Al-Bazzi read ﴿سَحابُ ظُلُماتٍ﴾ with the genitive construction. Qunbul read (sahābun) with tanwīn and (ẓulumātin) in the genitive, as a substitute for (ẓulumātin), and ﴿بَعْضُها فَوْقَ بَعْضٍ﴾ is a subject and predicate in the position of a qualifier for "like darknesses."

Al-Hawfi said: It is permissible, on the nominative reading of (ẓulumātun), for (baʿḍuhā) to be a substitute for it, but this is not permissible from the viewpoint of meaning; because the intended meaning, Allah knows best, is the report that they are darknesses, and that some of those darknesses are above others, meaning they are piled-up darknesses. It is not a report that some darknesses are above others without a report that those preceding darknesses are piled-up darknesses. The discussion has already preceded concerning (kāda) when a negative particle enters upon it, at length in al-Baqarah in His saying: ﴿and they nearly did not do it﴾ [al-Baqarah: 71], so it suffices to not repeat it. The meaning here is the negation of nearly seeing, and it necessarily entails the negation of seeing. The view of one who believes that ﴿يَكَدْ﴾ is redundant, or that he sees it after difficulty, is not correct. Redundancy is the view of Ibn al-Anbari, and that he saw it only after great effort is the view of al-Mubarrad and al-Farra'.

Ibn 'Atiyyah said, in meaning: When the verb after (kāda) is negated, it indicates its affirmation, as in "kāda Zayd lā yaqūmu"; when affirmed, it indicates its negation, as in "kāda Zayd yaqūmu." And when negation precedes (kāda), it may be that the verb is negated: you say "al-mafluj lā yakādu yaskunu," and this includes the negation of stillness. And you say "rajulun munṣarifun lā yakādu yaskunu," and this includes the affirmation of stillness after exertion. End of quotation.

The apparent meaning is that this second similitude is the likening of the deeds of the disbelievers to these dense darknesses, without any correspondence in meaning between its parts and the parts of the thing likened.

Al-Zamakhshari said: He likened them, meaning their deeds, in their darkness and blackness, because they are false, and in their emptiness of the light of truth, to darknesses piled up from the depths of the sea, the waves and the clouds. Some noticed the correspondence and said: the darknesses are the corrupt deeds and false beliefs; the deep sea is the disbeliever's breast and heart; the waves are misguidance and ignorance that overwhelm his heart, and crooked thoughts; the clouds are his desire for disbelief and his turning away from faith. Al-Farra' said: This is a parable for the heart of the disbeliever, meaning that he reasons but does not see. It was said: The darknesses are his deeds, the sea is his desire. The (qiʿān) is near to drowning in it, and of great peril; the wave is what covers his heart of ignorance and heedlessness; the second wave is what covers him of doubt and dubiety; the clouds are what covers him of polytheism and bewilderment, which prevents him from being guided, contrary to what is in the light of religion. End of quotation. Explaining by correspondence of parts resembles the explanation of the Batiniyyah, and is a departure from the method of Arabic speech.

The commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 24, verses 39–40 (part 2 of 2):

When He had likened the deeds of the disbelievers to layered darkness, and mentioned that one can hardly see one's hand because of the intensity of the darkness, He said: ﴿And whoever Allah does not grant light, for him there is no light.﴾ That is, whoever Allah does not illuminate his heart with the light of faith and guide him to it, he is in darkness, has no light, and never finds guidance. This light is in this world. It has also been said that it refers to the Hereafter, meaning: whoever Allah does not illuminate with His pardon and does not show mercy to with His mercy, for him there is no mercy. That it refers to this world is more suitable to the wording of the verse. Moreover, the two meanings are interconnected, since the light of the Hereafter belongs to those whose hearts Allah has illuminated in this world.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "Whoever Allah does not confer upon him the light of His guidance (tawfiq), protection (ismah), and subtle kindness (lutf), he is in the darkness of falsehood, with no light for him." This statement is to be understood as a form of kinayat (allusive or metonymic expression), because divine kindnesses (alutaf) only follow faith and righteous action, or their being awaited. Do you not see His saying: ﴿And those who strive in Our cause, We will surely guide them to Our paths﴾ (Al-Ankabut 29:69), and His saying: ﴿And Allah leaves the wrongdoers astray﴾ (Ibrahim 14:27)? (p-463) End. This is in the manner of the Mu'tazila (al-I'tizal).
