End of quotation. So he made the thirsty one the disbeliever himself, so that the pronouns in (jā'ahu), ﴿لَمْ يَجِدْهُ﴾, (wajada), (ʿindahu) and ﴿فَوَفّاهُ﴾ all refer to one person. Others differentiated between the pronouns: the pronoun in (jā'ahu) and ﴿لَمْ يَجِدْهُ﴾ refers to the thirsty one. In (wajada) it refers to the disbeliever for whom the thirsty one was given as a parable, that is, this disbeliever found Allah's promise of recompense for his deed ready for him, ﴿and He paid him his account﴾, his deed for which He recompensed him. This is the meaning of the statement of Ubayy, Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, al-Hasan and Qatadah. The pronoun in (wajada) was made singular after the plural had preceded, taking into account each one of the disbelievers.

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: It is possible that the pronoun in (jā'ahu) returns to the mirage. Then there is much omitted in the speech that the apparent meaning indicates, its estimate being: and likewise the disbeliever on the Day of Resurrection thinks his deed beneficial, ﴿until, when he comes to it, he finds it to be nothing﴾. The pronoun may also return to the deed indicated by His saying (a'māluhum), and the completion of the parable is at His saying (māʾan). On this interpretation the speech needs no omission, but there is in the parable concision and brevity, because the intended meaning is clear.

﴿And he finds Allah with him﴾, that is, with recompense. The pronoun in (ʿindahu) returns to the deed. End of quotation. What appears to me is that He, exalted is He, likened their deeds, in their not benefiting them, to a mirage with such-and-such a description, and that the pronouns after ﴿الظَّمْآنُ﴾ refer to it. The meaning of ﴿وَجَدَ اللَّهَ عِنْدَهُ﴾ is: (wajada) the decree of Allah concerning him of destruction by thirst; (ʿindahu), that is, at the place of the mirage; ﴿فَوَفّاهُ﴾ what was written for him of that, which is what was reckoned for him; and Allah hastens his reckoning and does not delay it from him. Thus the speech is coherent, each part holding the next, through the connection of the pronouns to one thing. This similitude corresponds to their deeds in that they believed them beneficial, but they did not benefit them, and destruction befell them immediately after they were reckoned. As for al-Zamakhsharī's view, although he made the pronouns refer to the thirsty one, he made the thirsty one the disbeliever himself, which is likening a thing to itself, as he said. And he likened the water after the exertion to the water. As for the view of others, it involves disjointing the speech, since they differentiated between the pronouns, and the arrangement of the speech was broken by making some of it slip away from the rest.

﴿Or like darknesses﴾: this is the second similitude for their deeds. The first concerns what their deeds lead to in the Hereafter, and this second concerns their state in the present world. He began with the first similitude because it is more emphatic in the report, for it mentions what their affair leads to of everlasting punishment and eternal torment. Then He followed it with this parable, which alerts them to what their deeds are like, that perhaps they will return to faith and reflect upon the light of Allah which the Messenger ﷺ brought. The apparent meaning is that it is a likening of their deeds and their misguidance to dense darknesses.

Abu 'Ali al-Farisi said: The estimate is: "or like one of darknesses" (aw ka-dhī ẓulumāt). He said: What indicates this omitted modifier is His saying: ﴿when he extends his hand﴾; so the pronoun returns to the omitted modifier. Thus the comparison, according to Abu 'Ali, falls on the disbeliever and not on the deeds, which is contrary to the apparent meaning. It may be imagined in explaining his speech that the estimate is "or like those who are as those in darknesses," so the first similitude is for their deeds and the second for them in their state of misguidance. Abu al-Baqa' said: There are two possibilities for the estimate. One: "or like the deeds of one of darknesses," so "one of darknesses" is estimated so that the pronoun in His saying ﴿when he extends his hand﴾ returns to it, and "deeds" is estimated so that the likening of the deeds of the disbelievers to the deeds of the owner of darkness is sound, since there is no sense in likening a deed to the owner of darkness. The second: there is no omission in it; the meaning is that He likened the deeds of the disbelievers to darkness in its obstructing between the heart and what it is guided to. As for the pronoun in His saying ﴿when he extends his hand﴾, it returns to an unmentioned referent that was omitted relying on the meaning; its estimate is "when he extends his hand, one who is in them."

Al-Jurjani said: The first verse is about the deeds of the disbelievers, and the second is about their disbelief. He coordinated disbelief with their deeds, because disbelief is also among their deeds. And He, exalted is He, has said: ﴿He brings them out of the darknesses into the light﴾ [al-Baqarah: 257], from disbelief to faith. So the parable falls on their deeds through the disbelief of the disbeliever, and (their deeds) includes their disbelief; thus He likened their deeds to darknesses. The coordinating particle ("aw") here is for variety and detail, not that "aw" indicates doubt. Al-Kirmani said: ("aw") is for choice, on the estimate: liken the deeds of the disbelievers to whichever of the two you wish.

Sufyan ibn Husayn recited ﴿أوَ كَظُلُماتٍ﴾ with a fatḥah on the waw, making it a coordinating waw preceded by the hamzah which serves to establish the comparison, free of pure interrogation. The apparent meaning is that the pronoun in ﴿يَغْشاهُ﴾ returns to ﴿بَحْرٍ لُجِّيٍّ﴾, that is, it covers that sea, meaning some of it covers others, in the sense that one wave comes followed by another, so it is turbulent and does not calm, and it is most frightening when its waves follow one another. Above this wave is (clouds), which is greater for fear, because it hides the stars by which one is guided, and because of the wind and rain that arise together with the clouds. Whoever estimated "or like one of darknesses" returns the pronoun in ﴿يَغْشاهُ﴾ to the omitted "one of", that is, it covers the owner of the darknesses.

The majority read (sahābun) with tanwīn and (ẓulumātun) in the nominative, on the estimate of a predicate for an omitted subject, that is: these or those are (ẓulumātun). Al-Hawfi permitted that it be a subject, and ﴿بَعْضُها فَوْقَ بَعْضٍ﴾ is a subject whose predicate is in the position of the predicate of (ẓulumātun). The apparent meaning is that this is not permissible, for lack of a justification for beginning with an indefinite noun, unless an omitted qualifier is estimated: "darknesses, many or great, ﴿some above others﴾."

Al-Bazzi read ﴿سَحابُ ظُلُماتٍ﴾ with the genitive construction. Qunbul read (sahābun) with tanwīn and (ẓulumātin) in the genitive, as a substitute for (ẓulumātin), and ﴿بَعْضُها فَوْقَ بَعْضٍ﴾ is a subject and predicate in the position of a qualifier for "like darknesses."

Al-Hawfi said: It is permissible, on the nominative reading of (ẓulumātun), for (baʿḍuhā) to be a substitute for it, but this is not permissible from the viewpoint of meaning; because the intended meaning, Allah knows best, is the report that they are darknesses, and that some of those darknesses are above others, meaning they are piled-up darknesses. It is not a report that some darknesses are above others without a report that those preceding darknesses are piled-up darknesses. The discussion has already preceded concerning (kāda) when a negative particle enters upon it, at length in al-Baqarah in His saying: ﴿and they nearly did not do it﴾ [al-Baqarah: 71], so it suffices to not repeat it. The meaning here is the negation of nearly seeing, and it necessarily entails the negation of seeing. The view of one who believes that ﴿يَكَدْ﴾ is redundant, or that he sees it after difficulty, is not correct. Redundancy is the view of Ibn al-Anbari, and that he saw it only after great effort is the view of al-Mubarrad and al-Farra'.

Ibn 'Atiyyah said, in meaning: When the verb after (kāda) is negated, it indicates its affirmation, as in "kāda Zayd lā yaqūmu"; when affirmed, it indicates its negation, as in "kāda Zayd yaqūmu." And when negation precedes (kāda), it may be that the verb is negated: you say "al-mafluj lā yakādu yaskunu," and this includes the negation of stillness. And you say "rajulun munṣarifun lā yakādu yaskunu," and this includes the affirmation of stillness after exertion. End of quotation.

The apparent meaning is that this second similitude is the likening of the deeds of the disbelievers to these dense darknesses, without any correspondence in meaning between its parts and the parts of the thing likened.

Al-Zamakhshari said: He likened them, meaning their deeds, in their darkness and blackness, because they are false, and in their emptiness of the light of truth, to darknesses piled up from the depths of the sea, the waves and the clouds. Some noticed the correspondence and said: the darknesses are the corrupt deeds and false beliefs; the deep sea is the disbeliever's breast and heart; the waves are misguidance and ignorance that overwhelm his heart, and crooked thoughts; the clouds are his desire for disbelief and his turning away from faith. Al-Farra' said: This is a parable for the heart of the disbeliever, meaning that he reasons but does not see. It was said: The darknesses are his deeds, the sea is his desire. The (qiʿān) is near to drowning in it, and of great peril; the wave is what covers his heart of ignorance and heedlessness; the second wave is what covers him of doubt and dubiety; the clouds are what covers him of polytheism and bewilderment, which prevents him from being guided, contrary to what is in the light of religion. End of quotation. Explaining by correspondence of parts resembles the explanation of the Batiniyyah, and is a departure from the method of Arabic speech.

The commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 24, verses 39–40 (part 2 of 2):

When He had likened the deeds of the disbelievers to layered darkness, and mentioned that one can hardly see one's hand because of the intensity of the darkness, He said: ﴿And whoever Allah does not grant light, for him there is no light.﴾ That is, whoever Allah does not illuminate his heart with the light of faith and guide him to it, he is in darkness, has no light, and never finds guidance. This light is in this world. It has also been said that it refers to the Hereafter, meaning: whoever Allah does not illuminate with His pardon and does not show mercy to with His mercy, for him there is no mercy. That it refers to this world is more suitable to the wording of the verse. Moreover, the two meanings are interconnected, since the light of the Hereafter belongs to those whose hearts Allah has illuminated in this world.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "Whoever Allah does not confer upon him the light of His guidance (tawfiq), protection (ismah), and subtle kindness (lutf), he is in the darkness of falsehood, with no light for him." This statement is to be understood as a form of kinayat (allusive or metonymic expression), because divine kindnesses (alutaf) only follow faith and righteous action, or their being awaited. Do you not see His saying: ﴿And those who strive in Our cause, We will surely guide them to Our paths﴾ (Al-Ankabut 29:69), and His saying: ﴿And Allah leaves the wrongdoers astray﴾ (Ibrahim 14:27)? (p-463) End. This is in the manner of the Mu'tazila (al-I'tizal).

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 24, verse 41–46 (part 1 of 2):

﴿Have you not seen that to Allah glorify whoever is in the heavens and the earth, and the birds in flight? Each has known its prayer and its glorification. And Allah is Knowing of what they do.﴾ ﴿To Allah belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth, and to Allah is the return.﴾ ﴿Have you not seen that Allah drives the clouds, then joins them together, then makes them into a heap, so that you see the rain coming out from within them? And He sends down from the sky mountains [of hail] wherein is hail, and strikes with it whom He wills and averts it from whom He wills. The flash of its lightning nearly takes away the sight.﴾ ﴿Allah alternates the night and the day. Indeed in that is a lesson for those of vision.﴾ ﴿And Allah created every creature from water. Among them are those that walk on their bellies, and among them are those that walk on two legs, and among them are those that walk on four. Allah creates what He wills. Indeed Allah is over all things competent.﴾ ﴿We have certainly sent down verses that make things clear, and Allah guides whom He wills to a straight path.﴾

When the Exalted mentioned the parable of the believer and the disbeliever, and that guidance and misguidance are both referred back to Him, He followed it with mention of the proofs of His power and His oneness. The apparent reading is to take the glorification (tasbih) in its literal sense, and to restrict (man) in His saying "and whoever is on the earth" to those among the two categories (jinn and humans) who obey Allah, the Exalted. It has been said: (man) is general for every existent, with rational beings given precedence over non-rational ones, so non-rational beings are included in it, and the meaning of glorification is that their existence indicates that Allah, the Exalted, is exempt from deficiencies and described by the attributes of perfection. It has also been said: the meaning of glorification is exaltation (ta'zim), so from those possessing religion it is by speech and prayer, and from others, among the accountable and inanimate, it is by indication; so this is a common measure between them, namely exaltation. Sufyan said: the glorification of everything is by its obedience and submission.

﴿And the birds in flight﴾ means: they spread their wings in the air for flying. He specifically mentioned the birds because when they fly they are between the sky and the earth, so they are outside the general category of ﴿whoever is in the heavens and the earth﴾ during their flight. The majority (al-Jumhur) read (wa-al-tayr) in the nominative, coordinated with (man), and (saffat) in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal). Al-A'raj read (wa-al-tayra) in the accusative as an object with (ma'a, "together with"). Al-Hasan and Kharijah, from Nafi', read ﴿wa-al-tayru saffatin﴾ with both in the nominative, as a subject and predicate, the implied verb being (yusabbihna). It has been said: the glorification of the birds is literal; this is what the majority said. Al-Zamakhshari said: it is not far-fetched that Allah inspires the birds with His supplication and glorification, just as He inspired them with the various subtle knowledges that intelligent beings can hardly reach. Al-Hasan and others said: it is a metaphor; their glorification is the manifestation of wisdom in them, and so it calls to glorification.

(Kullun) means: each of those mentioned, which includes the birds. The apparent reading is that the pronoun subject in (ʿalima) and in ﴿ṣalātahu wa-tasbīḥahu﴾ refers to (kullun). Al-Hasan said this, and said: so it is constant in performing both of them. Al-Zajjaj said: the pronoun in (ʿalima) and in ﴿ṣalātahu wa-tasbīḥahu﴾ refers to (kullun). It has been said: the pronoun in (ʿalima) refers to (kullun), and in ﴿ṣalātahu wa-tasbīḥahu﴾ refers to Allah, meaning the prayer of Allah and His glorification which He commanded and guided them to, so this is an attribution of creation to the Creator. Mujahid said: prayer is for humankind, and glorification is for all others.

Al-Hasan, ʿIsa, Sallam, and Harun, from Abu ʿAmr, read (wa-taf'alūna) with the second-person address (ta' of address), and in it is a warning and intimidation. ﴿To Allah belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth﴾ is an announcement that all created beings are under His dominion; He disposes of them as He wills, with the disposal of the Irresistible, the Dominant. ﴿And to Him is the return (al-masir)﴾, that is, to His recompense of reward and punishment. In this there is reminder and intimidation.

When He mentioned the submission to Him of whoever is in the heavens and the earth, and the birds, and mentioned His dominion over this world and their return to Him, He confirmed that with a wondrous thing of His actions, indicating a transition from one state to another. It came after His saying "and to Him is the return," and He informed of a transition to the resurrection (al-maʿad). So He conjoined to it what indicates His disposal in transferring things from one state to another. The meaning of (yuzji) is: he drives slowly, little by little, and it is used for driving something heavy gently, like clouds and camels. (Al-sahab) is a collective noun, its singular being (sahabah), and the meaning is: he drives one cloud to another cloud.

﴿Then He joins it together﴾, that is, its parts together, for it is a cloud joined to another cloud, so He makes it cohere by joining one part to another. Warsh read (yuwallifu) with a waw, and the rest of the seven read it with a hamza, which is the original form. ﴿Then makes it a heap (rukaman)﴾, that is, densely piled, one part upon another, and compressed by that. ﴿From within it (min khilalihi)﴾, that is, from its openings and outlets which came about through accumulation and compression. (Khilal): it has been said to be singular, and it has been said to be the plural of (khalal), like (jibal) and (jabal). Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn ʿAbbas, al-Dahhak, Mu'adh al-ʿAnbari, from Abu ʿAmr and al-Zaʿfarani, read (min khalalihi) in the singular. The apparent reading is that in the sky there are mountains of hail; this is what Mujahid, al-Kalbi, and most of the exegetes said, Allah having created them just as He created mountains of stone on the earth. It has been said: (jibal) is a metaphor for abundance, not that there are literal mountains in the sky, just as you say: so-and-so owns mountains of gold, and he has mountains of knowledge; meaning abundance. It has been said: or it is by omission of the particle of comparison.

(Al-sama') here means the clouds, i.e., (from the sky) which is mountains, i.e., like mountains, as in His saying: ﴿until when He makes it fire﴾ [al-Kahf: 96], i.e., like fire; this is what al-Zajjaj said. So he made "the sky" to be the elevated cloud, named so for its loftiness and height. According to the first view, the meaning of "sky" is the specific blue body, which is what comes first to the mind. From its metaphorical use of "mountains" for abundance is the verse of Ibn Muqbil:

"When I die, away from the mention of poetry, you will not find for it a poet from me more excellent and more knowing of it,
And one who has more verses, a poet for whom the valleys of the mountains of poetry were struck until it was made easy."

They agreed that the first (min) is for the beginning of the extent. As for ﴿min jibalin﴾, al-Hawfi said: it is a substitute (badal) for (al-sama'), then he said: and it is partitive, and this is an error; because the first is for the beginning of the extent in what it governs, and if the second is a substitute, it must be like the first, for the beginning of the extent; if you said: "I left Baghdad from al-Karkh," both would have to be for the beginning of the extent together. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn ʿAtiyyah said: it is partitive, so on their view it is in the position of the object of (yunazzilu). Al-Hawfi and al-Zamakhshari said: and the second is explanatory (lil-bayan), end of quote. So the meaning would be: and He sends down from the sky some of the mountains that are in it, which are hail; so what is sent down is hail, since some hail is hail, and thus the object of (yunazzilu) is ﴿min jibalin﴾.

Al-Zamakhshari said: or the first and the second are for the beginning of the extent and the last is partitive; its meaning is that He sends down hail from the sky from mountains in it, end of quote. Then ﴿min jibalin﴾ is a substitute for (min al-sama').

It has been said: the second and third (min) are superfluous (za'idatan); this was said by al-Akhfash, and they are in the position of the accusative in his view, as if he said: and He sends down from the sky mountains in it, i.e., in the sky, hail; and (baradan) is a substitute, i.e., the hail of mountains. Al-Farra' said: they are both superfluous, i.e., mountains in which is hail, not pebbles or stones in them; i.e., the hail gathers and becomes like mountains for awe-inspiration; so (baradun) is the subject and (fiha) its predicate. The pronoun in (fiha) refers to the mountains, or it is the agent of the prepositional phrase, since it has been relied upon by being in the position of a description of (jibalin). It has been said: the first and second (min) are for the beginning of the extent, and the third is superfluous, i.e., and He sends down from the sky from mountains of the sky hail. Al-Zajjaj said: its meaning: and He sends down from the sky from mountains hail in them, just as you say: this is a ring in my hand of iron, i.e., a ring of iron in my hand; and you came in this and in the verse with (min) when you distinguished; and because when you say "this is a ring of iron," the meaning is one, end of quote. On this view, ﴿min baradin﴾ is in the position of a description of (jibal), just as (min) in ﴿min hadid﴾ [al-Hajj: 21] is a description of (khatam), so it is in the genitive position, and the object of (yunazzilu) is ﴿min jibalin﴾; and if the mountains are ﴿min baradin﴾, the sent-down thing must be hail.

The apparent reading is that the pronoun in (bihi) refers back to the hail, though it is possible that by it is meant both the rain (wadq) and the hail, and it follows the way of the demonstrative. It is as if he said: "He strikes with that," and rain is more general and more prevalent in striking; while averting is more eloquent in benefit and in bestowing favor.

The majority read ﴿sana﴾ (light) as a short vowel form, and ﴿barqihi﴾ in the singular. Talhah ibn Musarrif read (sana'a) with a long vowel, and ﴿buraqihi﴾ with a damma on the ba' and a fatha on the ra', the plural of (buqrah) with a damma on the ba', which is the amount of lightning like a mouthful (ghurfah) and a morsel (luqmah); and from him also with a damma on both the ba' and the ra', making the vowel of the ra' follow the vowel of the ba', as was done in (zulumat), whose original form is with sukun. (Al-sana') with the long vowel is the elevation of rank; as if he likened the perceptible part of the lightning, because of its height in the air, to the imperceptible part of a human, for that is a flash which no eye perceives. The majority read ﴿yadhhabu﴾ with a fatha on the ya' and the ha'; and Abu Ja'far read ﴿yudhhibu﴾ with a damma on the ya' and a kasra on the ha'. Al-Akhfash and Abu Hatim went to declare Abu Ja'far's reading in error, saying: because the ya' replaces the hamza; and this is not correct, because he would not read except what was transmitted. He took the reading from the leaders of the Successors, who took from the great Companions, Ubayy and others, and Abu Ja'far did not stand alone in it; rather Shaybah also read it so, and it is explained as the addition of the ba', i.e., it takes away the sights; or on the basis that the ba' has the meaning of min, and the object is omitted, its implied sense being: it takes away the light from the sights, as he said:

"The drinking of one drunk with the cold of the water of al-Hashraj."

He meant: from cold. The alternation of night and day consists of two signs, one after the other; or it is the increase of this and the decrease of that; or it alters the day with the darkness of clouds at one time and the light of the sun at another, and alters the night with the intensifying of its darkness at one time and the light of the moon at another; or by the variation of what is decreed in them of good and benefit, hardship and blessing, security and their opposites, and the like. Four views are reported. That in that is an indication of the proofs previously mentioned which point to His oneness: from the glorification from remembrance, and the subjugation of the clouds, and what the Exalted brings about in them of His actions until He sends down rain, dividing His mercy among His creatures, and showing them the lightning in the clouds which nearly snatches away the sights, and alternates the night and the day.

(La'ibrah) means: a lesson, that is, admonition. The people of sight (ulu al-absar) were singled out for admonition, because sight and insight, when employed, arrive at the perception of truth, as in His saying: ﴿Only those of understanding remember﴾ [al-Ra'd: 19].

The majority read (khalaqa) as a past-tense verb, with (kulla) in the accusative. Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, Ibn Thabit, and al-A'mash read (khaliqu) as an active participle attributed to (kulli). (Al-dabbah) is that which moves forward on its feet, and it includes birds. The poet said:

"The crawling of the sandgrouse of al-Batha' in every watering place."

Al-Hut (the fish). In a hadith it is said: "a creature of the sea, like the dharib (a kind of lizard)." The phrase "every creature" (kulla dabbah) includes the one who discerns and others, so the distinction is easily made with "those" (man, the relative pronoun for rational beings) and "that which" (ma, for non-rational beings), when the non-rational is included in the general term. Thus a judgment is applied to it as though all the creatures were discerning. The apparent meaning is that "from water" (min ma') is connected to "created" (khalaqa). The "min" here indicates the starting point, meaning He began its creation from water.

It has been said: since most animals are created from water, either because they are generated from a drop of semen or because they cannot live except by water, the word "every" (kull) is used, treating the majority as if it were the whole. This excludes what was created from light, namely the angels, and what was created from fire, namely the jinn, and what was created from earth, namely Adam. Jesus was created from the Spirit, and many animals are not generated from a drop of semen.

It has also been said that "every creature" is general over all these things, and that the origin of all created beings is water. It is related that the first thing God created was a jewel, and He looked at it with the eye of awe, and it became water. Then from that water He created fire, air, and light. Since the purpose of this verse is to explain the origin of creation, and the first origin was water, He said: "He created every creature from water."

Al-Qaffal said: "from water" is not connected to "created." Rather, it is in the position of a description of "every creature." So the meaning is an announcement that He, exalted is He, created every creature generated from water, that is, generated from water and created by God, exalted is He. Water is indefinite here but definite in "And We made from water every living thing" (al-Anbiya: 30), because the meaning here (p-466) "He created every creature" from a kind of water specific to this creature, or "from water" specifically, which is the drop of semen. Then He varied the created beings from the drop of semen: insects, beasts, and humans, as He said: "watered with one water, yet We make some of them excel others in produce" (al-Ra'd). Here He intends that all kinds of animals are created from this genus, which is the genus of water, because it is the origin, even if intermediaries came between them and it, as it was said: the origin of light, fire, and earth is water.

Crawling on the belly is called walking, either because of its similarity to what follows, the mention of those who walk, or as a metaphor, as they say: "this matter has walked" and "affairs are going well for so-and-so," just as they used the word for lip (mushaffar) for lip and lip for the large lip (jahfalah). Those who walk "on their bellies" are snakes, fish, and the like, and worms and others. "On two legs" are humans and birds, and "on four" are all other land animals, beasts and others. If one is found that has more than four, it was said that its reliance is only on four, and it does not need all of them for its walking. And He mentioned first what is most evident in power and most wondrous, namely that which walks without any instrument, like one who has feet and limbs, then that which walks on two, then that which walks on four. In the codex of Ubayy: "and among them is one that walks on more," thereby generalizing this addition to all animals, but it is not established as Qur'an. Perhaps he cited it not as Qur'an but as an indication that God created those that walk on more than four: such as the spider, the scorpion, the centipede, the creature with forty-four legs, and the one called the ear-creature. Because this kind is rare, it was not mentioned.

"God creates what He wills" is an indication that whatever His will has been directed to create, He brings into being and originates. In this there is a reminder of the multitude of animals, and that just as they differ in manner of walking, they differ in other respects.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 24, verse 41–46 (part 1 of 2):

﴿Have you not seen that to Allah glorify whoever is in the heavens and the earth, and the birds in flight? Each has known its prayer and its glorification. And Allah is Knowing of what they do.﴾ ﴿To Allah belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth, and to Allah is the return.﴾ ﴿Have you not seen that Allah drives the clouds, then joins them together, then makes them into a heap, so that you see the rain coming out from within them? And He sends down from the sky mountains [of hail] wherein is hail, and strikes with it whom He wills and averts it from whom He wills. The flash of its lightning nearly takes away the sight.﴾ ﴿Allah alternates the night and the day. Indeed in that is a lesson for those of vision.﴾ ﴿And Allah created every creature from water. Among them are those that walk on their bellies, and among them are those that walk on two legs, and among them are those that walk on four. Allah creates what He wills. Indeed Allah is over all things competent.﴾ ﴿We have certainly sent down verses that make things clear, and Allah guides whom He wills to a straight path.﴾

When the Exalted mentioned the parable of the believer and the disbeliever, and that guidance and misguidance are both referred back to Him, He followed it with mention of the proofs of His power and His oneness. The apparent reading is to take the glorification (tasbih) in its literal sense, and to restrict (man) in His saying "and whoever is on the earth" to those among the two categories (jinn and humans) who obey Allah, the Exalted. It has been said: (man) is general for every existent, with rational beings given precedence over non-rational ones, so non-rational beings are included in it, and the meaning of glorification is that their existence indicates that Allah, the Exalted, is exempt from deficiencies and described by the attributes of perfection. It has also been said: the meaning of glorification is exaltation (ta'zim), so from those possessing religion it is by speech and prayer, and from others, among the accountable and inanimate, it is by indication; so this is a common measure between them, namely exaltation. Sufyan said: the glorification of everything is by its obedience and submission.

﴿And the birds in flight﴾ means: they spread their wings in the air for flying. He specifically mentioned the birds because when they fly they are between the sky and the earth, so they are outside the general category of ﴿whoever is in the heavens and the earth﴾ during their flight. The majority (al-Jumhur) read (wa-al-tayr) in the nominative, coordinated with (man), and (saffat) in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal). Al-A'raj read (wa-al-tayra) in the accusative as an object with (ma'a, "together with"). Al-Hasan and Kharijah, from Nafi', read ﴿wa-al-tayru saffatin﴾ with both in the nominative, as a subject and predicate, the implied verb being (yusabbihna). It has been said: the glorification of the birds is literal; this is what the majority said. Al-Zamakhshari said: it is not far-fetched that Allah inspires the birds with His supplication and glorification, just as He inspired them with the various subtle knowledges that intelligent beings can hardly reach. Al-Hasan and others said: it is a metaphor; their glorification is the manifestation of wisdom in them, and so it calls to glorification.

(Kullun) means: each of those mentioned, which includes the birds. The apparent reading is that the pronoun subject in (ʿalima) and in ﴿ṣalātahu wa-tasbīḥahu﴾ refers to (kullun). Al-Hasan said this, and said: so it is constant in performing both of them. Al-Zajjaj said: the pronoun in (ʿalima) and in ﴿ṣalātahu wa-tasbīḥahu﴾ refers to (kullun). It has been said: the pronoun in (ʿalima) refers to (kullun), and in ﴿ṣalātahu wa-tasbīḥahu﴾ refers to Allah, meaning the prayer of Allah and His glorification which He commanded and guided them to, so this is an attribution of creation to the Creator. Mujahid said: prayer is for humankind, and glorification is for all others.

Al-Hasan, ʿIsa, Sallam, and Harun, from Abu ʿAmr, read (wa-taf'alūna) with the second-person address (ta' of address), and in it is a warning and intimidation. ﴿To Allah belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth﴾ is an announcement that all created beings are under His dominion; He disposes of them as He wills, with the disposal of the Irresistible, the Dominant. ﴿And to Him is the return (al-masir)﴾, that is, to His recompense of reward and punishment. In this there is reminder and intimidation.

When He mentioned the submission to Him of whoever is in the heavens and the earth, and the birds, and mentioned His dominion over this world and their return to Him, He confirmed that with a wondrous thing of His actions, indicating a transition from one state to another. It came after His saying "and to Him is the return," and He informed of a transition to the resurrection (al-maʿad). So He conjoined to it what indicates His disposal in transferring things from one state to another. The meaning of (yuzji) is: he drives slowly, little by little, and it is used for driving something heavy gently, like clouds and camels. (Al-sahab) is a collective noun, its singular being (sahabah), and the meaning is: he drives one cloud to another cloud.

﴿Then He joins it together﴾, that is, its parts together, for it is a cloud joined to another cloud, so He makes it cohere by joining one part to another. Warsh read (yuwallifu) with a waw, and the rest of the seven read it with a hamza, which is the original form. ﴿Then makes it a heap (rukaman)﴾, that is, densely piled, one part upon another, and compressed by that. ﴿From within it (min khilalihi)﴾, that is, from its openings and outlets which came about through accumulation and compression. (Khilal): it has been said to be singular, and it has been said to be the plural of (khalal), like (jibal) and (jabal). Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn ʿAbbas, al-Dahhak, Mu'adh al-ʿAnbari, from Abu ʿAmr and al-Zaʿfarani, read (min khalalihi) in the singular. The apparent reading is that in the sky there are mountains of hail; this is what Mujahid, al-Kalbi, and most of the exegetes said, Allah having created them just as He created mountains of stone on the earth. It has been said: (jibal) is a metaphor for abundance, not that there are literal mountains in the sky, just as you say: so-and-so owns mountains of gold, and he has mountains of knowledge; meaning abundance. It has been said: or it is by omission of the particle of comparison.

(Al-sama') here means the clouds, i.e., (from the sky) which is mountains, i.e., like mountains, as in His saying: ﴿until when He makes it fire﴾ [al-Kahf: 96], i.e., like fire; this is what al-Zajjaj said. So he made "the sky" to be the elevated cloud, named so for its loftiness and height. According to the first view, the meaning of "sky" is the specific blue body, which is what comes first to the mind. From its metaphorical use of "mountains" for abundance is the verse of Ibn Muqbil:

"When I die, away from the mention of poetry, you will not find for it a poet from me more excellent and more knowing of it,
And one who has more verses, a poet for whom the valleys of the mountains of poetry were struck until it was made easy."

They agreed that the first (min) is for the beginning of the extent. As for ﴿min jibalin﴾, al-Hawfi said: it is a substitute (badal) for (al-sama'), then he said: and it is partitive, and this is an error; because the first is for the beginning of the extent in what it governs, and if the second is a substitute, it must be like the first, for the beginning of the extent; if you said: "I left Baghdad from al-Karkh," both would have to be for the beginning of the extent together. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn ʿAtiyyah said: it is partitive, so on their view it is in the position of the object of (yunazzilu). Al-Hawfi and al-Zamakhshari said: and the second is explanatory (lil-bayan), end of quote. So the meaning would be: and He sends down from the sky some of the mountains that are in it, which are hail; so what is sent down is hail, since some hail is hail, and thus the object of (yunazzilu) is ﴿min jibalin﴾.

Al-Zamakhshari said: or the first and the second are for the beginning of the extent and the last is partitive; its meaning is that He sends down hail from the sky from mountains in it, end of quote. Then ﴿min jibalin﴾ is a substitute for (min al-sama').

It has been said: the second and third (min) are superfluous (za'idatan); this was said by al-Akhfash, and they are in the position of the accusative in his view, as if he said: and He sends down from the sky mountains in it, i.e., in the sky, hail; and (baradan) is a substitute, i.e., the hail of mountains. Al-Farra' said: they are both superfluous, i.e., mountains in which is hail, not pebbles or stones in them; i.e., the hail gathers and becomes like mountains for awe-inspiration; so (baradun) is the subject and (fiha) its predicate. The pronoun in (fiha) refers to the mountains, or it is the agent of the prepositional phrase, since it has been relied upon by being in the position of a description of (jibalin). It has been said: the first and second (min) are for the beginning of the extent, and the third is superfluous, i.e., and He sends down from the sky from mountains of the sky hail. Al-Zajjaj said: its meaning: and He sends down from the sky from mountains hail in them, just as you say: this is a ring in my hand of iron, i.e., a ring of iron in my hand; and you came in this and in the verse with (min) when you distinguished; and because when you say "this is a ring of iron," the meaning is one, end of quote. On this view, ﴿min baradin﴾ is in the position of a description of (jibal), just as (min) in ﴿min hadid﴾ [al-Hajj: 21] is a description of (khatam), so it is in the genitive position, and the object of (yunazzilu) is ﴿min jibalin﴾; and if the mountains are ﴿min baradin﴾, the sent-down thing must be hail.

The apparent reading is that the pronoun in (bihi) refers back to the hail, though it is possible that by it is meant both the rain (wadq) and the hail, and it follows the way of the demonstrative. It is as if he said: "He strikes with that," and rain is more general and more prevalent in striking; while averting is more eloquent in benefit and in bestowing favor.

The majority read ﴿sana﴾ (light) as a short vowel form, and ﴿barqihi﴾ in the singular. Talhah ibn Musarrif read (sana'a) with a long vowel, and ﴿buraqihi﴾ with a damma on the ba' and a fatha on the ra', the plural of (buqrah) with a damma on the ba', which is the amount of lightning like a mouthful (ghurfah) and a morsel (luqmah); and from him also with a damma on both the ba' and the ra', making the vowel of the ra' follow the vowel of the ba', as was done in (zulumat), whose original form is with sukun. (Al-sana') with the long vowel is the elevation of rank; as if he likened the perceptible part of the lightning, because of its height in the air, to the imperceptible part of a human, for that is a flash which no eye perceives. The majority read ﴿yadhhabu﴾ with a fatha on the ya' and the ha'; and Abu Ja'far read ﴿yudhhibu﴾ with a damma on the ya' and a kasra on the ha'. Al-Akhfash and Abu Hatim went to declare Abu Ja'far's reading in error, saying: because the ya' replaces the hamza; and this is not correct, because he would not read except what was transmitted. He took the reading from the leaders of the Successors, who took from the great Companions, Ubayy and others, and Abu Ja'far did not stand alone in it; rather Shaybah also read it so, and it is explained as the addition of the ba', i.e., it takes away the sights; or on the basis that the ba' has the meaning of min, and the object is omitted, its implied sense being: it takes away the light from the sights, as he said:

"The drinking of one drunk with the cold of the water of al-Hashraj."

He meant: from cold. The alternation of night and day consists of two signs, one after the other; or it is the increase of this and the decrease of that; or it alters the day with the darkness of clouds at one time and the light of the sun at another, and alters the night with the intensifying of its darkness at one time and the light of the moon at another; or by the variation of what is decreed in them of good and benefit, hardship and blessing, security and their opposites, and the like. Four views are reported. That in that is an indication of the proofs previously mentioned which point to His oneness: from the glorification from remembrance, and the subjugation of the clouds, and what the Exalted brings about in them of His actions until He sends down rain, dividing His mercy among His creatures, and showing them the lightning in the clouds which nearly snatches away the sights, and alternates the night and the day.

(La'ibrah) means: a lesson, that is, admonition. The people of sight (ulu al-absar) were singled out for admonition, because sight and insight, when employed, arrive at the perception of truth, as in His saying: ﴿Only those of understanding remember﴾ [al-Ra'd: 19].

The majority read (khalaqa) as a past-tense verb, with (kulla) in the accusative. Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, Ibn Thabit, and al-A'mash read (khaliqu) as an active participle attributed to (kulli). (Al-dabbah) is that which moves forward on its feet, and it includes birds. The poet said:

"The crawling of the sandgrouse of al-Batha' in every watering place."

Al-Hut (the fish). In a hadith it is said: "a creature of the sea, like the dharib (a kind of lizard)." The phrase "every creature" (kulla dabbah) includes the one who discerns and others, so the distinction is easily made with "those" (man, the relative pronoun for rational beings) and "that which" (ma, for non-rational beings), when the non-rational is included in the general term. Thus a judgment is applied to it as though all the creatures were discerning. The apparent meaning is that "from water" (min ma') is connected to "created" (khalaqa). The "min" here indicates the starting point, meaning He began its creation from water.

It has been said: since most animals are created from water, either because they are generated from a drop of semen or because they cannot live except by water, the word "every" (kull) is used, treating the majority as if it were the whole. This excludes what was created from light, namely the angels, and what was created from fire, namely the jinn, and what was created from earth, namely Adam. Jesus was created from the Spirit, and many animals are not generated from a drop of semen.

It has also been said that "every creature" is general over all these things, and that the origin of all created beings is water. It is related that the first thing God created was a jewel, and He looked at it with the eye of awe, and it became water. Then from that water He created fire, air, and light. Since the purpose of this verse is to explain the origin of creation, and the first origin was water, He said: "He created every creature from water."

Al-Qaffal said: "from water" is not connected to "created." Rather, it is in the position of a description of "every creature." So the meaning is an announcement that He, exalted is He, created every creature generated from water, that is, generated from water and created by God, exalted is He. Water is indefinite here but definite in "And We made from water every living thing" (al-Anbiya: 30), because the meaning here (p-466) "He created every creature" from a kind of water specific to this creature, or "from water" specifically, which is the drop of semen. Then He varied the created beings from the drop of semen: insects, beasts, and humans, as He said: "watered with one water, yet We make some of them excel others in produce" (al-Ra'd). Here He intends that all kinds of animals are created from this genus, which is the genus of water, because it is the origin, even if intermediaries came between them and it, as it was said: the origin of light, fire, and earth is water.

Crawling on the belly is called walking, either because of its similarity to what follows, the mention of those who walk, or as a metaphor, as they say: "this matter has walked" and "affairs are going well for so-and-so," just as they used the word for lip (mushaffar) for lip and lip for the large lip (jahfalah). Those who walk "on their bellies" are snakes, fish, and the like, and worms and others. "On two legs" are humans and birds, and "on four" are all other land animals, beasts and others. If one is found that has more than four, it was said that its reliance is only on four, and it does not need all of them for its walking. And He mentioned first what is most evident in power and most wondrous, namely that which walks without any instrument, like one who has feet and limbs, then that which walks on two, then that which walks on four. Perhaps he cited it not as Qur'an but as an indication that God created those that walk on more than four: such as the spider, the scorpion, the centipede, the creature with forty-four legs, and the one called the ear-creature. Al-Akhfash and Abu Hatim went to declare Abu Ja'far's reading in error, saying: because the ya' replaces the hamza; and this is not correct, because he would not read except what was transmitted. "The drinking of one drunk with the cold of the water of al-Hashraj."

He meant: from cold. The alternation of night and day consists of two signs, one after the other; or it is the increase of this and the decrease of that; or it alters the day with the darkness of clouds at one time and the light of the sun at another, and alters the night with the intensifying of its darkness at one time and the light of the moon at another; or by the variation of what is decreed in them of good and benefit, hardship and blessing, security and their opposites, and the like. Four views are reported. That in that is an indication of the proofs previously mentioned which point to His oneness: from the glorification from remembrance, and the subjugation of the clouds, and what the Exalted brings about in them of His actions until He sends down rain, dividing His mercy among His creatures, and showing them the lightning in the clouds which nearly snatches away the sights, and alternates the night and the day.

(La'ibrah) means: a lesson, that is, admonition. The people of sight (ulu al-absar) were singled out for admonition, because sight and insight, when employed, arrive at the perception of truth, as in His saying: ﴿Only those of understanding remember﴾ [al-Ra'd: 19].

The majority read (khalaqa) as a past-tense verb, with (kulla) in the accusative. Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, Ibn Thabit, and al-A'mash read (khaliqu) as an active participle attributed to (kulli). (Al-dabbah) is that which moves forward on its feet, and it includes birds. The poet said:

"The crawling of the sandgrouse of al-Batha' in every watering place."

Al-Hut (the fish). In a hadith it is said: "a creature of the sea, like the dharib (a kind of lizard)." The phrase "every creature" (kulla dabbah) includes the one who discerns and others, so the distinction is easily made with "those" (man, the relative pronoun for rational beings) and "that which" (ma, for non-rational beings), when the non-rational is included in the general term. The "min" here indicates the starting point, meaning He began its creation from water.

This excludes what was created from light, namely the angels, and what was created from fire, namely the jinn, and what was created from earth, namely Adam. So the meaning is an announcement that He, exalted is He, created every creature generated from water, that is, generated from water and created by God, exalted is He. And He sends down from the sky mountains [of hail] wherein is hail, and strikes with it whom He wills and averts it from whom He wills. The flash of its lightning nearly takes away the sight.﴾ ﴿Allah alternates the night and the day. Indeed in that is a lesson for those of vision.﴾ ﴿And Allah created every creature from water. Among them are those that walk on their bellies, and among them are those that walk on two legs, and among them are those that walk on four. Allah creates what He wills. Indeed Allah is over all things competent.﴾ ﴿We have certainly sent down verses that make things clear, and Allah guides whom He wills to a straight path.﴾

It has been said: (man) is general for every existent, with rational beings given precedence over non-rational ones, so non-rational beings are included in it, and the meaning of glorification is that their existence indicates that Allah, the Exalted, is exempt from deficiencies and described by the attributes of perfection. It has also been said: the meaning of glorification is exaltation (ta'zim), so from those possessing religion it is by speech and prayer, and from others, among the accountable and inanimate, it is by indication; so this is a common measure between them, namely exaltation. Sufyan said: the glorification of everything is by its obedience and submission.

﴿And the birds in flight﴾ means: they spread their wings in the air for flying. He specifically mentioned the birds because when they fly they are between the sky and the earth, so they are outside the general category of ﴿whoever is in the heavens and the earth﴾ during their flight. The majority (al-Jumhur) read (wa-al-tayr) in the nominative, coordinated with (man), and (saffat) in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal). Al-A'raj read (wa-al-tayra) in the accusative as an object with (ma'a, "together with"). Al-Hasan and Kharijah, from Nafi', read ﴿wa-al-tayru saffatin﴾ with both in the nominative, as a subject and predicate, the implied verb being (yusabbihna). It has been said: the glorification of the birds is literal; this is what the majority said. Al-Zamakhshari said: it is not far-fetched that Allah inspires the birds with His supplication and glorification, just as He inspired them with the various subtle knowledges that intelligent beings can hardly reach. Al-Hasan and others said: it is a metaphor; their glorification is the manifestation of wisdom in them, and so it calls to glorification.

(Kullun) means: each of those mentioned, which includes the birds. The apparent reading is that the pronoun subject in (ʿalima) and in ﴿ṣalātahu wa-tasbīḥahu﴾ refers to (kullun). Al-Hasan said this, and said: so it is constant in performing both of them. Al-Zajjaj said: the pronoun in (ʿalima) and in ﴿ṣalātahu wa-tasbīḥahu﴾ refers to (kullun). It has been said: the pronoun in (ʿalima) refers to (kullun), and in ﴿ṣalātahu wa-tasbīḥahu﴾ refers to Allah, meaning the prayer of Allah and His glorification which He commanded and guided them to, so this is an attribution of creation to the Creator. Mujahid said: prayer is for humankind, and glorification is for all others.

Al-Hasan, ʿIsa, Sallam, and Harun, from Abu ʿAmr, read (wa-taf'alūna) with the second-person address (ta' of address), and in it is a warning and intimidation. ﴿To Allah belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth﴾ is an announcement that all created beings are under His dominion; He disposes of them as He wills, with the disposal of the Irresistible, the Dominant. ﴿And to Him is the return (al-masir)﴾, that is, to His recompense of reward and punishment. In this there is reminder and intimidation.

When He mentioned the submission to Him of whoever is in the heavens and the earth, and the birds, and mentioned His dominion over this world and their return to Him, He confirmed that with a wondrous thing of His actions, indicating a transition from one state to another. It came after His saying "and to Him is the return," and He informed of a transition to the resurrection (al-maʿad). So He conjoined to it what indicates His disposal in transferring things from one state to another. The meaning of (yuzji) is: he drives slowly, little by little, and it is used for driving something heavy gently, like clouds and camels. (Al-sahab) is a collective noun, its singular being (sahabah), and the meaning is: he drives one cloud to another cloud.

﴿Then He joins it together﴾, that is, its parts together, for it is a cloud joined to another cloud, so He makes it cohere by joining one part to another. Warsh read (yuwallifu) with a waw, and the rest of the seven read it with a hamza, which is the original form. ﴿Then makes it a heap (rukaman)﴾, that is, densely piled, one part upon another, and compressed by that. ﴿From within it (min khilalihi)﴾, that is, from its openings and outlets which came about through accumulation and compression. Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn ʿAbbas, al-Dahhak, Mu'adh al-ʿAnbari, from Abu ʿAmr and al-Zaʿfarani, read (min khalalihi) in the singular. The apparent reading is that in the sky there are mountains of hail; this is what Mujahid, al-Kalbi, and most of the exegetes said, Allah having created them just as He created mountains of stone on the earth. It has been said: (jibal) is a metaphor for abundance, not that there are literal mountains in the sky, just as you say: so-and-so owns mountains of gold, and he has mountains of knowledge; meaning abundance. It has been said: or it is by omission of the particle of comparison.

(Al-sama') here means the clouds, i.e., (from the sky) which is mountains, i.e., like mountains, as in His saying: ﴿until when He makes it fire﴾ [al-Kahf: 96], i.e., like fire; this is what al-Zajjaj said. So he made "the sky" to be the elevated cloud, named so for its loftiness and height. According to the first view, the meaning of "sky" is the specific blue body, which is what comes first to the mind. From its metaphorical use of "mountains" for abundance is the verse of Ibn Muqbil:

"When I die, away from the mention of poetry, you will not find for it a poet from me more excellent and more knowing of it,
And one who has more verses, a poet for whom the valleys of the mountains of poetry were struck until it was made easy."

They agreed that the first (min) is for the beginning of the extent. As for ﴿min jibalin﴾, al-Hawfi said: it is a substitute (badal) for (al-sama'), then he said: and it is partitive, and this is an error; because the first is for the beginning of the extent in what it governs, and if the second is a substitute, it must be like the first, for the beginning of the extent; if you said: "I left Baghdad from al-Karkh," both would have to be for the beginning of the extent together. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn ʿAtiyyah said: it is partitive, so on their view it is in the position of the object of (yunazzilu). Al-Hawfi and al-Zamakhshari said: and the second is explanatory (lil-bayan), end of quote. So the meaning would be: and He sends down from the sky some of the mountains that are in it, which are hail; so what is sent down is hail, since some hail is hail, and thus the object of (yunazzilu) is ﴿min jibalin﴾.

It has been said: the first and second (min) are for the beginning of the extent, and the third is superfluous, i.e., and He sends down from the sky from mountains of the sky hail. On this view, ﴿min baradin﴾ is in the position of a description of (jibal), just as (min) in ﴿min hadid﴾ [al-Hajj: 21] is a description of (khatam), so it is in the genitive position, and the object of (yunazzilu) is ﴿min jibalin﴾; and if the mountains are ﴿min baradin﴾, the sent-down thing must be hail.

The apparent reading is that the pronoun in (bihi) refers back to the hail, though it is possible that by it is meant both the rain (wadq) and the hail, and it follows the way of the demonstrative. It is as if he said: "He strikes with that," and rain is more general and more prevalent in striking; while averting is more eloquent in benefit and in bestowing favor.

So He conjoined to it what indicates His disposal in transferring things from one state to another. The meaning of (yuzji) is: he drives slowly, little by little, and it is used for driving something heavy gently, like clouds and camels. (Al-sahab) is a collective noun, its singular being (sahabah), and the meaning is: he drives one cloud to another cloud.

﴿Then He joins it together﴾, that is, its parts together, for it is a cloud joined to another cloud, so He makes it cohere by joining one part to another. Warsh read (yuwallifu) with a waw, and the rest of the seven read it with a hamza, which is the original form. ﴿Then makes it a heap (rukaman)﴾, that is, densely piled, one part upon another, and compressed by that. ﴿From within it (min khilalihi)﴾, that is, from its openings and outlets which came about through accumulation and compression. (Khilal): it has been said to be singular, and it has been said to be the plural of (khalal), like (jibal) and (jabal). Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn ʿAbbas, al-Dahhak, Mu'adh al-ʿAnbari, from Abu ʿAmr and al-Zaʿfarani, read (min khalalihi) in the singular. The apparent reading is that in the sky there are mountains of hail; this is what Mujahid, al-Kalbi, and most of the exegetes said, Allah having created them just as He created mountains of stone on the earth. It has been said: (jibal) is a metaphor for abundance, not that there are literal mountains in the sky, just as you say: so-and-so owns mountains of gold, and he has mountains of knowledge; meaning abundance. It has been said: or it is by omission of the particle of comparison.

(Al-sama') here means the clouds, i.e., (from the sky) which is mountains, i.e., like mountains, as in His saying: ﴿until when He makes it fire﴾ [al-Kahf: 96], i.e., like fire; this is what al-Zajjaj said. So he made "the sky" to be the elevated cloud, named so for its loftiness and height. According to the first view, the meaning of "sky" is the specific blue body, which is what comes first to the mind. From its metaphorical use of "mountains" for abundance is the verse of Ibn Muqbil:

"When I die, away from the mention of poetry, you will not find for it a poet from me more excellent and more knowing of it,
And one who has more verses, a poet for whom the valleys of the mountains of poetry were struck until it was made easy."

They agreed that the first (min) is for the beginning of the extent. As for ﴿min jibalin﴾, al-Hawfi said: it is a substitute (badal) for (al-sama'), then he said: and it is partitive, and this is an error; because the first is for the beginning of the extent in what it governs, and if the second is a substitute, it must be like the first, for the beginning of the extent; if you said: "I left Baghdad from al-Karkh," both would have to be for the beginning of the extent together. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn ʿAtiyyah said: it is partitive, so on their view it is in the position of the object of (yunazzilu). Al-Hawfi and al-Zamakhshari said: and the second is explanatory (lil-bayan), end of quote. So the meaning would be: and He sends down from the sky some of the mountains that are in it, which are hail; so what is sent down is hail, since some hail is hail, and thus the object of (yunazzilu) is ﴿min jibalin﴾.

Al-Zamakhshari said: or the first and the second are for the beginning of the extent and the last is partitive; its meaning is that He sends down hail from the sky from mountains in it, end of quote. Then ﴿min jibalin﴾ is a substitute for (min al-sama').

It has been said: the second and third (min) are superfluous (za'idatan); this was said by al-Akhfash, and they are in the position of the accusative in his view, as if he said: and He sends down from the sky mountains in it, i.e., in the sky, hail; and (baradan) is a substitute, i.e., the hail of mountains. Al-Farra' said: they are both superfluous, i.e., mountains in which is hail, not pebbles or stones in them; i.e., the hail gathers and becomes like mountains for awe-inspiration; so (baradun) is the subject and (fiha) its predicate. The pronoun in (fiha) refers to the mountains, or it is the agent of the prepositional phrase, since it has been relied upon by being in the position of a description of (jibalin). It has been said: the first and second (min) are for the beginning of the extent, and the third is superfluous, i.e., and He sends down from the sky from mountains of the sky hail. Al-Zajjaj said: its meaning: and He sends down from the sky from mountains hail in them, just as you say: this is a ring in my hand of iron, i.e., a ring of iron in my hand; and you came in this and in the verse with (min) when you distinguished; and because when you say "this is a ring of iron," the meaning is one, end of quote. On this view, ﴿min baradin﴾ is in the position of a description of (jibal), just as (min) in ﴿min hadid﴾ [al-Hajj: 21] is a description of (khatam), so it is in the genitive position, and the object of (yunazzilu) is ﴿min jibalin﴾; and if the mountains are ﴿min baradin﴾, the sent-down thing must be hail.

The apparent reading is that the pronoun in (bihi) refers back to the hail, though it is possible that by it is meant both the rain (wadq) and the hail, and it follows the way of the demonstrative. It is as if he said: "He strikes with that," and rain is more general and more prevalent in striking; while averting is more eloquent in benefit and in bestowing favor.

The majority read ﴿sana﴾ (light) as a short vowel form, and ﴿barqihi﴾ in the singular. Talhah ibn Musarrif read (sana'a) with a long vowel, and ﴿buraqihi﴾ with a damma on the ba' and a fatha on the ra', the plural of (buqrah) with a damma on the ba', which is the amount of lightning like a mouthful (ghurfah) and a morsel (luqmah); and from him also with a damma on both the ba' and the ra', making the vowel of the ra' follow the vowel of the ba', as was done in (zulumat), whose original form is with sukun. (Al-sana') with the long vowel is the elevation of rank; as if he likened the perceptible part of the lightning, because of its height in the air, to the imperceptible part of a human, for that is a flash which no eye perceives. The majority read ﴿yadhhabu﴾ with a fatha on the ya' and the ha'; and Abu Ja'far read ﴿yudhhibu﴾ with a damma on the ya' and a kasra on the ha'. Al-Akhfash and Abu Hatim went to declare Abu Ja'far's reading in error, saying: because the ya' replaces the hamza; and this is not correct, because he would not read except what was transmitted. He took the reading from the leaders of the Successors, who took from the great Companions, Ubayy and others, and Abu Ja'far did not stand alone in it; rather Shaybah also read it so, and it is explained as the addition of the ba', i.e., it takes away the sights; or on the basis that the ba' has the meaning of min, and the object is omitted, its implied sense being: it takes away the light from the sights, as he said:

"The drinking of one drunk with the cold of the water of al-Hashraj."

He meant: from cold. The alternation of night and day consists of two signs, one after the other; or it is the increase of this and the decrease of that; or it alters the day with the darkness of clouds at one time and the light of the sun at another, and alters the night with the intensifying of its darkness at one time and the light of the moon at another; or by the variation of what is decreed in them of good and benefit, hardship and blessing, security and their opposites, and the like. Four views are reported. That in that is an indication of the proofs previously mentioned which point to His oneness: from the glorification from remembrance, and the subjugation of the clouds, and what the Exalted brings about in them of His actions until He sends down rain, dividing His mercy among His creatures, and showing them the lightning in the clouds which nearly snatches away the sights, and alternates the night and the day.

(La'ibrah) means: a lesson, that is, admonition. The people of sight (ulu al-absar) were singled out for admonition, because sight and insight, when employed, arrive at the perception of truth, as in His saying: ﴿Only those of understanding remember﴾ [al-Ra'd: 19].

The majority read (khalaqa) as a past-tense verb, with (kulla) in the accusative. Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, Ibn Thabit, and al-A'mash read (khaliqu) as an active participle attributed to (kulli). (Al-dabbah) is that which moves forward on its feet, and it includes birds. The poet said:

"The crawling of the sandgrouse of al-Batha' in every watering place."

Al-Hut (the fish). In a hadith it is said: "a creature of the sea, like the dharib (a kind of lizard)." The phrase "every creature" (kulla dabbah) includes the one who discerns and others, so the distinction is easily made with "those" (man, the relative pronoun for rational beings) and "that which" (ma, for non-rational beings), when the non-rational is included in the general term. Thus a judgment is applied to it as though all the creatures were discerning. The apparent meaning is that "from water" (min ma') is connected to "created" (khalaqa). The "min" here indicates the starting point, meaning He began its creation from water.

It has been said: since most animals are created from water, either because they are generated from a drop of semen or because they cannot live except by water, the word "every" (kull) is used, treating the majority as if it were the whole. This excludes what was created from light, namely the angels, and what was created from fire, namely the jinn, and what was created from earth, namely Adam. Jesus was created from the Spirit, and many animals are not generated from a drop of semen.

It has also been said that "every creature" is general over all these things, and that the origin of all created beings is water. It is related that the first thing God created was a jewel, and He looked at it with the eye of awe, and it became water. Then from that water He created fire, air, and light. Since the purpose of this verse is to explain the origin of creation, and the first origin was water, He said: "He created every creature from water."

Al-Qaffal said: "from water" is not connected to "created." Rather, it is in the position of a description of "every creature." So the meaning is an announcement that He, exalted is He, created every creature generated from water, that is, generated from water and created by God, exalted is He. Water is indefinite here but definite in "And We made from water every living thing" (al-Anbiya: 30), because the meaning here (p-466) "He created every creature" from a kind of water specific to this creature, or "from water" specifically, which is the drop of semen. Then He varied the created beings from the drop of semen: insects, beasts, and humans, as He said: "watered with one water, yet We make some of them excel others in produce" (al-Ra'd). Here He intends that all kinds of animals are created from this genus, which is the genus of water, because it is the origin, even if intermediaries came between them and it, as it was said: the origin of light, fire, and earth is water.

Crawling on the belly is called walking, either because of its similarity to what follows, the mention of those who walk, or as a metaphor, as they say: "this matter has walked" and "affairs are going well for so-and-so," just as they used the word for lip (mushaffar) for lip and lip for the large lip (jahfalah). Those who walk "on their bellies" are snakes, fish, and the like, and worms and others. "On two legs" are humans and birds, and "on four" are all other land animals, beasts and others. If one is found that has more than four, it was said that its reliance is only on four, and it does not need all of them for its walking. And He mentioned first what is most evident in power and most wondrous, namely that which walks without any instrument, like one who has feet and limbs, then that which walks on two, then that which walks on four. In the codex of Ubayy: "and among them is one that walks on more," thereby generalizing this addition to all animals, but it is not established as Qur'an. Perhaps he cited it not as Qur'an but as an indication that God created those that walk on more than four: such as the spider, the scorpion, the centipede, the creature with forty-four legs, and the one called the ear-creature. Because this kind is rare, it was not mentioned.

"God creates what He wills" is an indication that whatever His will has been directed to create, He brings into being and originates. In this there is a reminder of the multitude of animals, and that just as they differ in manner of walking, they differ in other respects.

And Allah is Knowing of what they do.﴾ ﴿To Allah belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth, and to Allah is the return.﴾ ﴿Have you not seen that Allah drives the clouds, then joins them together, then makes them into a heap, so that you see the rain coming out from within them? And He sends down from the sky mountains [of hail] wherein is hail, and strikes with it whom He wills and averts it from whom He wills. The flash of its lightning nearly takes away the sight.﴾ ﴿Allah alternates the night and the day. Indeed in that is a lesson for those of vision.﴾ ﴿And Allah created every creature from water. Among them are those that walk on their bellies, and among them are those that walk on two legs, and among them are those that walk on four. Allah creates what He wills. Indeed Allah is over all things competent.﴾ ﴿We have certainly sent down verses that make things clear, and Allah guides whom He wills to a straight path.﴾

It has been said: (man) is general for every existent, with rational beings given precedence over non-rational ones, so non-rational beings are included in it, and the meaning of glorification is that their existence indicates that Allah, the Exalted, is exempt from deficiencies and described by the attributes of perfection. It has also been said: the meaning of glorification is exaltation (ta'zim), so from those possessing religion it is by speech and prayer, and from others, among the accountable and inanimate, it is by indication; so this is a common measure between them, namely exaltation. Sufyan said: the glorification of everything is by its obedience and submission.

﴿And the birds in flight﴾ means: they spread their wings in the air for flying. Al-Hasan and others said: it is a metaphor; their glorification is the manifestation of wisdom in them, and so it calls to glorification.

It has been said: the pronoun in (ʿalima) refers to (kullun), and in ﴿ṣalātahu wa-tasbīḥahu﴾ refers to Allah, meaning the prayer of Allah and His glorification which He commanded and guided them to, so this is an attribution of creation to the Creator. Here He intends that all kinds of animals are created from this genus, which is the genus of water, because it is the origin, even if intermediaries came between them and it, as it was said: the origin of light, fire, and earth is water.

Crawling on the belly is called walking, either because of its similarity to what follows, the mention of those who walk, or as a metaphor, as they say: "this matter has walked" and "affairs are going well for so-and-so," just as they used the word for lip (mushaffar) for lip and lip for the large lip (jahfalah). Those who walk "on their bellies" are snakes, fish, and the like, and worms and others. "On two legs" are humans and birds, and "on four" are all other land animals, beasts and others. If one is found that has more than four, it was said that its reliance is only on four, and it does not need all of them for its walking. And He mentioned first what is most evident in power and most wondrous, namely that which walks without any instrument, like one who has feet and limbs, then that which walks on two, then that which walks on four. In the codex of Ubayy: "and among them is one that walks on more," thereby generalizing this addition to all animals, but it is not established as Qur'an. Perhaps he cited it not as Qur'an but as an indication that God created those that walk on more than four: such as the spider, the scorpion, the centipede, the creature with forty-four legs, and the one called the ear-creature. Because this kind is rare, it was not mentioned.

"God creates what He wills" is an indication that whatever His will has been directed to create, He brings into being and originates. In this there is a reminder of the multitude of animals, and that just as they differ in manner of walking, they differ in other respects.

(p. 467) It was revealed, up to His saying ﴿the clear delivery alone﴾, concerning the hypocrites, because of a hypocrite named Bishr. A Jew had a dispute with him and invited him to the Messenger ﷺ, but he invited the Jew to Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf, and so it was revealed.

When the Exalted mentioned the proofs of tawhid (the oneness of God), He followed that with a rebuke of a people who professed faith with their tongues but not with their beliefs.

﴿Then a faction of them turns away﴾ from faith.

﴿after that﴾, i.e., after their saying: "We believe."

﴿And those are not believers﴾. The word "those" refers to the speakers, so faith is negated from all of them. Or it refers to the faction that turns away, so that the faith they had previously was not faith but a mere claim with the tongue, without agreement of the heart.

He used the singular pronoun in ﴿to judge between them﴾, although earlier He had said: "to God and His Messenger," because the Messenger's judgment is from God. Al-Zamakhshari said: "Like your saying: 'Zayd impressed me, and his generosity,' meaning the generosity of Zayd." And from this is the line of verse:

"And a watering place in the desert, in its midst,
I reached it before the sandgrouse and its advance."

He meant: before the advance of the sandgrouse, i.e., before the sandgrouse came to it. End of quote.

Abu Ja'far read (لِيُحْكَمَ) in both places in the passive voice, and (إذا) the second is for sudden occurrence (إذا الفجائية, "idha" of surprise). The answer to the first (إذا), the conditional one, is... This is one of the proofs that the answer (jawab) does not govern the conditional (إذا الشرطية), contrary to most grammarians, because the sudden (إذا الفجائية) is not governed by what follows it in what precedes it. This has been settled in the science of grammar.

The apparent reading is that (إليه) is connected to (يأتوا). The pronoun in (إليه) refers to the Messenger ﷺ. Al-Zamakhshari allowed that (إليه) be connected to (مذعنين), saying: "Because it means hastening in obedience. This is better, because its complement is placed first and it indicates exclusivity." We have refuted him on that, and on what he preferred, namely preparing the governing word for action and detaching it from its action, which is weak. The meaning is that, knowing that with him there is nothing but bitter truth and pure justice, they turn away from being judged by you when the truth weighs upon them, lest you take it from them by your ruling against them in favour of their opponents. But if the right is established for them against an opponent, they all hasten to you and are content only with your judgment.

﴿Is there sickness in their hearts, or have they doubted, or do they fear that God and His Messenger will oppress them?﴾ Here (أم) is disjunctive (منقطعة), and the implied meaning is: "Rather, have they doubted? Rather, do they fear?" It is an interrogation of censure and rebuke, so that they admit to one of these aspects, and with admitting them there is what there is against them. This kind of questioning is used for matters that are apparent, by which one is rebuked and blamed, or by which one is praised. It is very eloquent. From the exaggeration in blame is the saying of the poet:

"Are you not of the people who made a covenant
for baseness and indecency in the ancient age?"

And from the exaggeration in praise is the saying of Jarir:

"Are you not the best of those who rode mounts,
and the most generous of all people in filling bellies?"

The Exalted divided the directions of their aversion from His judgment, saying: ﴿Is there sickness in their hearts﴾, i.e., hypocrisy and lack of sincerity.

﴿or have they doubted﴾, i.e., doubt and suspicion about his prophethood came upon them after they had been sincere.

﴿or do they fear﴾, i.e., there comes upon them the fear of injustice in judgment, so that would be an injustice to them. Then He corrected Himself with "Rather" (بل): ﴿They are the wrongdoers﴾.

ʿAlī, Ibn Abi Ishaq and al-Hasan read (إنما كان قولُ) in the nominative, while the majority read it in the accusative. Al-Zamakhshari said: "The accusative is stronger, because the more defined of the two nouns is more suitable to be the noun of (كان), and ﴿that they say﴾ is more defined, since it has no way of being indefinite, unlike the saying of the believers. This is of the kind of (كان) in His saying: ﴿It is not for God to take a son﴾ [Maryam 19:35] and ﴿It is not for us to speak of this﴾ [al-Nur 24:16]." End of quote. Sibawayh stated explicitly that when the noun and predicate of (كان) are both definite, you have the choice of making whichever you wish the noun and the other the predicate, without any condition or preference in that.

Abu Ja'far, al-Jahdari and Khalid ibn Ilyas read (لِيُحْكَمَ بينهم), in the passive voice. The object that was not named as agent is the pronoun of the verbal noun, i.e., (ليُحكَم) is (هو), i.e., the judgment. The meaning is: "so that judgment may be carried out (بينهم) between them." Similar is their saying: "He brought them together (جمع بينهما)" and "He united them (ألّف بينهما)," and His saying: ﴿and a barrier was placed between them﴾ [Saba' 34:54]. Al-Zamakhshari said: "Similar to it is ﴿Your bond has been severed﴾ [al-An'am 6:94] for the one who read (بينكم) in the accusative, i.e., the severance took place between you." End of quote. What he said about this verse is not definite, since the agent may be a pronoun referring to something before it, and the discussion of that has already passed in its place.

﴿that they say: "We hear and we obey"﴾, i.e., the words of the Messenger, (and we obey), i.e., his command. It is recited: ﴿wa-yattaqhi﴾ with full vowel, with partial vowel (الاختلاس), and with sukun. It is also recited ﴿wa-yattaqhi﴾ with sukun on the qaf and kasra on the ha without full vowel. The grammarian treated the separated predicate of (كان) as if it were joined, so just as it is made sukun in (علِمَ), one says (علْمَ), so also it is made sukun in (يتقه), because it is (تَقِهِ) like (علِمَ). As the poet said:

"Sulayma said: 'Buy us some sawiq (a kind of porridge).'"

He means: "Buy for us (اشترِ لنا)."
