﴿And whoever obeys God﴾ in His obligations, ﴿and His Messenger﴾ in his practices, ﴿and fears God﴾ [Fatir 35:28] regarding what has passed of his sins, ﴿and keeps his duty to Him﴾ regarding what is to come. It is reported that some king asked for a sufficient verse, and this one was recited to him.

When what God revealed about the hypocrites reached them, they came to the Messenger ﷺ and swore by God an oath, up to its end, i.e., (they will certainly go out) from their homes, their wealth and their women. And ﴿if you command them﴾ to jihad, (they will certainly go out) to it. The discussion of ﴿the most solemn of their oaths﴾ [al-An'am 6:109] has passed in al-An'am. The Exalted forbade them from their oath, since He knows that it is not true.

﴿Obedience, known﴾, i.e., known and not doubted, like the obedience of the sincere believers whose inner state matches their outer. Not oaths you swear with your mouths while your hearts are contrary to them. Or: your obedience is an obedience known by speech without action. Or: an obedience that is known, better and more fitting for you than these false oaths; this is said by al-Zamakhshari. Ibn 'Atiyya said: "It admits several meanings:

The first: a prohibition of the false oath, since He knew that their obedience was corrupt and bad, so it is as if He said: 'Do not deceive, for He knows what you are upon.'

The second: do not labour at the oath; obedience that is known, moderate, according to capacity, is better and more useful for you. In this aspect there is a sparing of them.

The third: do not be content with the oath; obedience which is recognised from you and manifest upon you is what is sought from you.

The fourth: do not be content, for your own selves, with pleasing us by swearing; the obedience of God is known, and the striving against His enemy is a clear path." End of quote.

(Obedience) is a subject (مبتدأ, mubtada'), and (known) is an adjective, and the predicate is omitted, i.e., "better and more fitting," or the predicate of an omitted subject, i.e., "our command" or "what is required is: known obedience." Abu al-Baqa' said: "If it were read in the accusative, it would be permissible in Arabic, on the basis of the verbal noun, i.e., obey obedience." End of quote. Zayd ibn 'Ali and al-Yazidi read it in the accusative. Some have assumed the nominative by supposing an implied "let there be" (ولتكن): "known obedience," but this is weak, because the verb is not omitted while the agent remains, unless there is some indication of it, such as "men" after the passive (يُسبَّح), i.e., men glorify Him; or it is answered by a negation, such as "Yes, Zayd," to one who said: "No one came"; or by an interrogation, as in the saying of the poet:

"Has not a messenger come to Umm al-Huwayrith?
Yes, Khalid, if the obstacles do not prevent him."

I.e., Khalid came to her.

﴿Indeed God is All-Aware of what you do﴾, i.e., He is informed of your inner secrets, so He will expose you. He turned from the third person to the second, because that is more forceful in rebuking them.

When He rebuked them by saying that He is informed of their inner secrets, He treated them kindly, and commanded them to obey God and the Messenger, which is a general command for the hypocrites and others.

﴿But if they turn away﴾, i.e., if you turn away.

﴿then upon him is what he has been charged with﴾, i.e., upon the Messenger is what he was charged with, namely the delivery and confronting people with the message and exerting effort in warning them.

﴿and upon you is what you have been charged with﴾, namely hearing and obeying and following the truth. Then He made their guidance conditional upon obeying him, so it does not happen except by obeying him. ﴿And upon the Messenger is only the clear delivery﴾. The discussion of a similar phrase has passed in al-Ma'ida.

It is reported that some of the Companions complained of the hardship of confronting the enemy and the fear they were in, and that they could not lay down their weapons, so there was revealed: ﴿God has promised those among you who believe and do righteous deeds﴾. It is also reported that when some of them said: "No day has come upon us when we were secure and laid down our weapons," he ﷺ said: "You will not wait but a little until a man among you sits in the great assembly, reclining, with no iron weapon with him." Ibn 'Abbas said: "This promise, God promised it to the community of Muhammad ﷺ in the Torah and the Gospel."

The address in (منكم) is to the Messenger and his followers, and (من) is explanatory (للبيان), i.e., those who are you; God promised them that He would make Islam victorious over disbelief, bequeath them the earth, and make them successors. His saying ﴿in the earth﴾ refers to the lands bordering them, which is the Arabian Peninsula; then they conquered the lands of the East and the West, broke the kingdom of the Persian kings, possessed their treasures, and gained mastery over the world. In the authentic collection: "The earth was folded up for me, so I was shown its eastern and western parts, and the dominion of my community will reach what was folded up for me of it." Some scholars said: "For this reason Islam spread widely in the East and the West, more than it spread in the South and the North." (I say): Especially in our time, with the conversion of most of the world in the East, such as the Turkish tribes, and in the West, such as the lands of the Sudan, Takrur and Abyssinia, and the lands of India.

﴿as He made successors of those before them﴾, i.e., the Children of Israel, when He bequeathed to them Egypt and the Levant after the destruction of the tyrants. It was said: it is what happened in the time of David and Solomon, peace be upon them, when the believers were dominant over the earth. It is recited: ﴿as he was made successor﴾ in the passive voice. The lam in ﴿He will surely make them successors﴾ answers an implied oath, i.e., "And He swore, He will surely make them successors," or the promise of God, for its certainty, is treated as an oath, so it is answered with what an oath is answered with. According to the reading in which the object of (وعد) is omitted, the oath is omitted, its object being your succession and the establishment of your religion, and the answer of the omitted oath indicates it. Al-Dahhak said: "This verse includes the caliphate of Abu Bakr, 'Umar, 'Uthman and 'Ali, because they are the people of faith and righteous deeds." And he said: "The caliphate after me is thirty years." End of quote. Included among those who went in their way in justice are those from Quraysh who were made successors, such as 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-Aziz from the Umayyads, and those rightly guided by God among the 'Abbasids.

And He will surely establish for them their religion ﴿ولَيُمَكِّنَنَّ لَهم دِينَهُمُ﴾, meaning He will make it firm and secure by making it manifest, by strengthening its people, and by humbling polytheism and its adherents. The phrase ﴿the religion He has approved for them﴾ ﴿الَّذِي ارْتَضى لَهُمْ﴾ is a sublime description of praise. This community has reached the utmost limit in establishing this religion, through the conquests and the sciences that Allah manifested at their hands, in which they surpassed the entire world from the time of Adam until this Muhammadan community.

The majority (al-Jumhur) read ﴿ولَيُبَدِّلَنَّهُمْ﴾ with the doubled letter (tashdid). Ibn Kathir, Abu Bakr, al-Hasan, and Ibn Muhaysin read it without doubling (takhfif).

Abu al-Aliyah said: When Allah, Mighty and Majestic, made His Messenger ﷺ victorious over the Arabian Peninsula, they laid down their weapons and believed. Then Allah took His Prophet, peace be upon him, and they remained secure. Likewise during the caliphates of Abu Bakr, Umar, and Uthman, until they fell into what they fell into and became ungrateful for the blessing. So Allah brought fear upon them, and they changed, and Allah changed what was with them.

﴿يَعْبُدُونَنِي﴾ (they worship Me). Apparently it is a resumptive clause (isti'naf, a new independent sentence), so it has no place in grammatical parsing (i'rab). It is as if it were said: "What is the matter with them that they are made successors and given security?" Then He said: ﴿They worship Me﴾. This was stated by al-Zamakhshari. Ibn Atiyyah said: ﴿They worship Me﴾ is a resumptive verb, meaning: they are ﴿worshipping Me﴾, and by "resumption" he means the sentence, not the verb alone. Al-Hawfi also said this, adding: It may also be resumptive as a form of praise for them, meaning: they are ﴿worshipping Me﴾.

Al-Zamakhshari also said: If you make it a circumstantial clause (hal) relating to His promise to them, meaning: Allah promised them that while they were worshipping and sincere, then its position is in the accusative case (nasb). He concluded. Al-Hawfi had said this before him. Abu al-Baqa' said: ﴿They worship Me﴾ is a circumstantial clause from the object of ﴿He will surely make them successors﴾ (لَيَسْتَخْلِفَنَّهُمْ), and (لَيُبَدِّلَنَّهم) and (لا يُشْرِكُونَ) (they will not associate anything with Me) is a substitute (badal) for ﴿they worship Me﴾, or a circumstantial clause from the subject in ﴿they worship Me﴾, meaning as monotheists (muwahhidin). He concluded.

Apparently, whenever disbelief (kufr) is used without qualification, it stands opposite to Islam and faith (iman). This is the apparent meaning of the statement of Hudhayfah, who said: Hypocrisy existed in the time of the Prophet ﷺ, and it has gone; nothing remains but disbelief after faith. Ibn Atiyyah said: It is possible that he means the disbelief of these blessings when they occur, and in this case, immorality (fisq) does not exclude one from the religion (millah). It was said that this appeared among the killers of Uthman.

Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿And whoever disbelieves﴾ (ومَن كَفَرَ) means ingratitude for the blessing (kufran al-ni'mah), like His saying: ﴿then it denied the favours of Allah﴾ ﴿فَكَفَرَتْ بِأنْعُمِ اللَّهِ﴾ (an-Nahl 16:112), and ﴿those are the defiantly disobedient﴾ ﴿فَأُولَئِكَ هُمُ الفاسِقُونَ﴾, meaning they are the complete transgressors, since they denied this great blessing.

Apparently, His saying (وأقِيمُوا), "and establish," is a shift (iltifat) from the third person (ghaybah) to the second person (khitab). The address in (مِنكم), "among you," makes this shift good. Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿And establish the prayer﴾ ﴿وأقِيمُوا الصَّلاةَ﴾ is conjoined (ma'tuf) to ﴿Obey Allah and obey the Messenger﴾ ﴿أطِيعُوا اللَّهَ وأطِيعُوا الرَّسُولَ﴾, and it is not far-fetched for a separation to occur between the conjoined element and what it is conjoined to, even if it is long, because the conjoined element is supposed to be other than what it is conjoined to. The obedience to the Messenger is repeated to emphasize its obligation. He concluded.

The majority read (لا تَحْسَبَنَّ), "do not think," with the second-person ta' (khitab). The implied subject is you (أيُّها المُخاطَبُ), the addressee, and the Messenger is not included in it. Some said it is addressed to the Messenger, but this is not good, because such a supposition cannot be conceived of him, peace be upon him.

Hamzah and Ibn Amir read (لا يَحْسَبَنَّ), with the third-person ya' (ghaybah), meaning: let no thinker (hasib) think. The Messenger is not included in "thinker." Some said that the pronoun of the subject refers to the Messenger, because his mention preceded in ﴿Obey the Messenger﴾ ﴿وأطِيعُوا الرَّسُولَ﴾. This was said by Abu Ali and al-Zamakhshari. But this is not good, for the reason we mentioned concerning the ta' reading.

Al-Nahhas said: I know of no one among the grammarians, whether of Basra or Kufa, who does not reject the reading of Hamzah. Some say it is a grammatical error (lahn), because it only takes one object (maf'ul) with (يَحْسَبَنَّ). Among those who said this is Abu Hatim. He concluded. Al-Farra' said: It is weak, but he permitted it by omitting the second object, which is the view of the Basrans, its estimate being: themselves (أنْفُسَهم). (مُعْجِزِينَ), "frustrating," is the second object.

Ali ibn Sulayman said: ﴿Those who disbelieved﴾ ﴿الَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا﴾ is in the accusative position. He said: The meaning would be: let not those who disbelieve think ﴿that they can frustrate [Allah] on earth﴾ ﴿مُعْجِزِينَ في الأرْضِ﴾. The Kufans said: (مُعْجِزِينَ) is the first object and (في الأرْضِ) the second. It was said that this is an error, because the apparent connection of (في الأرْضِ) is with (مُعْجِزِينَ), so it cannot be a second object. Al-Zamakhshari followed the Kufans' view and derived it thus: ﴿frustrating on earth﴾ ﴿مُعْجِزِينَ في الأرْضِ﴾ are the two objects, and the meaning is: let not those who disbelieve think that anyone can frustrate Allah on earth, so that they hope for the like of that. This is a strong and good meaning. He also said: The original would be: let not ﴿those who disbelieve﴾ ﴿الَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا﴾ think them ﴿frustrating﴾ ﴿مُعْجِزِينَ﴾, and then the pronoun that is the first object was omitted. What made this permissible is that the subject and the two objects, being like one thing, are satisfied with mentioning two instead of the third. He concluded. I have already rejected this derivation in Al 'Imran, in his saying: (لا يَحْسَبَنَّ الَّذِينَ يَفْرَحُونَ بِما أتَوْا), "Let not those who rejoice in what they have done think," in the reading of whoever reads with the third-person ya', and makes the subject ﴿those who rejoice﴾ ﴿الَّذِينَ يَفْرَحُونَ﴾ (Al 'Imran 3:188). Its summary is that this is not among the pronouns that are explained by what follows them, so one cannot estimate (لا يَحْسَبَنَّهم), since it is not permitted to say (ظَنَّهُ زَيْدٌ قائِمًا) on the basis of raising Zayd with (ظَنَّهُ).

﴿And their refuge is the Fire﴾ ﴿ومَأْواهُمُ النّارُ﴾. Al-Zamakhshari said: It is conjoined (ma'tuf) to ﴿do not think﴾ ﴿لا تَحْسَبَنَّ﴾, as if it were said: those who disbelieve will not escape Allah, ﴿and their refuge is the Fire﴾ ﴿ومَأْواهُمُ النّارُ﴾. The intended ones are those who swear by Allah with their strongest oaths. He concluded. The author of al-Nazm said: It cannot be that (ومَأْواهُمُ) is connected to His saying ﴿Let not those who disbelieved think they can frustrate [Allah] on earth﴾ ﴿لا تَحْسَبَنَّ الَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا مُعْجِزِينَ في الأرْضِ﴾; rather, they are overpowered, ﴿and their refuge is the Fire﴾ ﴿ومَأْواهُمُ النّارُ﴾. He concluded.

The conjunction was considered unlikely on the ground that ﴿do not think﴾ (لا تَحْسَبَنَّ) is a prohibition, while ﴿and their refuge is the Fire﴾ (ومَأْواهُمُ النّارُ) is a declarative sentence. So in his view it was not appropriate to conjoin a declarative sentence to a prohibitive one, because they are different. This is the position of a group. When al-Zamakhshari sensed this, he said: It is as if it were said: those who disbelieve will not escape Allah, so he interpreted the prohibitive sentence as a declarative one so that the connection would be appropriate. The correct view is that this is not a requirement; rather, it is permitted to conjoin sentences that differ from one another, even if they do not share the same type. This is the view of Sibawayh.

(p. 467) It was revealed, up to His saying ﴿the clear delivery alone﴾, concerning the hypocrites, because of a hypocrite named Bishr. A Jew had a dispute with him and invited him to the Messenger ﷺ, but he invited the Jew to Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf, and so it was revealed.

When the Exalted mentioned the proofs of tawhid (the oneness of God), He followed that with a rebuke of a people who professed faith with their tongues but not with their beliefs.

﴿Then a faction of them turns away﴾ from faith.

﴿after that﴾, i.e., after their saying: "We believe."

﴿And those are not believers﴾. The word "those" refers to the speakers, so faith is negated from all of them. Or it refers to the faction that turns away, so that the faith they had previously was not faith but a mere claim with the tongue, without agreement of the heart.

He used the singular pronoun in ﴿to judge between them﴾, although earlier He had said: "to God and His Messenger," because the Messenger's judgment is from God. Al-Zamakhshari said: "Like your saying: 'Zayd impressed me, and his generosity,' meaning the generosity of Zayd." And from this is the line of verse:

"And a watering place in the desert, in its midst,
I reached it before the sandgrouse and its advance."

He meant: before the advance of the sandgrouse, i.e., before the sandgrouse came to it. End of quote.

Abu Ja'far read (لِيُحْكَمَ) in both places in the passive voice, and (إذا) the second is for sudden occurrence (إذا الفجائية, "idha" of surprise). The answer to the first (إذا), the conditional one, is... This is one of the proofs that the answer (jawab) does not govern the conditional (إذا الشرطية), contrary to most grammarians, because the sudden (إذا الفجائية) is not governed by what follows it in what precedes it. This has been settled in the science of grammar.

The apparent reading is that (إليه) is connected to (يأتوا). The pronoun in (إليه) refers to the Messenger ﷺ. Al-Zamakhshari allowed that (إليه) be connected to (مذعنين), saying: "Because it means hastening in obedience. This is better, because its complement is placed first and it indicates exclusivity." We have refuted him on that, and on what he preferred, namely preparing the governing word for action and detaching it from its action, which is weak. The meaning is that, knowing that with him there is nothing but bitter truth and pure justice, they turn away from being judged by you when the truth weighs upon them, lest you take it from them by your ruling against them in favour of their opponents. But if the right is established for them against an opponent, they all hasten to you and are content only with your judgment.

﴿Is there sickness in their hearts, or have they doubted, or do they fear that God and His Messenger will oppress them?﴾ Here (أم) is disjunctive (منقطعة), and the implied meaning is: "Rather, have they doubted? Rather, do they fear?" It is an interrogation of censure and rebuke, so that they admit to one of these aspects, and with admitting them there is what there is against them. This kind of questioning is used for matters that are apparent, by which one is rebuked and blamed, or by which one is praised. It is very eloquent. From the exaggeration in blame is the saying of the poet:

"Are you not of the people who made a covenant
for baseness and indecency in the ancient age?"

And from the exaggeration in praise is the saying of Jarir:

"Are you not the best of those who rode mounts,
and the most generous of all people in filling bellies?"

The Exalted divided the directions of their aversion from His judgment, saying: ﴿Is there sickness in their hearts﴾, i.e., hypocrisy and lack of sincerity.

﴿or have they doubted﴾, i.e., doubt and suspicion about his prophethood came upon them after they had been sincere.

﴿or do they fear﴾, i.e., there comes upon them the fear of injustice in judgment, so that would be an injustice to them. Then He corrected Himself with "Rather" (بل): ﴿They are the wrongdoers﴾.

ʿAlī, Ibn Abi Ishaq and al-Hasan read (إنما كان قولُ) in the nominative, while the majority read it in the accusative. Al-Zamakhshari said: "The accusative is stronger, because the more defined of the two nouns is more suitable to be the noun of (كان), and ﴿that they say﴾ is more defined, since it has no way of being indefinite, unlike the saying of the believers. This is of the kind of (كان) in His saying: ﴿It is not for God to take a son﴾ [Maryam 19:35] and ﴿It is not for us to speak of this﴾ [al-Nur 24:16]." End of quote. Sibawayh stated explicitly that when the noun and predicate of (كان) are both definite, you have the choice of making whichever you wish the noun and the other the predicate, without any condition or preference in that.

Abu Ja'far, al-Jahdari and Khalid ibn Ilyas read (لِيُحْكَمَ بينهم), in the passive voice. The object that was not named as agent is the pronoun of the verbal noun, i.e., (ليُحكَم) is (هو), i.e., the judgment. The meaning is: "so that judgment may be carried out (بينهم) between them." Similar is their saying: "He brought them together (جمع بينهما)" and "He united them (ألّف بينهما)," and His saying: ﴿and a barrier was placed between them﴾ [Saba' 34:54]. Al-Zamakhshari said: "Similar to it is ﴿Your bond has been severed﴾ [al-An'am 6:94] for the one who read (بينكم) in the accusative, i.e., the severance took place between you." End of quote. What he said about this verse is not definite, since the agent may be a pronoun referring to something before it, and the discussion of that has already passed in its place.

﴿that they say: "We hear and we obey"﴾, i.e., the words of the Messenger, (and we obey), i.e., his command. It is recited: ﴿wa-yattaqhi﴾ with full vowel, with partial vowel (الاختلاس), and with sukun. It is also recited ﴿wa-yattaqhi﴾ with sukun on the qaf and kasra on the ha without full vowel. The grammarian treated the separated predicate of (كان) as if it were joined, so just as it is made sukun in (علِمَ), one says (علْمَ), so also it is made sukun in (يتقه), because it is (تَقِهِ) like (علِمَ). As the poet said:

"Sulayma said: 'Buy us some sawiq (a kind of porridge).'"

He means: "Buy for us (اشترِ لنا)."

﴿And whoever obeys God﴾ in His obligations, ﴿and His Messenger﴾ in his practices, ﴿and fears God﴾ [Fatir 35:28] regarding what has passed of his sins, ﴿and keeps his duty to Him﴾ regarding what is to come. It is reported that some king asked for a sufficient verse, and this one was recited to him.

When what God revealed about the hypocrites reached them, they came to the Messenger ﷺ and swore by God an oath, up to its end, i.e., (they will certainly go out) from their homes, their wealth and their women. And ﴿if you command them﴾ to jihad, (they will certainly go out) to it. The discussion of ﴿the most solemn of their oaths﴾ [al-An'am 6:109] has passed in al-An'am. The Exalted forbade them from their oath, since He knows that it is not true.

﴿Obedience, known﴾, i.e., known and not doubted, like the obedience of the sincere believers whose inner state matches their outer. Not oaths you swear with your mouths while your hearts are contrary to them. Or: your obedience is an obedience known by speech without action. Or: an obedience that is known, better and more fitting for you than these false oaths; this is said by al-Zamakhshari. Ibn 'Atiyya said: "It admits several meanings:

The first: a prohibition of the false oath, since He knew that their obedience was corrupt and bad, so it is as if He said: 'Do not deceive, for He knows what you are upon.'

The second: do not labour at the oath; obedience that is known, moderate, according to capacity, is better and more useful for you. In this aspect there is a sparing of them.

The third: do not be content with the oath; obedience which is recognised from you and manifest upon you is what is sought from you.

The fourth: do not be content, for your own selves, with pleasing us by swearing; the obedience of God is known, and the striving against His enemy is a clear path." End of quote.

(Obedience) is a subject (مبتدأ, mubtada'), and (known) is an adjective, and the predicate is omitted, i.e., "better and more fitting," or the predicate of an omitted subject, i.e., "our command" or "what is required is: known obedience." Abu al-Baqa' said: "If it were read in the accusative, it would be permissible in Arabic, on the basis of the verbal noun, i.e., obey obedience." End of quote. Zayd ibn 'Ali and al-Yazidi read it in the accusative. Some have assumed the nominative by supposing an implied "let there be" (ولتكن): "known obedience," but this is weak, because the verb is not omitted while the agent remains, unless there is some indication of it, such as "men" after the passive (يُسبَّح), i.e., men glorify Him; or it is answered by a negation, such as "Yes, Zayd," to one who said: "No one came"; or by an interrogation, as in the saying of the poet:

"Has not a messenger come to Umm al-Huwayrith?
Yes, Khalid, if the obstacles do not prevent him."

I.e., Khalid came to her.

﴿Indeed God is All-Aware of what you do﴾, i.e., He is informed of your inner secrets, so He will expose you. He turned from the third person to the second, because that is more forceful in rebuking them.

When He rebuked them by saying that He is informed of their inner secrets, He treated them kindly, and commanded them to obey God and the Messenger, which is a general command for the hypocrites and others.

﴿But if they turn away﴾, i.e., if you turn away.

﴿then upon him is what he has been charged with﴾, i.e., upon the Messenger is what he was charged with, namely the delivery and confronting people with the message and exerting effort in warning them.

﴿and upon you is what you have been charged with﴾, namely hearing and obeying and following the truth. Then He made their guidance conditional upon obeying him, so it does not happen except by obeying him. ﴿And upon the Messenger is only the clear delivery﴾. The discussion of a similar phrase has passed in al-Ma'ida.

It is reported that some of the Companions complained of the hardship of confronting the enemy and the fear they were in, and that they could not lay down their weapons, so there was revealed: ﴿God has promised those among you who believe and do righteous deeds﴾. It is also reported that when some of them said: "No day has come upon us when we were secure and laid down our weapons," he ﷺ said: "You will not wait but a little until a man among you sits in the great assembly, reclining, with no iron weapon with him." Ibn 'Abbas said: "This promise, God promised it to the community of Muhammad ﷺ in the Torah and the Gospel."

The address in (منكم) is to the Messenger and his followers, and (من) is explanatory (للبيان), i.e., those who are you; God promised them that He would make Islam victorious over disbelief, bequeath them the earth, and make them successors. His saying ﴿in the earth﴾ refers to the lands bordering them, which is the Arabian Peninsula; then they conquered the lands of the East and the West, broke the kingdom of the Persian kings, possessed their treasures, and gained mastery over the world. In the authentic collection: "The earth was folded up for me, so I was shown its eastern and western parts, and the dominion of my community will reach what was folded up for me of it." Some scholars said: "For this reason Islam spread widely in the East and the West, more than it spread in the South and the North." (I say): Especially in our time, with the conversion of most of the world in the East, such as the Turkish tribes, and in the West, such as the lands of the Sudan, Takrur and Abyssinia, and the lands of India.

﴿as He made successors of those before them﴾, i.e., the Children of Israel, when He bequeathed to them Egypt and the Levant after the destruction of the tyrants. It was said: it is what happened in the time of David and Solomon, peace be upon them, when the believers were dominant over the earth. It is recited: ﴿as he was made successor﴾ in the passive voice. The lam in ﴿He will surely make them successors﴾ answers an implied oath, i.e., "And He swore, He will surely make them successors," or the promise of God, for its certainty, is treated as an oath, so it is answered with what an oath is answered with. According to the reading in which the object of (وعد) is omitted, the oath is omitted, its object being your succession and the establishment of your religion, and the answer of the omitted oath indicates it. Al-Dahhak said: "This verse includes the caliphate of Abu Bakr, 'Umar, 'Uthman and 'Ali, because they are the people of faith and righteous deeds." And he said: "The caliphate after me is thirty years." End of quote. Included among those who went in their way in justice are those from Quraysh who were made successors, such as 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-Aziz from the Umayyads, and those rightly guided by God among the 'Abbasids.

And He will surely establish for them their religion ﴿ولَيُمَكِّنَنَّ لَهم دِينَهُمُ﴾, meaning He will make it firm and secure by making it manifest, by strengthening its people, and by humbling polytheism and its adherents. The phrase ﴿the religion He has approved for them﴾ ﴿الَّذِي ارْتَضى لَهُمْ﴾ is a sublime description of praise. This community has reached the utmost limit in establishing this religion, through the conquests and the sciences that Allah manifested at their hands, in which they surpassed the entire world from the time of Adam until this Muhammadan community.

The majority (al-Jumhur) read ﴿ولَيُبَدِّلَنَّهُمْ﴾ with the doubled letter (tashdid). Ibn Kathir, Abu Bakr, al-Hasan, and Ibn Muhaysin read it without doubling (takhfif).

Abu al-Aliyah said: When Allah, Mighty and Majestic, made His Messenger ﷺ victorious over the Arabian Peninsula, they laid down their weapons and believed. Then Allah took His Prophet, peace be upon him, and they remained secure. Likewise during the caliphates of Abu Bakr, Umar, and Uthman, until they fell into what they fell into and became ungrateful for the blessing. So Allah brought fear upon them, and they changed, and Allah changed what was with them.

﴿يَعْبُدُونَنِي﴾ (they worship Me). Apparently it is a resumptive clause (isti'naf, a new independent sentence), so it has no place in grammatical parsing (i'rab). It is as if it were said: "What is the matter with them that they are made successors and given security?" Then He said: ﴿They worship Me﴾. This was stated by al-Zamakhshari. Ibn Atiyyah said: ﴿They worship Me﴾ is a resumptive verb, meaning: they are ﴿worshipping Me﴾, and by "resumption" he means the sentence, not the verb alone. Al-Hawfi also said this, adding: It may also be resumptive as a form of praise for them, meaning: they are ﴿worshipping Me﴾.

Al-Zamakhshari also said: If you make it a circumstantial clause (hal) relating to His promise to them, meaning: Allah promised them that while they were worshipping and sincere, then its position is in the accusative case (nasb). He concluded. Al-Hawfi had said this before him. Abu al-Baqa' said: ﴿They worship Me﴾ is a circumstantial clause from the object of ﴿He will surely make them successors﴾ (لَيَسْتَخْلِفَنَّهُمْ), and (لَيُبَدِّلَنَّهم) and (لا يُشْرِكُونَ) (they will not associate anything with Me) is a substitute (badal) for ﴿they worship Me﴾, or a circumstantial clause from the subject in ﴿they worship Me﴾, meaning as monotheists (muwahhidin). He concluded.

Apparently, whenever disbelief (kufr) is used without qualification, it stands opposite to Islam and faith (iman). This is the apparent meaning of the statement of Hudhayfah, who said: Hypocrisy existed in the time of the Prophet ﷺ, and it has gone; nothing remains but disbelief after faith. Ibn Atiyyah said: It is possible that he means the disbelief of these blessings when they occur, and in this case, immorality (fisq) does not exclude one from the religion (millah). It was said that this appeared among the killers of Uthman.

Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿And whoever disbelieves﴾ (ومَن كَفَرَ) means ingratitude for the blessing (kufran al-ni'mah), like His saying: ﴿then it denied the favours of Allah﴾ ﴿فَكَفَرَتْ بِأنْعُمِ اللَّهِ﴾ (an-Nahl 16:112), and ﴿those are the defiantly disobedient﴾ ﴿فَأُولَئِكَ هُمُ الفاسِقُونَ﴾, meaning they are the complete transgressors, since they denied this great blessing.

Apparently, His saying (وأقِيمُوا), "and establish," is a shift (iltifat) from the third person (ghaybah) to the second person (khitab). The address in (مِنكم), "among you," makes this shift good. Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿And establish the prayer﴾ ﴿وأقِيمُوا الصَّلاةَ﴾ is conjoined (ma'tuf) to ﴿Obey Allah and obey the Messenger﴾ ﴿أطِيعُوا اللَّهَ وأطِيعُوا الرَّسُولَ﴾, and it is not far-fetched for a separation to occur between the conjoined element and what it is conjoined to, even if it is long, because the conjoined element is supposed to be other than what it is conjoined to. The obedience to the Messenger is repeated to emphasize its obligation. He concluded.

The majority read (لا تَحْسَبَنَّ), "do not think," with the second-person ta' (khitab). The implied subject is you (أيُّها المُخاطَبُ), the addressee, and the Messenger is not included in it. Some said it is addressed to the Messenger, but this is not good, because such a supposition cannot be conceived of him, peace be upon him.

Hamzah and Ibn Amir read (لا يَحْسَبَنَّ), with the third-person ya' (ghaybah), meaning: let no thinker (hasib) think. The Messenger is not included in "thinker." Some said that the pronoun of the subject refers to the Messenger, because his mention preceded in ﴿Obey the Messenger﴾ ﴿وأطِيعُوا الرَّسُولَ﴾. This was said by Abu Ali and al-Zamakhshari. But this is not good, for the reason we mentioned concerning the ta' reading.

Al-Nahhas said: I know of no one among the grammarians, whether of Basra or Kufa, who does not reject the reading of Hamzah. Some say it is a grammatical error (lahn), because it only takes one object (maf'ul) with (يَحْسَبَنَّ). Among those who said this is Abu Hatim. He concluded. Al-Farra' said: It is weak, but he permitted it by omitting the second object, which is the view of the Basrans, its estimate being: themselves (أنْفُسَهم). (مُعْجِزِينَ), "frustrating," is the second object.

Ali ibn Sulayman said: ﴿Those who disbelieved﴾ ﴿الَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا﴾ is in the accusative position. He said: The meaning would be: let not those who disbelieve think ﴿that they can frustrate [Allah] on earth﴾ ﴿مُعْجِزِينَ في الأرْضِ﴾. The Kufans said: (مُعْجِزِينَ) is the first object and (في الأرْضِ) the second. It was said that this is an error, because the apparent connection of (في الأرْضِ) is with (مُعْجِزِينَ), so it cannot be a second object. Al-Zamakhshari followed the Kufans' view and derived it thus: ﴿frustrating on earth﴾ ﴿مُعْجِزِينَ في الأرْضِ﴾ are the two objects, and the meaning is: let not those who disbelieve think that anyone can frustrate Allah on earth, so that they hope for the like of that. This is a strong and good meaning. He also said: The original would be: let not ﴿those who disbelieve﴾ ﴿الَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا﴾ think them ﴿frustrating﴾ ﴿مُعْجِزِينَ﴾, and then the pronoun that is the first object was omitted. What made this permissible is that the subject and the two objects, being like one thing, are satisfied with mentioning two instead of the third. He concluded. I have already rejected this derivation in Al 'Imran, in his saying: (لا يَحْسَبَنَّ الَّذِينَ يَفْرَحُونَ بِما أتَوْا), "Let not those who rejoice in what they have done think," in the reading of whoever reads with the third-person ya', and makes the subject ﴿those who rejoice﴾ ﴿الَّذِينَ يَفْرَحُونَ﴾ (Al 'Imran 3:188). Its summary is that this is not among the pronouns that are explained by what follows them, so one cannot estimate (لا يَحْسَبَنَّهم), since it is not permitted to say (ظَنَّهُ زَيْدٌ قائِمًا) on the basis of raising Zayd with (ظَنَّهُ).

﴿And their refuge is the Fire﴾ ﴿ومَأْواهُمُ النّارُ﴾. Al-Zamakhshari said: It is conjoined (ma'tuf) to ﴿do not think﴾ ﴿لا تَحْسَبَنَّ﴾, as if it were said: those who disbelieve will not escape Allah, ﴿and their refuge is the Fire﴾ ﴿ومَأْواهُمُ النّارُ﴾. The intended ones are those who swear by Allah with their strongest oaths. He concluded. The author of al-Nazm said: It cannot be that (ومَأْواهُمُ) is connected to His saying ﴿Let not those who disbelieved think they can frustrate [Allah] on earth﴾ ﴿لا تَحْسَبَنَّ الَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا مُعْجِزِينَ في الأرْضِ﴾; rather, they are overpowered, ﴿and their refuge is the Fire﴾ ﴿ومَأْواهُمُ النّارُ﴾. He concluded.

The conjunction was considered unlikely on the ground that ﴿do not think﴾ (لا تَحْسَبَنَّ) is a prohibition, while ﴿and their refuge is the Fire﴾ (ومَأْواهُمُ النّارُ) is a declarative sentence. So in his view it was not appropriate to conjoin a declarative sentence to a prohibitive one, because they are different. This is the position of a group. When al-Zamakhshari sensed this, he said: It is as if it were said: those who disbelieve will not escape Allah, so he interpreted the prohibitive sentence as a declarative one so that the connection would be appropriate. The correct view is that this is not a requirement; rather, it is permitted to conjoin sentences that differ from one another, even if they do not share the same type. This is the view of Sibawayh.

(p. 467) It was revealed, up to His saying ﴿the clear delivery alone﴾, concerning the hypocrites, because of a hypocrite named Bishr. A Jew had a dispute with him and invited him to the Messenger ﷺ, but he invited the Jew to Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf, and so it was revealed.

When the Exalted mentioned the proofs of tawhid (the oneness of God), He followed that with a rebuke of a people who professed faith with their tongues but not with their beliefs.

﴿Then a faction of them turns away﴾ from faith.

﴿after that﴾, i.e., after their saying: "We believe."

﴿And those are not believers﴾. The word "those" refers to the speakers, so faith is negated from all of them. Or it refers to the faction that turns away, so that the faith they had previously was not faith but a mere claim with the tongue, without agreement of the heart.

He used the singular pronoun in ﴿to judge between them﴾, although earlier He had said: "to God and His Messenger," because the Messenger's judgment is from God. Al-Zamakhshari said: "Like your saying: 'Zayd impressed me, and his generosity,' meaning the generosity of Zayd." And from this is the line of verse:

"And a watering place in the desert, in its midst,
I reached it before the sandgrouse and its advance."

He meant: before the advance of the sandgrouse, i.e., before the sandgrouse came to it. End of quote.

Abu Ja'far read (لِيُحْكَمَ) in both places in the passive voice, and (إذا) the second is for sudden occurrence (إذا الفجائية, "idha" of surprise). The answer to the first (إذا), the conditional one, is... This is one of the proofs that the answer (jawab) does not govern the conditional (إذا الشرطية), contrary to most grammarians, because the sudden (إذا الفجائية) is not governed by what follows it in what precedes it. This has been settled in the science of grammar.

The apparent reading is that (إليه) is connected to (يأتوا). The pronoun in (إليه) refers to the Messenger ﷺ. Al-Zamakhshari allowed that (إليه) be connected to (مذعنين), saying: "Because it means hastening in obedience. This is better, because its complement is placed first and it indicates exclusivity." We have refuted him on that, and on what he preferred, namely preparing the governing word for action and detaching it from its action, which is weak. The meaning is that, knowing that with him there is nothing but bitter truth and pure justice, they turn away from being judged by you when the truth weighs upon them, lest you take it from them by your ruling against them in favour of their opponents. But if the right is established for them against an opponent, they all hasten to you and are content only with your judgment.

﴿Is there sickness in their hearts, or have they doubted, or do they fear that God and His Messenger will oppress them?﴾ Here (أم) is disjunctive (منقطعة), and the implied meaning is: "Rather, have they doubted? Rather, do they fear?" It is an interrogation of censure and rebuke, so that they admit to one of these aspects, and with admitting them there is what there is against them. This kind of questioning is used for matters that are apparent, by which one is rebuked and blamed, or by which one is praised. It is very eloquent. From the exaggeration in blame is the saying of the poet:

"Are you not of the people who made a covenant
for baseness and indecency in the ancient age?"

And from the exaggeration in praise is the saying of Jarir:

"Are you not the best of those who rode mounts,
and the most generous of all people in filling bellies?"

The Exalted divided the directions of their aversion from His judgment, saying: ﴿Is there sickness in their hearts﴾, i.e., hypocrisy and lack of sincerity.

﴿or have they doubted﴾, i.e., doubt and suspicion about his prophethood came upon them after they had been sincere.

﴿or do they fear﴾, i.e., there comes upon them the fear of injustice in judgment, so that would be an injustice to them. Then He corrected Himself with "Rather" (بل): ﴿They are the wrongdoers﴾.

ʿAlī, Ibn Abi Ishaq and al-Hasan read (إنما كان قولُ) in the nominative, while the majority read it in the accusative. Al-Zamakhshari said: "The accusative is stronger, because the more defined of the two nouns is more suitable to be the noun of (كان), and ﴿that they say﴾ is more defined, since it has no way of being indefinite, unlike the saying of the believers. This is of the kind of (كان) in His saying: ﴿It is not for God to take a son﴾ [Maryam 19:35] and ﴿It is not for us to speak of this﴾ [al-Nur 24:16]." End of quote. Sibawayh stated explicitly that when the noun and predicate of (كان) are both definite, you have the choice of making whichever you wish the noun and the other the predicate, without any condition or preference in that.

Abu Ja'far, al-Jahdari and Khalid ibn Ilyas read (لِيُحْكَمَ بينهم), in the passive voice. The object that was not named as agent is the pronoun of the verbal noun, i.e., (ليُحكَم) is (هو), i.e., the judgment. The meaning is: "so that judgment may be carried out (بينهم) between them." Similar is their saying: "He brought them together (جمع بينهما)" and "He united them (ألّف بينهما)," and His saying: ﴿and a barrier was placed between them﴾ [Saba' 34:54]. Al-Zamakhshari said: "Similar to it is ﴿Your bond has been severed﴾ [al-An'am 6:94] for the one who read (بينكم) in the accusative, i.e., the severance took place between you." End of quote. What he said about this verse is not definite, since the agent may be a pronoun referring to something before it, and the discussion of that has already passed in its place.

﴿that they say: "We hear and we obey"﴾, i.e., the words of the Messenger, (and we obey), i.e., his command. It is recited: ﴿wa-yattaqhi﴾ with full vowel, with partial vowel (الاختلاس), and with sukun. It is also recited ﴿wa-yattaqhi﴾ with sukun on the qaf and kasra on the ha without full vowel. The grammarian treated the separated predicate of (كان) as if it were joined, so just as it is made sukun in (علِمَ), one says (علْمَ), so also it is made sukun in (يتقه), because it is (تَقِهِ) like (علِمَ). As the poet said:

"Sulayma said: 'Buy us some sawiq (a kind of porridge).'"

He means: "Buy for us (اشترِ لنا)."

﴿And whoever obeys God﴾ in His obligations, ﴿and His Messenger﴾ in his practices, ﴿and fears God﴾ [Fatir 35:28] regarding what has passed of his sins, ﴿and keeps his duty to Him﴾ regarding what is to come. It is reported that some king asked for a sufficient verse, and this one was recited to him.

When what God revealed about the hypocrites reached them, they came to the Messenger ﷺ and swore by God an oath, up to its end, i.e., (they will certainly go out) from their homes, their wealth and their women. And ﴿if you command them﴾ to jihad, (they will certainly go out) to it. The discussion of ﴿the most solemn of their oaths﴾ [al-An'am 6:109] has passed in al-An'am. The Exalted forbade them from their oath, since He knows that it is not true.

﴿Obedience, known﴾, i.e., known and not doubted, like the obedience of the sincere believers whose inner state matches their outer. Not oaths you swear with your mouths while your hearts are contrary to them. Or: your obedience is an obedience known by speech without action. Or: an obedience that is known, better and more fitting for you than these false oaths; this is said by al-Zamakhshari. Ibn 'Atiyya said: "It admits several meanings:

The first: a prohibition of the false oath, since He knew that their obedience was corrupt and bad, so it is as if He said: 'Do not deceive, for He knows what you are upon.'

The second: do not labour at the oath; obedience that is known, moderate, according to capacity, is better and more useful for you. In this aspect there is a sparing of them.

The third: do not be content with the oath; obedience which is recognised from you and manifest upon you is what is sought from you.

The fourth: do not be content, for your own selves, with pleasing us by swearing; the obedience of God is known, and the striving against His enemy is a clear path." End of quote.

(Obedience) is a subject (مبتدأ, mubtada'), and (known) is an adjective, and the predicate is omitted, i.e., "better and more fitting," or the predicate of an omitted subject, i.e., "our command" or "what is required is: known obedience." Abu al-Baqa' said: "If it were read in the accusative, it would be permissible in Arabic, on the basis of the verbal noun, i.e., obey obedience." End of quote. Zayd ibn 'Ali and al-Yazidi read it in the accusative. Some have assumed the nominative by supposing an implied "let there be" (ولتكن): "known obedience," but this is weak, because the verb is not omitted while the agent remains, unless there is some indication of it, such as "men" after the passive (يُسبَّح), i.e., men glorify Him; or it is answered by a negation, such as "Yes, Zayd," to one who said: "No one came"; or by an interrogation, as in the saying of the poet:

"Has not a messenger come to Umm al-Huwayrith?
Yes, Khalid, if the obstacles do not prevent him."

I.e., Khalid came to her.

﴿Indeed God is All-Aware of what you do﴾, i.e., He is informed of your inner secrets, so He will expose you. He turned from the third person to the second, because that is more forceful in rebuking them.

When He rebuked them by saying that He is informed of their inner secrets, He treated them kindly, and commanded them to obey God and the Messenger, which is a general command for the hypocrites and others.

﴿But if they turn away﴾, i.e., if you turn away.

﴿then upon him is what he has been charged with﴾, i.e., upon the Messenger is what he was charged with, namely the delivery and confronting people with the message and exerting effort in warning them.

﴿and upon you is what you have been charged with﴾, namely hearing and obeying and following the truth. Then He made their guidance conditional upon obeying him, so it does not happen except by obeying him. ﴿And upon the Messenger is only the clear delivery﴾. The discussion of a similar phrase has passed in al-Ma'ida.

It is reported that some of the Companions complained of the hardship of confronting the enemy and the fear they were in, and that they could not lay down their weapons, so there was revealed: ﴿God has promised those among you who believe and do righteous deeds﴾. It is also reported that when some of them said: "No day has come upon us when we were secure and laid down our weapons," he ﷺ said: "You will not wait but a little until a man among you sits in the great assembly, reclining, with no iron weapon with him." Ibn 'Abbas said: "This promise, God promised it to the community of Muhammad ﷺ in the Torah and the Gospel."

The address in (منكم) is to the Messenger and his followers, and (من) is explanatory (للبيان), i.e., those who are you; God promised them that He would make Islam victorious over disbelief, bequeath them the earth, and make them successors. His saying ﴿in the earth﴾ refers to the lands bordering them, which is the Arabian Peninsula; then they conquered the lands of the East and the West, broke the kingdom of the Persian kings, possessed their treasures, and gained mastery over the world. In the authentic collection: "The earth was folded up for me, so I was shown its eastern and western parts, and the dominion of my community will reach what was folded up for me of it." Some scholars said: "For this reason Islam spread widely in the East and the West, more than it spread in the South and the North." (I say): Especially in our time, with the conversion of most of the world in the East, such as the Turkish tribes, and in the West, such as the lands of the Sudan, Takrur and Abyssinia, and the lands of India.

﴿as He made successors of those before them﴾, i.e., the Children of Israel, when He bequeathed to them Egypt and the Levant after the destruction of the tyrants. It was said: it is what happened in the time of David and Solomon, peace be upon them, when the believers were dominant over the earth. It is recited: ﴿as he was made successor﴾ in the passive voice. The lam in ﴿He will surely make them successors﴾ answers an implied oath, i.e., "And He swore, He will surely make them successors," or the promise of God, for its certainty, is treated as an oath, so it is answered with what an oath is answered with. According to the reading in which the object of (وعد) is omitted, the oath is omitted, its object being your succession and the establishment of your religion, and the answer of the omitted oath indicates it. Al-Dahhak said: "This verse includes the caliphate of Abu Bakr, 'Umar, 'Uthman and 'Ali, because they are the people of faith and righteous deeds." And he said: "The caliphate after me is thirty years." End of quote. Included among those who went in their way in justice are those from Quraysh who were made successors, such as 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-Aziz from the Umayyads, and those rightly guided by God among the 'Abbasids.

And He will surely establish for them their religion ﴿ولَيُمَكِّنَنَّ لَهم دِينَهُمُ﴾, meaning He will make it firm and secure by making it manifest, by strengthening its people, and by humbling polytheism and its adherents. The phrase ﴿the religion He has approved for them﴾ ﴿الَّذِي ارْتَضى لَهُمْ﴾ is a sublime description of praise. This community has reached the utmost limit in establishing this religion, through the conquests and the sciences that Allah manifested at their hands, in which they surpassed the entire world from the time of Adam until this Muhammadan community.

The majority (al-Jumhur) read ﴿ولَيُبَدِّلَنَّهُمْ﴾ with the doubled letter (tashdid). Ibn Kathir, Abu Bakr, al-Hasan, and Ibn Muhaysin read it without doubling (takhfif).

Abu al-Aliyah said: When Allah, Mighty and Majestic, made His Messenger ﷺ victorious over the Arabian Peninsula, they laid down their weapons and believed. Then Allah took His Prophet, peace be upon him, and they remained secure. Likewise during the caliphates of Abu Bakr, Umar, and Uthman, until they fell into what they fell into and became ungrateful for the blessing. So Allah brought fear upon them, and they changed, and Allah changed what was with them.

﴿يَعْبُدُونَنِي﴾ (they worship Me). Apparently it is a resumptive clause (isti'naf, a new independent sentence), so it has no place in grammatical parsing (i'rab). It is as if it were said: "What is the matter with them that they are made successors and given security?" Then He said: ﴿They worship Me﴾. This was stated by al-Zamakhshari. Ibn Atiyyah said: ﴿They worship Me﴾ is a resumptive verb, meaning: they are ﴿worshipping Me﴾, and by "resumption" he means the sentence, not the verb alone. Al-Hawfi also said this, adding: It may also be resumptive as a form of praise for them, meaning: they are ﴿worshipping Me﴾.

Al-Zamakhshari also said: If you make it a circumstantial clause (hal) relating to His promise to them, meaning: Allah promised them that while they were worshipping and sincere, then its position is in the accusative case (nasb). He concluded. Al-Hawfi had said this before him. Abu al-Baqa' said: ﴿They worship Me﴾ is a circumstantial clause from the object of ﴿He will surely make them successors﴾ (لَيَسْتَخْلِفَنَّهُمْ), and (لَيُبَدِّلَنَّهم) and (لا يُشْرِكُونَ) (they will not associate anything with Me) is a substitute (badal) for ﴿they worship Me﴾, or a circumstantial clause from the subject in ﴿they worship Me﴾, meaning as monotheists (muwahhidin). He concluded.

Apparently, whenever disbelief (kufr) is used without qualification, it stands opposite to Islam and faith (iman). This is the apparent meaning of the statement of Hudhayfah, who said: Hypocrisy existed in the time of the Prophet ﷺ, and it has gone; nothing remains but disbelief after faith. Ibn Atiyyah said: It is possible that he means the disbelief of these blessings when they occur, and in this case, immorality (fisq) does not exclude one from the religion (millah). It was said that this appeared among the killers of Uthman.

Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿And whoever disbelieves﴾ (ومَن كَفَرَ) means ingratitude for the blessing (kufran al-ni'mah), like His saying: ﴿then it denied the favours of Allah﴾ ﴿فَكَفَرَتْ بِأنْعُمِ اللَّهِ﴾ (an-Nahl 16:112), and ﴿those are the defiantly disobedient﴾ ﴿فَأُولَئِكَ هُمُ الفاسِقُونَ﴾, meaning they are the complete transgressors, since they denied this great blessing.

Apparently, His saying (وأقِيمُوا), "and establish," is a shift (iltifat) from the third person (ghaybah) to the second person (khitab). The address in (مِنكم), "among you," makes this shift good. Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿And establish the prayer﴾ ﴿وأقِيمُوا الصَّلاةَ﴾ is conjoined (ma'tuf) to ﴿Obey Allah and obey the Messenger﴾ ﴿أطِيعُوا اللَّهَ وأطِيعُوا الرَّسُولَ﴾, and it is not far-fetched for a separation to occur between the conjoined element and what it is conjoined to, even if it is long, because the conjoined element is supposed to be other than what it is conjoined to. The obedience to the Messenger is repeated to emphasize its obligation. He concluded.

The majority read (لا تَحْسَبَنَّ), "do not think," with the second-person ta' (khitab). The implied subject is you (أيُّها المُخاطَبُ), the addressee, and the Messenger is not included in it. Some said it is addressed to the Messenger, but this is not good, because such a supposition cannot be conceived of him, peace be upon him.

Hamzah and Ibn Amir read (لا يَحْسَبَنَّ), with the third-person ya' (ghaybah), meaning: let no thinker (hasib) think. The Messenger is not included in "thinker." Some said that the pronoun of the subject refers to the Messenger, because his mention preceded in ﴿Obey the Messenger﴾ ﴿وأطِيعُوا الرَّسُولَ﴾. This was said by Abu Ali and al-Zamakhshari. But this is not good, for the reason we mentioned concerning the ta' reading.

Al-Nahhas said: I know of no one among the grammarians, whether of Basra or Kufa, who does not reject the reading of Hamzah. Some say it is a grammatical error (lahn), because it only takes one object (maf'ul) with (يَحْسَبَنَّ). Among those who said this is Abu Hatim. He concluded. Al-Farra' said: It is weak, but he permitted it by omitting the second object, which is the view of the Basrans, its estimate being: themselves (أنْفُسَهم). (مُعْجِزِينَ), "frustrating," is the second object.

Ali ibn Sulayman said: ﴿Those who disbelieved﴾ ﴿الَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا﴾ is in the accusative position. He said: The meaning would be: let not those who disbelieve think ﴿that they can frustrate [Allah] on earth﴾ ﴿مُعْجِزِينَ في الأرْضِ﴾. The Kufans said: (مُعْجِزِينَ) is the first object and (في الأرْضِ) the second. It was said that this is an error, because the apparent connection of (في الأرْضِ) is with (مُعْجِزِينَ), so it cannot be a second object. Al-Zamakhshari followed the Kufans' view and derived it thus: ﴿frustrating on earth﴾ ﴿مُعْجِزِينَ في الأرْضِ﴾ are the two objects, and the meaning is: let not those who disbelieve think that anyone can frustrate Allah on earth, so that they hope for the like of that. This is a strong and good meaning. He also said: The original would be: let not ﴿those who disbelieve﴾ ﴿الَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا﴾ think them ﴿frustrating﴾ ﴿مُعْجِزِينَ﴾, and then the pronoun that is the first object was omitted. What made this permissible is that the subject and the two objects, being like one thing, are satisfied with mentioning two instead of the third. He concluded. I have already rejected this derivation in Al 'Imran, in his saying: (لا يَحْسَبَنَّ الَّذِينَ يَفْرَحُونَ بِما أتَوْا), "Let not those who rejoice in what they have done think," in the reading of whoever reads with the third-person ya', and makes the subject ﴿those who rejoice﴾ ﴿الَّذِينَ يَفْرَحُونَ﴾ (Al 'Imran 3:188). Its summary is that this is not among the pronouns that are explained by what follows them, so one cannot estimate (لا يَحْسَبَنَّهم), since it is not permitted to say (ظَنَّهُ زَيْدٌ قائِمًا) on the basis of raising Zayd with (ظَنَّهُ).

﴿And their refuge is the Fire﴾ ﴿ومَأْواهُمُ النّارُ﴾. Al-Zamakhshari said: It is conjoined (ma'tuf) to ﴿do not think﴾ ﴿لا تَحْسَبَنَّ﴾, as if it were said: those who disbelieve will not escape Allah, ﴿and their refuge is the Fire﴾ ﴿ومَأْواهُمُ النّارُ﴾. The intended ones are those who swear by Allah with their strongest oaths. He concluded. The author of al-Nazm said: It cannot be that (ومَأْواهُمُ) is connected to His saying ﴿Let not those who disbelieved think they can frustrate [Allah] on earth﴾ ﴿لا تَحْسَبَنَّ الَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا مُعْجِزِينَ في الأرْضِ﴾; rather, they are overpowered, ﴿and their refuge is the Fire﴾ ﴿ومَأْواهُمُ النّارُ﴾. He concluded.

The conjunction was considered unlikely on the ground that ﴿do not think﴾ (لا تَحْسَبَنَّ) is a prohibition, while ﴿and their refuge is the Fire﴾ (ومَأْواهُمُ النّارُ) is a declarative sentence. So in his view it was not appropriate to conjoin a declarative sentence to a prohibitive one, because they are different. This is the position of a group. When al-Zamakhshari sensed this, he said: It is as if it were said: those who disbelieve will not escape Allah, so he interpreted the prohibitive sentence as a declarative one so that the connection would be appropriate. The correct view is that this is not a requirement; rather, it is permitted to conjoin sentences that differ from one another, even if they do not share the same type. This is the view of Sibawayh.

(p. 467) It was revealed, up to His saying ﴿the clear delivery alone﴾, concerning the hypocrites, because of a hypocrite named Bishr. A Jew had a dispute with him and invited him to the Messenger ﷺ, but he invited the Jew to Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf, and so it was revealed.

When the Exalted mentioned the proofs of tawhid (the oneness of God), He followed that with a rebuke of a people who professed faith with their tongues but not with their beliefs.

﴿Then a faction of them turns away﴾ from faith.

﴿after that﴾, i.e., after their saying: "We believe."

﴿And those are not believers﴾. The word "those" refers to the speakers, so faith is negated from all of them. Or it refers to the faction that turns away, so that the faith they had previously was not faith but a mere claim with the tongue, without agreement of the heart.

He used the singular pronoun in ﴿to judge between them﴾, although earlier He had said: "to God and His Messenger," because the Messenger's judgment is from God. Al-Zamakhshari said: "Like your saying: 'Zayd impressed me, and his generosity,' meaning the generosity of Zayd." And from this is the line of verse:

"And a watering place in the desert, in its midst,
I reached it before the sandgrouse and its advance."

He meant: before the advance of the sandgrouse, i.e., before the sandgrouse came to it. End of quote.

Abu Ja'far read (لِيُحْكَمَ) in both places in the passive voice, and (إذا) the second is for sudden occurrence (إذا الفجائية, "idha" of surprise). The answer to the first (إذا), the conditional one, is... This is one of the proofs that the answer (jawab) does not govern the conditional (إذا الشرطية), contrary to most grammarians, because the sudden (إذا الفجائية) is not governed by what follows it in what precedes it. This has been settled in the science of grammar.

The apparent reading is that (إليه) is connected to (يأتوا). The pronoun in (إليه) refers to the Messenger ﷺ. Al-Zamakhshari allowed that (إليه) be connected to (مذعنين), saying: "Because it means hastening in obedience. This is better, because its complement is placed first and it indicates exclusivity." We have refuted him on that, and on what he preferred, namely preparing the governing word for action and detaching it from its action, which is weak. The meaning is that, knowing that with him there is nothing but bitter truth and pure justice, they turn away from being judged by you when the truth weighs upon them, lest you take it from them by your ruling against them in favour of their opponents. But if the right is established for them against an opponent, they all hasten to you and are content only with your judgment.

﴿Is there sickness in their hearts, or have they doubted, or do they fear that God and His Messenger will oppress them?﴾ Here (أم) is disjunctive (منقطعة), and the implied meaning is: "Rather, have they doubted? Rather, do they fear?" It is an interrogation of censure and rebuke, so that they admit to one of these aspects, and with admitting them there is what there is against them. This kind of questioning is used for matters that are apparent, by which one is rebuked and blamed, or by which one is praised. It is very eloquent. From the exaggeration in blame is the saying of the poet:

"Are you not of the people who made a covenant
for baseness and indecency in the ancient age?"

And from the exaggeration in praise is the saying of Jarir:

"Are you not the best of those who rode mounts,
and the most generous of all people in filling bellies?"

The Exalted divided the directions of their aversion from His judgment, saying: ﴿Is there sickness in their hearts﴾, i.e., hypocrisy and lack of sincerity.

﴿or have they doubted﴾, i.e., doubt and suspicion about his prophethood came upon them after they had been sincere.

﴿or do they fear﴾, i.e., there comes upon them the fear of injustice in judgment, so that would be an injustice to them. Then He corrected Himself with "Rather" (بل): ﴿They are the wrongdoers﴾.

ʿAlī, Ibn Abi Ishaq and al-Hasan read (إنما كان قولُ) in the nominative, while the majority read it in the accusative. Al-Zamakhshari said: "The accusative is stronger, because the more defined of the two nouns is more suitable to be the noun of (كان), and ﴿that they say﴾ is more defined, since it has no way of being indefinite, unlike the saying of the believers. This is of the kind of (كان) in His saying: ﴿It is not for God to take a son﴾ [Maryam 19:35] and ﴿It is not for us to speak of this﴾ [al-Nur 24:16]." End of quote. Sibawayh stated explicitly that when the noun and predicate of (كان) are both definite, you have the choice of making whichever you wish the noun and the other the predicate, without any condition or preference in that.

Abu Ja'far, al-Jahdari and Khalid ibn Ilyas read (لِيُحْكَمَ بينهم), in the passive voice. The object that was not named as agent is the pronoun of the verbal noun, i.e., (ليُحكَم) is (هو), i.e., the judgment. The meaning is: "so that judgment may be carried out (بينهم) between them." Similar is their saying: "He brought them together (جمع بينهما)" and "He united them (ألّف بينهما)," and His saying: ﴿and a barrier was placed between them﴾ [Saba' 34:54]. Al-Zamakhshari said: "Similar to it is ﴿Your bond has been severed﴾ [al-An'am 6:94] for the one who read (بينكم) in the accusative, i.e., the severance took place between you." End of quote. What he said about this verse is not definite, since the agent may be a pronoun referring to something before it, and the discussion of that has already passed in its place.

﴿that they say: "We hear and we obey"﴾, i.e., the words of the Messenger, (and we obey), i.e., his command. It is recited: ﴿wa-yattaqhi﴾ with full vowel, with partial vowel (الاختلاس), and with sukun. It is also recited ﴿wa-yattaqhi﴾ with sukun on the qaf and kasra on the ha without full vowel. The grammarian treated the separated predicate of (كان) as if it were joined, so just as it is made sukun in (علِمَ), one says (علْمَ), so also it is made sukun in (يتقه), because it is (تَقِهِ) like (علِمَ). As the poet said:

"Sulayma said: 'Buy us some sawiq (a kind of porridge).'"

He means: "Buy for us (اشترِ لنا)."

﴿And whoever obeys God﴾ in His obligations, ﴿and His Messenger﴾ in his practices, ﴿and fears God﴾ [Fatir 35:28] regarding what has passed of his sins, ﴿and keeps his duty to Him﴾ regarding what is to come. It is reported that some king asked for a sufficient verse, and this one was recited to him.

When what God revealed about the hypocrites reached them, they came to the Messenger ﷺ and swore by God an oath, up to its end, i.e., (they will certainly go out) from their homes, their wealth and their women. And ﴿if you command them﴾ to jihad, (they will certainly go out) to it. The discussion of ﴿the most solemn of their oaths﴾ [al-An'am 6:109] has passed in al-An'am. The Exalted forbade them from their oath, since He knows that it is not true.

﴿Obedience, known﴾, i.e., known and not doubted, like the obedience of the sincere believers whose inner state matches their outer. Not oaths you swear with your mouths while your hearts are contrary to them. Or: your obedience is an obedience known by speech without action. Or: an obedience that is known, better and more fitting for you than these false oaths; this is said by al-Zamakhshari. Ibn 'Atiyya said: "It admits several meanings:

The first: a prohibition of the false oath, since He knew that their obedience was corrupt and bad, so it is as if He said: 'Do not deceive, for He knows what you are upon.'

The second: do not labour at the oath; obedience that is known, moderate, according to capacity, is better and more useful for you. In this aspect there is a sparing of them.

The third: do not be content with the oath; obedience which is recognised from you and manifest upon you is what is sought from you.

The fourth: do not be content, for your own selves, with pleasing us by swearing; the obedience of God is known, and the striving against His enemy is a clear path." End of quote.

(Obedience) is a subject (مبتدأ, mubtada'), and (known) is an adjective, and the predicate is omitted, i.e., "better and more fitting," or the predicate of an omitted subject, i.e., "our command" or "what is required is: known obedience." Abu al-Baqa' said: "If it were read in the accusative, it would be permissible in Arabic, on the basis of the verbal noun, i.e., obey obedience." End of quote. Zayd ibn 'Ali and al-Yazidi read it in the accusative. Some have assumed the nominative by supposing an implied "let there be" (ولتكن): "known obedience," but this is weak, because the verb is not omitted while the agent remains, unless there is some indication of it, such as "men" after the passive (يُسبَّح), i.e., men glorify Him; or it is answered by a negation, such as "Yes, Zayd," to one who said: "No one came"; or by an interrogation, as in the saying of the poet:

"Has not a messenger come to Umm al-Huwayrith?
Yes, Khalid, if the obstacles do not prevent him."

I.e., Khalid came to her.

﴿Indeed God is All-Aware of what you do﴾, i.e., He is informed of your inner secrets, so He will expose you. He turned from the third person to the second, because that is more forceful in rebuking them.

When He rebuked them by saying that He is informed of their inner secrets, He treated them kindly, and commanded them to obey God and the Messenger, which is a general command for the hypocrites and others.

﴿But if they turn away﴾, i.e., if you turn away.

﴿then upon him is what he has been charged with﴾, i.e., upon the Messenger is what he was charged with, namely the delivery and confronting people with the message and exerting effort in warning them.

﴿and upon you is what you have been charged with﴾, namely hearing and obeying and following the truth. Then He made their guidance conditional upon obeying him, so it does not happen except by obeying him. ﴿And upon the Messenger is only the clear delivery﴾. The discussion of a similar phrase has passed in al-Ma'ida.

It is reported that some of the Companions complained of the hardship of confronting the enemy and the fear they were in, and that they could not lay down their weapons, so there was revealed: ﴿God has promised those among you who believe and do righteous deeds﴾. It is also reported that when some of them said: "No day has come upon us when we were secure and laid down our weapons," he ﷺ said: "You will not wait but a little until a man among you sits in the great assembly, reclining, with no iron weapon with him." Ibn 'Abbas said: "This promise, God promised it to the community of Muhammad ﷺ in the Torah and the Gospel."

The address in (منكم) is to the Messenger and his followers, and (من) is explanatory (للبيان), i.e., those who are you; God promised them that He would make Islam victorious over disbelief, bequeath them the earth, and make them successors. His saying ﴿in the earth﴾ refers to the lands bordering them, which is the Arabian Peninsula; then they conquered the lands of the East and the West, broke the kingdom of the Persian kings, possessed their treasures, and gained mastery over the world. In the authentic collection: "The earth was folded up for me, so I was shown its eastern and western parts, and the dominion of my community will reach what was folded up for me of it." Some scholars said: "For this reason Islam spread widely in the East and the West, more than it spread in the South and the North." (I say): Especially in our time, with the conversion of most of the world in the East, such as the Turkish tribes, and in the West, such as the lands of the Sudan, Takrur and Abyssinia, and the lands of India.

﴿as He made successors of those before them﴾, i.e., the Children of Israel, when He bequeathed to them Egypt and the Levant after the destruction of the tyrants. It was said: it is what happened in the time of David and Solomon, peace be upon them, when the believers were dominant over the earth. It is recited: ﴿as he was made successor﴾ in the passive voice. The lam in ﴿He will surely make them successors﴾ answers an implied oath, i.e., "And He swore, He will surely make them successors," or the promise of God, for its certainty, is treated as an oath, so it is answered with what an oath is answered with. According to the reading in which the object of (وعد) is omitted, the oath is omitted, its object being your succession and the establishment of your religion, and the answer of the omitted oath indicates it. Al-Dahhak said: "This verse includes the caliphate of Abu Bakr, 'Umar, 'Uthman and 'Ali, because they are the people of faith and righteous deeds." And he said: "The caliphate after me is thirty years." End of quote. Included among those who went in their way in justice are those from Quraysh who were made successors, such as 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-Aziz from the Umayyads, and those rightly guided by God among the 'Abbasids.

And He will surely establish for them their religion ﴿ولَيُمَكِّنَنَّ لَهم دِينَهُمُ﴾, meaning He will make it firm and secure by making it manifest, by strengthening its people, and by humbling polytheism and its adherents. The phrase ﴿the religion He has approved for them﴾ ﴿الَّذِي ارْتَضى لَهُمْ﴾ is a sublime description of praise. This community has reached the utmost limit in establishing this religion, through the conquests and the sciences that Allah manifested at their hands, in which they surpassed the entire world from the time of Adam until this Muhammadan community.

The majority (al-Jumhur) read ﴿ولَيُبَدِّلَنَّهُمْ﴾ with the doubled letter (tashdid). Ibn Kathir, Abu Bakr, al-Hasan, and Ibn Muhaysin read it without doubling (takhfif).

Abu al-Aliyah said: When Allah, Mighty and Majestic, made His Messenger ﷺ victorious over the Arabian Peninsula, they laid down their weapons and believed. Then Allah took His Prophet, peace be upon him, and they remained secure. Likewise during the caliphates of Abu Bakr, Umar, and Uthman, until they fell into what they fell into and became ungrateful for the blessing. So Allah brought fear upon them, and they changed, and Allah changed what was with them.

﴿يَعْبُدُونَنِي﴾ (they worship Me). Apparently it is a resumptive clause (isti'naf, a new independent sentence), so it has no place in grammatical parsing (i'rab). It is as if it were said: "What is the matter with them that they are made successors and given security?" Then He said: ﴿They worship Me﴾. This was stated by al-Zamakhshari. Ibn Atiyyah said: ﴿They worship Me﴾ is a resumptive verb, meaning: they are ﴿worshipping Me﴾, and by "resumption" he means the sentence, not the verb alone. Al-Hawfi also said this, adding: It may also be resumptive as a form of praise for them, meaning: they are ﴿worshipping Me﴾.

Al-Zamakhshari also said: If you make it a circumstantial clause (hal) relating to His promise to them, meaning: Allah promised them that while they were worshipping and sincere, then its position is in the accusative case (nasb). He concluded. Al-Hawfi had said this before him. Abu al-Baqa' said: ﴿They worship Me﴾ is a circumstantial clause from the object of ﴿He will surely make them successors﴾ (لَيَسْتَخْلِفَنَّهُمْ), and (لَيُبَدِّلَنَّهم) and (لا يُشْرِكُونَ) (they will not associate anything with Me) is a substitute (badal) for ﴿they worship Me﴾, or a circumstantial clause from the subject in ﴿they worship Me﴾, meaning as monotheists (muwahhidin). He concluded.

Apparently, whenever disbelief (kufr) is used without qualification, it stands opposite to Islam and faith (iman). This is the apparent meaning of the statement of Hudhayfah, who said: Hypocrisy existed in the time of the Prophet ﷺ, and it has gone; nothing remains but disbelief after faith. Ibn Atiyyah said: It is possible that he means the disbelief of these blessings when they occur, and in this case, immorality (fisq) does not exclude one from the religion (millah). It was said that this appeared among the killers of Uthman.

Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿And whoever disbelieves﴾ (ومَن كَفَرَ) means ingratitude for the blessing (kufran al-ni'mah), like His saying: ﴿then it denied the favours of Allah﴾ ﴿فَكَفَرَتْ بِأنْعُمِ اللَّهِ﴾ (an-Nahl 16:112), and ﴿those are the defiantly disobedient﴾ ﴿فَأُولَئِكَ هُمُ الفاسِقُونَ﴾, meaning they are the complete transgressors, since they denied this great blessing.

Apparently, His saying (وأقِيمُوا), "and establish," is a shift (iltifat) from the third person (ghaybah) to the second person (khitab). The address in (مِنكم), "among you," makes this shift good. Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿And establish the prayer﴾ ﴿وأقِيمُوا الصَّلاةَ﴾ is conjoined (ma'tuf) to ﴿Obey Allah and obey the Messenger﴾ ﴿أطِيعُوا اللَّهَ وأطِيعُوا الرَّسُولَ﴾, and it is not far-fetched for a separation to occur between the conjoined element and what it is conjoined to, even if it is long, because the conjoined element is supposed to be other than what it is conjoined to. The obedience to the Messenger is repeated to emphasize its obligation. He concluded.

The majority read (لا تَحْسَبَنَّ), "do not think," with the second-person ta' (khitab). The implied subject is you (أيُّها المُخاطَبُ), the addressee, and the Messenger is not included in it. Some said it is addressed to the Messenger, but this is not good, because such a supposition cannot be conceived of him, peace be upon him.

Hamzah and Ibn Amir read (لا يَحْسَبَنَّ), with the third-person ya' (ghaybah), meaning: let no thinker (hasib) think. The Messenger is not included in "thinker." Some said that the pronoun of the subject refers to the Messenger, because his mention preceded in ﴿Obey the Messenger﴾ ﴿وأطِيعُوا الرَّسُولَ﴾. This was said by Abu Ali and al-Zamakhshari. But this is not good, for the reason we mentioned concerning the ta' reading.

Al-Nahhas said: I know of no one among the grammarians, whether of Basra or Kufa, who does not reject the reading of Hamzah. Some say it is a grammatical error (lahn), because it only takes one object (maf'ul) with (يَحْسَبَنَّ). Among those who said this is Abu Hatim. He concluded. Al-Farra' said: It is weak, but he permitted it by omitting the second object, which is the view of the Basrans, its estimate being: themselves (أنْفُسَهم). (مُعْجِزِينَ), "frustrating," is the second object.

Ali ibn Sulayman said: ﴿Those who disbelieved﴾ ﴿الَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا﴾ is in the accusative position. He said: The meaning would be: let not those who disbelieve think ﴿that they can frustrate [Allah] on earth﴾ ﴿مُعْجِزِينَ في الأرْضِ﴾. The Kufans said: (مُعْجِزِينَ) is the first object and (في الأرْضِ) the second. It was said that this is an error, because the apparent connection of (في الأرْضِ) is with (مُعْجِزِينَ), so it cannot be a second object. Al-Zamakhshari followed the Kufans' view and derived it thus: ﴿frustrating on earth﴾ ﴿مُعْجِزِينَ في الأرْضِ﴾ are the two objects, and the meaning is: let not those who disbelieve think that anyone can frustrate Allah on earth, so that they hope for the like of that. This is a strong and good meaning. He also said: The original would be: let not ﴿those who disbelieve﴾ ﴿الَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا﴾ think them ﴿frustrating﴾ ﴿مُعْجِزِينَ﴾, and then the pronoun that is the first object was omitted. What made this permissible is that the subject and the two objects, being like one thing, are satisfied with mentioning two instead of the third. He concluded. I have already rejected this derivation in Al 'Imran, in his saying: (لا يَحْسَبَنَّ الَّذِينَ يَفْرَحُونَ بِما أتَوْا), "Let not those who rejoice in what they have done think," in the reading of whoever reads with the third-person ya', and makes the subject ﴿those who rejoice﴾ ﴿الَّذِينَ يَفْرَحُونَ﴾ (Al 'Imran 3:188). Its summary is that this is not among the pronouns that are explained by what follows them, so one cannot estimate (لا يَحْسَبَنَّهم), since it is not permitted to say (ظَنَّهُ زَيْدٌ قائِمًا) on the basis of raising Zayd with (ظَنَّهُ).

﴿And their refuge is the Fire﴾ ﴿ومَأْواهُمُ النّارُ﴾. Al-Zamakhshari said: It is conjoined (ma'tuf) to ﴿do not think﴾ ﴿لا تَحْسَبَنَّ﴾, as if it were said: those who disbelieve will not escape Allah, ﴿and their refuge is the Fire﴾ ﴿ومَأْواهُمُ النّارُ﴾. The intended ones are those who swear by Allah with their strongest oaths. He concluded. The author of al-Nazm said: It cannot be that (ومَأْواهُمُ) is connected to His saying ﴿Let not those who disbelieved think they can frustrate [Allah] on earth﴾ ﴿لا تَحْسَبَنَّ الَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا مُعْجِزِينَ في الأرْضِ﴾; rather, they are overpowered, ﴿and their refuge is the Fire﴾ ﴿ومَأْواهُمُ النّارُ﴾. He concluded.

The conjunction was considered unlikely on the ground that ﴿do not think﴾ (لا تَحْسَبَنَّ) is a prohibition, while ﴿and their refuge is the Fire﴾ (ومَأْواهُمُ النّارُ) is a declarative sentence. So in his view it was not appropriate to conjoin a declarative sentence to a prohibitive one, because they are different. This is the position of a group. When al-Zamakhshari sensed this, he said: It is as if it were said: those who disbelieve will not escape Allah, so he interpreted the prohibitive sentence as a declarative one so that the connection would be appropriate. The correct view is that this is not a requirement; rather, it is permitted to conjoin sentences that differ from one another, even if they do not share the same type. This is the view of Sibawayh.

(p. 467) It was revealed, up to His saying ﴿the clear delivery alone﴾, concerning the hypocrites, because of a hypocrite named Bishr. A Jew had a dispute with him and invited him to the Messenger ﷺ, but he invited the Jew to Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf, and so it was revealed.

When the Exalted mentioned the proofs of tawhid (the oneness of God), He followed that with a rebuke of a people who professed faith with their tongues but not with their beliefs.

﴿Then a faction of them turns away﴾ from faith.

﴿after that﴾, i.e., after their saying: "We believe."
