From Ibn 'Abbas: when the verse ﴿And do not consume your wealth among yourselves in falsehood﴾ [al-Baqarah: 188] was revealed, the Muslims became scrupulous about eating with the blind, because he cannot see the place of good food; and with the lame, because he cannot compete for food; and with the sick, because he cannot fully partake of food. So Allah revealed this verse. It is said: they also became scrupulous about eating the food of relatives, so it was revealed permitting all these kinds of food, and making clear that those prohibitions apply to transgression, gambling, what a believer eats from the property of one whose household he dislikes, or by a corrupt transaction, and the like. 'Ubayd Allah ibn 'Abd Allah ibn 'Utba ibn Mas'ud and Ibn al-Musayyab said: when they set out for the campaign and left the people with excuses in their homes and property, they became scrupulous about consuming the property of the absent, so it was revealed permitting them what their need requires from the property of the absent, when the absent has consented to that. Mujahid said: a man would take people with excuses to his house, and finding nothing in it, he would take them to the houses of his relatives, so the people of excuses became scrupulous about that, and it was revealed. It is also said: before the mission, the Arabs and those in Medina avoided eating with people of these excuses, some out of disgust at the place where the blind man's hand moves, some out of the sitting-together with the lame, and some out of the smell of the sick; and these are jahili manners and arrogance. Then it was revealed. This is considered unlikely, for if this were the cause, the construction would have been "there is no blame upon you that you eat with them," and it would not be "there is no blame upon the blind." Some answered that ﴿'ala﴾ means ﴿fi﴾, i.e., "in eating with the blind," but this is very far-fetched. In the book of al-Zahrawi, from Ibn 'Abbas, it is that the people of these excuses became scrupulous about eating with people on account of their excuse, so it was revealed. On all these views, the negation of blame concerns the people of excuse and those after them regarding foods. Al-Hasan and 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Zayd said: the blame negated for the people of excuse concerns sitting out from jihad and other things for which they were granted dispensation, while the blame negated for those after them concerns eating of what has been mentioned; it is separate from what precedes it, since the object of the two kinds of blame differs, even if both share the negation of blame. This view is the apparent one.

He did not mention the houses of children, being content with ﴿your houses﴾, because a man's child is part of him and his ruling is the ruling of himself, and his house is his house. In a hadith: "The best of what a man eats is from his earnings, and his child is from his earnings."

The meaning of ﴿from your houses﴾ is from the houses in which your wives and dependants are. The child is closer than a number of relatives, so if the reason for the dispensation is kinship, the one closest to them has greater claim. Talha read ('immahatikum) with a kasra on the hamza.

﴿Or that whose keys you possess﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: it is a man's agent, who may take from the dates and drink from the milk. Qatada said: the slave, since his property is yours. Mujahid and al-Dahhak said: the storerooms of your houses when you possess their keys. Ibn Jarir said: the disabled who hold authority over houses whose keys have been handed to them. It is also said: an orphan's guardian takes from his property by the measure Allah mentioned: ﴿And whoever is poor, let him eat in accordance with what is reasonable﴾ [al-Nisa': 6], and its keys are in his hand.

The majority read ﴿malaktum﴾ with a fatha on the mim and lam, lightly. Ibn Jubayr read it with a damma on the mim and a kasra on the lam, doubled. The majority read (mafatihahu), the plural of mifth; Ibn Jubayr read (mafatihahu), the plural of miftah; Qatada, Harun, and Abu 'Amr (by report) read (miftahahu) in the singular.

﴿أوْ صَدِيقِكُمْ﴾ It is read with a kasra on the ṣād (صِدِيقِكُمْ), by ittibā‘ (vowel harmonization, making the vowel of one letter match the adjacent one), i.e., following the kasra of the dāl. Ḥumayd al-Khazzāz reported this reading. God joined the close friend (ṣadīq) with pure kinship. It was said to one of them: "Who is more beloved to you, your brother or your friend?" He replied: "I do not love my brother unless he is my friend." Ma‘mar said: I said to Qatāda: "Shall I not drink from this grain?" He said: "You are my friend; so what is this asking of permission?" Ibn ‘Abbās said: "The friend is more emphatic than kinship. Do you not see the plea of the people of Hell: ﴿So we have no intercessors, nor any warm friend﴾ [al-Shu‘arā’: 100], and they did not plead with fathers and mothers." The meaning of ﴿أوْ صَدِيقِكُمْ﴾ is: or the houses of your friends. The word ṣadīq may be used for the singular and the plural, like khalīṭ and qaṭīn. A group of the companions of al-Ḥasan ate from his house while he was absent. When he came, he was pleased and said: "Thus we found them," meaning the senior Companions. A man would enter his friend's house, take from his purse, and free his slave-girl who had allowed him to do so. It is also reported from Ja‘far al-Ṣādiq: "Among the greatness of the sacredness of a friend is that God made him, in intimacy, trust, ease, and dropping formality, in the position of the self, the father, the son, and the brother." Hishām ibn ‘Abd al-Malik said: "I attained what I attained, even the caliphate, and I lacked a friend from whom I felt no shame." The people of knowledge (ahl al-‘ilm) said: "When the apparent circumstance indicates the owner's consent, it takes the place of explicit permission."

﴿جَمِيعًا أوْ أشْتاتًا﴾ is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (ḥāl), meaning gathered together or dispersed. al-Ḍaḥḥāk and Qatāda said: it was revealed concerning a tribe of Kinānah who scrupled that a man should eat alone. Thus they would sit for a meal before a man who could not find anyone to eat with him until evening, and he would be compelled to eat alone. One of the poets said:
"When you prepare the provision, seek for it a companion to eat with me, for I will not eat it alone."
‘Ikrimah said: it concerns a people of the Anṣār who, when a guest came to them, would not eat except with him. It was also said: it concerns people who scrupled to eat all together, for fear that one of them might eat more than another. It was also said: ﴿أوْ صَدِيقِكُمْ﴾ refers only to when he invites you to a wedding feast. It was said: this verse is mansūkh (abrogated, i.e., its ruling has been superseded) by his saying, peace be upon him: "Verily your blood and your property are sacred to you," and by his saying, peace be upon him, in the ḥadīth of Ibn ‘Umar: "No one should milk another's livestock except with his permission," and by God's saying: ﴿Do not enter houses other than your own until you have sought permission and greeted their inhabitants﴾ [al-Nūr: 27], etc.

﴿فَإذا دَخَلْتُمْ بُيُوتًا فَسَلِّمُوا عَلى أنْفُسِكُمْ﴾. Ibn ‘Abbās and al-Nakha‘ī said: the mosques. So greet those in them; if there is no one in them, he should say: "Peace be upon the Messenger of God." It was also said: he says, "Peace be upon you" meaning the angels, then he says, "Peace be upon us and upon the righteous servants of God." Jābir, Ibn ‘Abbās, and ‘Aṭā’ said: the inhabited houses; and they said that one may enter uninhabited ones, and he says, "Peace be upon us and upon the righteous servants of God." Ibn ‘Umar said: empty houses. al-Suddī said: ﴿عَلى أنْفُسِكُمْ﴾ means upon the people of your religion. Qatāda said: upon your families in the houses of your own selves. It was said: the houses of the unbelievers, ﴿so greet one another﴾. al-Zamakhsharī said: ﴿فَإذا دَخَلْتُمْ بُيُوتًا﴾ (p-475) of these houses in order to eat, so begin with greeting their people, who are of your religion and kin.

﴿تَحِيَّةً مِن عِنْدِ اللَّهِ﴾ means: established by His command, prescribed from Him; or because greeting and salutation are a request for safety and a life for the one greeted. He described it as blessed and good, because it is a believer's supplication for a believer, by which increase and good provision from God are hoped for, end of quote. Muqātil said: (blessed) in reward. It was also said: it is blessed with reward. al-Ḍaḥḥāk said: in the greeting are ten good deeds, with mercy twenty, and with blessings thirty.

تَحِيَّةً is in the accusative governed by ﴿فَسَلِّمُوا﴾, because its meaning is "then greet (ḥayyū)," like your saying: "I sat in sitting" (qa‘adtu julūsan).

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 24, verse 58–61 (part 1 of 2):

﴿O you who have believed, let those whom your right hands possess and those who have not yet reached puberty among you ask permission of you at three times: before the prayer of dawn, and when you put aside your clothing at midday, and after the prayer of 'Isha'. These are three times of nakedness (awrat) for you. There is no blame upon you or upon them beyond these, as they circulate among you, some of you attending to others. Thus does Allah make clear to you the verses, and Allah is Knowing and Wise.﴾ ﴿And when the children among you reach puberty, let them ask permission as those before them asked permission. Thus does Allah make clear to you His verses, and Allah is Knowing and Wise.﴾ ﴿And women past child-bearing who have no hope of marriage—there is no blame upon them if they put aside their outer garments without displaying adornment. But to refrain is better for them. And Allah is Hearing and Knowing.﴾ ﴿There is no blame upon the blind, nor upon the lame, nor upon the sick, nor upon yourselves, for eating from your houses, or the houses of your fathers, or the houses of your mothers, or the houses of your brothers, or the houses of your sisters, or the houses of your paternal uncles, or the houses of your paternal aunts, or the houses of your maternal uncles, or the houses of your maternal aunts, or from that whose keys you possess, or from the house of your friend. There is no blame upon you whether you eat together or separately. But when you enter houses, greet one another with a greeting from Allah, blessed and good. Thus does Allah make clear to you the verses, that you may understand.﴾

"It is related that 'Umar sent a young man of the Ansar, called Mudlij, to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and he was sleeping. He knocked on the door and entered, and he awoke and sat up, and something was uncovered of him. 'Umar said: 'I wish that Allah had forbidden our sons and our women from entering upon us at these hours except with permission.' Then he went to the Messenger and found that this verse had been revealed, so he fell down in prostration." (p-٤٧٢) It is also said: it was revealed concerning Asma' bint Abi Marthad. It is said that a large male servant of hers entered upon her at a time she disliked his entering, so she came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and said: "Our servants and our boys enter upon us in states we dislike."

﴿Let them ask permission﴾ is a command, and the apparent meaning is that it is obligatory, but the majority hold it to be recommended (nadb). It is also said that it was abrogated (naskh) when the houses came to have doors; this is related from Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn al-Musayyab. The apparent meaning of ﴿those whom your right hands possess﴾ is general, covering male and female slaves; this is the view of the majority. Ibn 'Umar and others said: male slaves only, not female slaves. Al-Sulami said: female slaves only, not male slaves.

﴿Those who have not yet reached puberty among you﴾ is general to children, whether slaves or free. Al-Hasan, Abu 'Amr (in one narration), and Talha read (al-hulm) with a sukun on the lam, which is the dialect of Tamim. It is also said that ﴿among you﴾ means among the free, whether males or females. The apparent meaning of ﴿three times﴾ is three occasions of seeking permission, because when you strike something three times, nothing is understood from it except three strikes; and the saying of the Prophet (peace be upon him) supports this: "Seeking permission is three." What the majority hold is that the meaning of ﴿three times﴾ is three periods of time, and they took what follows of the mention of those times as an explanation of ﴿three times﴾. This is not necessarily fixed; rather ﴿three times﴾ remains upon its literal meaning.

﴿Before the prayer of dawn﴾, because it is the time of rising from the beds, casting off the garments worn for sleep, and donning the garments of wakefulness, and the sleeper may be uncovered.

﴿And when you put aside your clothing at midday﴾, because it is the time of putting off clothes for the midday rest (qa'ilah), since the heat of the day is at its most intense at that time. Concerning the particle min in ﴿min al-zahira﴾, Abu al-Baqa' said: it is for specification of the kind, meaning that this time is the midday; he said: or it means "because of the heat of midday." And ﴿hina﴾ is conjoined to the position of ﴿min qabli﴾.

﴿And after the prayer of 'Isha'﴾, because it is the time of stripping off the garments of wakefulness and wrapping oneself in the garments of sleep.

﴿Three times of nakedness for you﴾: each of them is called awrah because people's covering and guarding of themselves is disturbed during them. The awrah is a flaw; from it come "a'wara al-faris" (the horseman was exposed) and "a'wara al-makan" (the place was defective), and al-a'war is one whose eye is defective.

Hamza and al-Kisa'i read ﴿thalatha﴾ with the accusative (fatha). They said it is a substitute (badal) for ﴿thalathu 'awrat﴾. Al-Hawfi, al-Zamakhshari, and Abu al-Baqa' estimated it as "times of three nakedness." Ibn 'Atiyya said: it is only valid as a substitute by estimating "times of nakedness," so the qualifying noun is omitted and the qualified noun is put in its place. The rest of the seven read it in the nominative, meaning: they are ﴿three times of nakedness﴾. Al-A'mash read (awarat) with a fatha on the waw, and it has been mentioned that this is the dialect of Hudhayl ibn Mudrika and Banu Tamim; and with the nominative on ﴿thalath﴾.

Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿laysa 'alaykum﴾ may be a clause in the position of a nominative, as a description, and the meaning is: they are ﴿three times of nakedness﴾ specified for seeking permission. But if you read it in the accusative, it has no position, and it is a statement affirming the command to seek permission in those states specifically.

﴿Ba'dahunna﴾ means: after their seeking permission during them; the agent and the preposition bi-fi were omitted, so it is "after their seeking permission," then the verbal noun was omitted. It is also said: ﴿laysa 'alaykum﴾ refers to the slaves, the female slaves, and those who have not reached puberty entering ﴿upon you﴾ without permission; ﴿junah﴾ (blame) is after these three times.

﴿Tawwafuna 'alaykum﴾ means they come and go. It is the predicate of an omitted subject; its estimate is "they are ﴿tawwafuna﴾," i.e., the slaves and the children ﴿circulate upon you﴾, meaning they enter upon you in the homes morning and evening without permission except in those times. As for ﴿ba'dukum 'ala ba'd﴾, they permitted it to be a subject and predicate, but as for the genitive they estimated "a circulating party over some," which is a particular state, so it may not be omitted. Al-Zamakhshari said: it was omitted because ﴿tawwafuna﴾ indicates it, and it may be nominative by an omitted verb whose estimate is "some of you circulate." Ibn 'Atiyya said: ﴿ba'dukum﴾ is a substitute for ﴿tawwafuna﴾, which is not valid; for if he meant a substitute for ﴿tawwafuna﴾ itself, it is not permitted, since the estimate becomes "they are (some of you upon some)," and this meaning is not valid. And if you make it a substitute for the pronoun in ﴿tawwafuna﴾, it is also not valid if the pronoun is estimated as a third-person pronoun for the estimated subject "they," since the estimate becomes "they circulate (some of you upon some)," which is not valid. If you make the estimate "you circulate ﴿upon you, some of you upon some﴾," this is countered by the fact that his saying "upon you" is a substitute, indicating that they are the ones circulated upon, while "you are circulating" indicates they are circulating, so the two conflict. Ibn Abi 'Abla read (tawwafina) with the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal) from the pronoun in ('alayhim). Al-Hasan said: if a man's servant spends the night with him, there is no seeking of permission from him, nor during these three times.

﴿And when the children reach puberty﴾, i.e., from your offspring and relatives, ﴿let them ask permission﴾, i.e., at all times, for before puberty they used to ask permission during the three times.

﴿As those before them asked permission﴾, meaning the adults. It is also said: the grown-up children of a man and his relatives. This indicates that the adult son and brother are like a stranger in this matter. They spoke here about what puberty is by, which is a question mentioned in jurisprudence (fiqh). ﴿Thus﴾ refers to what was mentioned before: the seeking of permission by the slaves and those who have not reached puberty.

When Allah the Exalted commanded women to guard themselves from men and from children who have not reached puberty, during the times that are liable to uncovering their nakedness, He made an exception for ﴿the women past child-bearing﴾, who have grown old and sat aside from desire for them and from being tempted by them. So He said: ﴿And the qawa'id (women past child-bearing)﴾, which is the plural of qa'id, an adjective for females. Ibn al-Sikkit said: a woman qa'id is one who has ceased from menstruation. Ibn Qutayba said: they were so named because after old age they frequently sit. Rabi'a said: it is because they have ceased to be enjoyed, so they have despaired and no hope of husbands remains for them. It is also said: they have ceased from menstruation and pregnancy. And ﴿their garments﴾ means the outer cloak (jilbab), the robe (rida'), the veil above the headscarf (qina'), the wrap above the garments (mula'), or the headscarves (khumur), or the robe and headscarf: these are the views. It is said of a woman when she grows old: "imra'a wad'," i.e., she has set down her headscarf.

﴿Without displaying adornment﴾ means without making a display of adornment so that they may be looked at. The true meaning of tabarruj is displaying what must be concealed; or, "not intending to display themselves by setting aside (garments)"; and many an old woman shows a desire to appear beautiful.

﴿But that they refrain﴾ from setting aside their garments and cover themselves as young women do, is better for them.

﴿And Allah is Hearing﴾ of what every speaker says, ﴿Knowing﴾ of intentions. The mention of these two attributes contains a warning and a threat.

From Ibn 'Abbas: when the verse ﴿And do not consume your wealth among yourselves in falsehood﴾ [al-Baqarah: 188] was revealed, the Muslims became scrupulous about eating with the blind, because he cannot see the place of good food; and with the lame, because he cannot compete for food; and with the sick, because he cannot fully partake of food. So Allah revealed this verse. It is said: they also became scrupulous about eating the food of relatives, so it was revealed permitting all these kinds of food, and making clear that those prohibitions apply to transgression, gambling, what a believer eats from the property of one whose household he dislikes, or by a corrupt transaction, and the like. 'Ubayd Allah ibn 'Abd Allah ibn 'Utba ibn Mas'ud and Ibn al-Musayyab said: when they set out for the campaign and left the people with excuses in their homes and property, they became scrupulous about consuming the property of the absent, so it was revealed permitting them what their need requires from the property of the absent, when the absent has consented to that. Mujahid said: a man would take people with excuses to his house, and finding nothing in it, he would take them to the houses of his relatives, so the people of excuses became scrupulous about that, and it was revealed. It is also said: before the mission, the Arabs and those in Medina avoided eating with people of these excuses, some out of disgust at the place where the blind man's hand moves, some out of the sitting-together with the lame, and some out of the smell of the sick; and these are jahili manners and arrogance. Then it was revealed. This is considered unlikely, for if this were the cause, the construction would have been "there is no blame upon you that you eat with them," and it would not be "there is no blame upon the blind." Some answered that ﴿'ala﴾ means ﴿fi﴾, i.e., "in eating with the blind," but this is very far-fetched. In the book of al-Zahrawi, from Ibn 'Abbas, it is that the people of these excuses became scrupulous about eating with people on account of their excuse, so it was revealed. On all these views, the negation of blame concerns the people of excuse and those after them regarding foods. Al-Hasan and 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Zayd said: the blame negated for the people of excuse concerns sitting out from jihad and other things for which they were granted dispensation, while the blame negated for those after them concerns eating of what has been mentioned; it is separate from what precedes it, since the object of the two kinds of blame differs, even if both share the negation of blame. This view is the apparent one.

He did not mention the houses of children, being content with ﴿your houses﴾, because a man's child is part of him and his ruling is the ruling of himself, and his house is his house. In a hadith: "The best of what a man eats is from his earnings, and his child is from his earnings."

The meaning of ﴿from your houses﴾ is from the houses in which your wives and dependants are. The child is closer than a number of relatives, so if the reason for the dispensation is kinship, the one closest to them has greater claim. Talha read ('immahatikum) with a kasra on the hamza.

﴿Or that whose keys you possess﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: it is a man's agent, who may take from the dates and drink from the milk. Qatada said: the slave, since his property is yours. Mujahid and al-Dahhak said: the storerooms of your houses when you possess their keys. Ibn Jarir said: the disabled who hold authority over houses whose keys have been handed to them. It is also said: an orphan's guardian takes from his property by the measure Allah mentioned: ﴿And whoever is poor, let him eat in accordance with what is reasonable﴾ [al-Nisa': 6], and its keys are in his hand.

The majority read ﴿malaktum﴾ with a fatha on the mim and lam, lightly. Ibn Jubayr read it with a damma on the mim and a kasra on the lam, doubled. The majority read (mafatihahu), the plural of mifth; Ibn Jubayr read (mafatihahu), the plural of miftah; Qatada, Harun, and Abu 'Amr (by report) read (miftahahu) in the singular.

﴿أوْ صَدِيقِكُمْ﴾ It is read with a kasra on the ṣād (صِدِيقِكُمْ), by ittibā‘ (vowel harmonization, making the vowel of one letter match the adjacent one), i.e., following the kasra of the dāl. Ḥumayd al-Khazzāz reported this reading. God joined the close friend (ṣadīq) with pure kinship. It was said to one of them: "Who is more beloved to you, your brother or your friend?" He replied: "I do not love my brother unless he is my friend." Ma‘mar said: I said to Qatāda: "Shall I not drink from this grain?" He said: "You are my friend; so what is this asking of permission?" Ibn ‘Abbās said: "The friend is more emphatic than kinship. Do you not see the plea of the people of Hell: ﴿So we have no intercessors, nor any warm friend﴾ [al-Shu‘arā’: 100], and they did not plead with fathers and mothers." The meaning of ﴿أوْ صَدِيقِكُمْ﴾ is: or the houses of your friends. The word ṣadīq may be used for the singular and the plural, like khalīṭ and qaṭīn. A group of the companions of al-Ḥasan ate from his house while he was absent. When he came, he was pleased and said: "Thus we found them," meaning the senior Companions. A man would enter his friend's house, take from his purse, and free his slave-girl who had allowed him to do so. It is also reported from Ja‘far al-Ṣādiq: "Among the greatness of the sacredness of a friend is that God made him, in intimacy, trust, ease, and dropping formality, in the position of the self, the father, the son, and the brother." Hishām ibn ‘Abd al-Malik said: "I attained what I attained, even the caliphate, and I lacked a friend from whom I felt no shame." The people of knowledge (ahl al-‘ilm) said: "When the apparent circumstance indicates the owner's consent, it takes the place of explicit permission."

﴿جَمِيعًا أوْ أشْتاتًا﴾ is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (ḥāl), meaning gathered together or dispersed. al-Ḍaḥḥāk and Qatāda said: it was revealed concerning a tribe of Kinānah who scrupled that a man should eat alone. Thus they would sit for a meal before a man who could not find anyone to eat with him until evening, and he would be compelled to eat alone. One of the poets said:
"When you prepare the provision, seek for it a companion to eat with me, for I will not eat it alone."
‘Ikrimah said: it concerns a people of the Anṣār who, when a guest came to them, would not eat except with him. It was also said: it concerns people who scrupled to eat all together, for fear that one of them might eat more than another. It was also said: ﴿أوْ صَدِيقِكُمْ﴾ refers only to when he invites you to a wedding feast. It was said: this verse is mansūkh (abrogated, i.e., its ruling has been superseded) by his saying, peace be upon him: "Verily your blood and your property are sacred to you," and by his saying, peace be upon him, in the ḥadīth of Ibn ‘Umar: "No one should milk another's livestock except with his permission," and by God's saying: ﴿Do not enter houses other than your own until you have sought permission and greeted their inhabitants﴾ [al-Nūr: 27], etc.

﴿فَإذا دَخَلْتُمْ بُيُوتًا فَسَلِّمُوا عَلى أنْفُسِكُمْ﴾. Ibn ‘Abbās and al-Nakha‘ī said: the mosques. So greet those in them; if there is no one in them, he should say: "Peace be upon the Messenger of God." It was also said: he says, "Peace be upon you" meaning the angels, then he says, "Peace be upon us and upon the righteous servants of God." Jābir, Ibn ‘Abbās, and ‘Aṭā’ said: the inhabited houses; and they said that one may enter uninhabited ones, and he says, "Peace be upon us and upon the righteous servants of God." Ibn ‘Umar said: empty houses. al-Suddī said: ﴿عَلى أنْفُسِكُمْ﴾ means upon the people of your religion. Qatāda said: upon your families in the houses of your own selves. It was said: the houses of the unbelievers, ﴿so greet one another﴾. al-Zamakhsharī said: ﴿فَإذا دَخَلْتُمْ بُيُوتًا﴾ (p-475) of these houses in order to eat, so begin with greeting their people, who are of your religion and kin.

﴿تَحِيَّةً مِن عِنْدِ اللَّهِ﴾ means: established by His command, prescribed from Him; or because greeting and salutation are a request for safety and a life for the one greeted. He described it as blessed and good, because it is a believer's supplication for a believer, by which increase and good provision from God are hoped for, end of quote. Muqātil said: (blessed) in reward. It was also said: it is blessed with reward. al-Ḍaḥḥāk said: in the greeting are ten good deeds, with mercy twenty, and with blessings thirty.

تَحِيَّةً is in the accusative governed by ﴿فَسَلِّمُوا﴾, because its meaning is "then greet (ḥayyū)," like your saying: "I sat in sitting" (qa‘adtu julūsan).

Ibn 'Atiyya said: ﴿ba'dukum﴾ is a substitute for ﴿tawwafuna﴾, which is not valid; for if he meant a substitute for ﴿tawwafuna﴾ itself, it is not permitted, since the estimate becomes "they are (some of you upon some)," and this meaning is not valid. And if you make it a substitute for the pronoun in ﴿tawwafuna﴾, it is also not valid if the pronoun is estimated as a third-person pronoun for the estimated subject "they," since the estimate becomes "they circulate (some of you upon some)," which is not valid. If you make the estimate "you circulate ﴿upon you, some of you upon some﴾," this is countered by the fact that his saying "upon you" is a substitute, indicating that they are the ones circulated upon, while "you are circulating" indicates they are circulating, so the two conflict. Ibn Abi 'Abla read (tawwafina) with the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal) from the pronoun in ('alayhim). Al-Hasan said: if a man's servant spends the night with him, there is no seeking of permission from him, nor during these three times.

﴿And when the children reach puberty﴾, i.e., from your offspring and relatives, ﴿let them ask permission﴾, i.e., at all times, for before puberty they used to ask permission during the three times.

﴿As those before them asked permission﴾, meaning the adults. It is also said: the grown-up children of a man and his relatives. This indicates that the adult son and brother are like a stranger in this matter. They spoke here about what puberty is by, which is a question mentioned in jurisprudence (fiqh). ﴿Thus﴾ refers to what was mentioned before: the seeking of permission by the slaves and those who have not reached puberty.

When Allah the Exalted commanded women to guard themselves from men and from children who have not reached puberty, during the times that are liable to uncovering their nakedness, He made an exception for ﴿the women past child-bearing﴾, who have grown old and sat aside from desire for them and from being tempted by them. So He said: ﴿And the qawa'id (women past child-bearing)﴾, which is the plural of qa'id, an adjective for females. Ibn al-Sikkit said: a woman qa'id is one who has ceased from menstruation. Ibn Qutayba said: they were so named because after old age they frequently sit. Rabi'a said: it is because they have ceased to be enjoyed, so they have despaired and no hope of husbands remains for them. It is also said: they have ceased from menstruation and pregnancy. And ﴿their garments﴾ means the outer cloak (jilbab), the robe (rida'), the veil above the headscarf (qina'), the wrap above the garments (mula'), or the headscarves (khumur), or the robe and headscarf: these are the views. It is said of a woman when she grows old: "imra'a wad'," i.e., she has set down her headscarf.

﴿Without displaying adornment﴾ means without making a display of adornment so that they may be looked at. The true meaning of tabarruj is displaying what must be concealed; or, "not intending to display themselves by setting aside (garments)"; and many an old woman shows a desire to appear beautiful.

﴿But that they refrain﴾ from setting aside their garments and cover themselves as young women do, is better for them.

﴿And Allah is Hearing﴾ of what every speaker says, ﴿Knowing﴾ of intentions. The mention of these two attributes contains a warning and a threat.

From Ibn 'Abbas: when the verse ﴿And do not consume your wealth among yourselves in falsehood﴾ [al-Baqarah: 188] was revealed, the Muslims became scrupulous about eating with the blind, because he cannot see the place of good food; and with the lame, because he cannot compete for food; and with the sick, because he cannot fully partake of food. So Allah revealed this verse. It is said: they also became scrupulous about eating the food of relatives, so it was revealed permitting all these kinds of food, and making clear that those prohibitions apply to transgression, gambling, what a believer eats from the property of one whose household he dislikes, or by a corrupt transaction, and the like. 'Ubayd Allah ibn 'Abd Allah ibn 'Utba ibn Mas'ud and Ibn al-Musayyab said: when they set out for the campaign and left the people with excuses in their homes and property, they became scrupulous about consuming the property of the absent, so it was revealed permitting them what their need requires from the property of the absent, when the absent has consented to that. Mujahid said: a man would take people with excuses to his house, and finding nothing in it, he would take them to the houses of his relatives, so the people of excuses became scrupulous about that, and it was revealed. It is also said: before the mission, the Arabs and those in Medina avoided eating with people of these excuses, some out of disgust at the place where the blind man's hand moves, some out of the sitting-together with the lame, and some out of the smell of the sick; and these are jahili manners and arrogance. Then it was revealed. This is considered unlikely, for if this were the cause, the construction would have been "there is no blame upon you that you eat with them," and it would not be "there is no blame upon the blind." Some answered that ﴿'ala﴾ means ﴿fi﴾, i.e., "in eating with the blind," but this is very far-fetched. In the book of al-Zahrawi, from Ibn 'Abbas, it is that the people of these excuses became scrupulous about eating with people on account of their excuse, so it was revealed. On all these views, the negation of blame concerns the people of excuse and those after them regarding foods. Al-Hasan and 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Zayd said: the blame negated for the people of excuse concerns sitting out from jihad and other things for which they were granted dispensation, while the blame negated for those after them concerns eating of what has been mentioned; it is separate from what precedes it, since the object of the two kinds of blame differs, even if both share the negation of blame. This view is the apparent one.

He did not mention the houses of children, being content with ﴿your houses﴾, because a man's child is part of him and his ruling is the ruling of himself, and his house is his house. In a hadith: "The best of what a man eats is from his earnings, and his child is from his earnings."

The meaning of ﴿from your houses﴾ is from the houses in which your wives and dependants are. The child is closer than a number of relatives, so if the reason for the dispensation is kinship, the one closest to them has greater claim. Talha read ('immahatikum) with a kasra on the hamza.

﴿Or that whose keys you possess﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: it is a man's agent, who may take from the dates and drink from the milk. Qatada said: the slave, since his property is yours. Mujahid and al-Dahhak said: the storerooms of your houses when you possess their keys. Ibn Jarir said: the disabled who hold authority over houses whose keys have been handed to them. It is also said: an orphan's guardian takes from his property by the measure Allah mentioned: ﴿And whoever is poor, let him eat in accordance with what is reasonable﴾ [al-Nisa': 6], and its keys are in his hand.

The majority read ﴿malaktum﴾ with a fatha on the mim and lam, lightly. Ibn Jubayr read it with a damma on the mim and a kasra on the lam, doubled. The majority read (mafatihahu), the plural of mifth; Ibn Jubayr read (mafatihahu), the plural of miftah; Qatada, Harun, and Abu 'Amr (by report) read (miftahahu) in the singular.

﴿أوْ صَدِيقِكُمْ﴾ It is read with a kasra on the ṣād (صِدِيقِكُمْ), by ittibā‘ (vowel harmonization, making the vowel of one letter match the adjacent one), i.e., following the kasra of the dāl. Ḥumayd al-Khazzāz reported this reading. God joined the close friend (ṣadīq) with pure kinship. It was said to one of them: "Who is more beloved to you, your brother or your friend?" He replied: "I do not love my brother unless he is my friend." Ma‘mar said: I said to Qatāda: "Shall I not drink from this grain?" He said: "You are my friend; so what is this asking of permission?" Ibn ‘Abbās said: "The friend is more emphatic than kinship. Do you not see the plea of the people of Hell: ﴿So we have no intercessors, nor any warm friend﴾ [al-Shu‘arā’: 100], and they did not plead with fathers and mothers." The meaning of ﴿أوْ صَدِيقِكُمْ﴾ is: or the houses of your friends. The word ṣadīq may be used for the singular and the plural, like khalīṭ and qaṭīn. A group of the companions of al-Ḥasan ate from his house while he was absent. When he came, he was pleased and said: "Thus we found them," meaning the senior Companions. A man would enter his friend's house, take from his purse, and free his slave-girl who had allowed him to do so. It is also reported from Ja‘far al-Ṣādiq: "Among the greatness of the sacredness of a friend is that God made him, in intimacy, trust, ease, and dropping formality, in the position of the self, the father, the son, and the brother." Hishām ibn ‘Abd al-Malik said: "I attained what I attained, even the caliphate, and I lacked a friend from whom I felt no shame." The people of knowledge (ahl al-‘ilm) said: "When the apparent circumstance indicates the owner's consent, it takes the place of explicit permission."

﴿جَمِيعًا أوْ أشْتاتًا﴾ is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (ḥāl), meaning gathered together or dispersed. al-Ḍaḥḥāk and Qatāda said: it was revealed concerning a tribe of Kinānah who scrupled that a man should eat alone. Thus they would sit for a meal before a man who could not find anyone to eat with him until evening, and he would be compelled to eat alone. One of the poets said:
"When you prepare the provision, seek for it a companion to eat with me, for I will not eat it alone."
‘Ikrimah said: it concerns a people of the Anṣār who, when a guest came to them, would not eat except with him. It was also said: it concerns people who scrupled to eat all together, for fear that one of them might eat more than another. It was also said: ﴿أوْ صَدِيقِكُمْ﴾ refers only to when he invites you to a wedding feast. It was said: this verse is mansūkh (abrogated, i.e., its ruling has been superseded) by his saying, peace be upon him: "Verily your blood and your property are sacred to you," and by his saying, peace be upon him, in the ḥadīth of Ibn ‘Umar: "No one should milk another's livestock except with his permission," and by God's saying: ﴿Do not enter houses other than your own until you have sought permission and greeted their inhabitants﴾ [al-Nūr: 27], etc.

﴿فَإذا دَخَلْتُمْ بُيُوتًا فَسَلِّمُوا عَلى أنْفُسِكُمْ﴾. Ibn ‘Abbās and al-Nakha‘ī said: the mosques. So greet those in them; if there is no one in them, he should say: "Peace be upon the Messenger of God." It was also said: he says, "Peace be upon you" meaning the angels, then he says, "Peace be upon us and upon the righteous servants of God." Jābir, Ibn ‘Abbās, and ‘Aṭā’ said: the inhabited houses; and they said that one may enter uninhabited ones, and he says, "Peace be upon us and upon the righteous servants of God." Ibn ‘Umar said: empty houses. al-Suddī said: ﴿عَلى أنْفُسِكُمْ﴾ means upon the people of your religion. Qatāda said: upon your families in the houses of your own selves. It was said: the houses of the unbelievers, ﴿so greet one another﴾. al-Zamakhsharī said: ﴿فَإذا دَخَلْتُمْ بُيُوتًا﴾ (p-475) of these houses in order to eat, so begin with greeting their people, who are of your religion and kin.

﴿تَحِيَّةً مِن عِنْدِ اللَّهِ﴾ means: established by His command, prescribed from Him; or because greeting and salutation are a request for safety and a life for the one greeted. He described it as blessed and good, because it is a believer's supplication for a believer, by which increase and good provision from God are hoped for, end of quote. Muqātil said: (blessed) in reward. It was also said: it is blessed with reward. al-Ḍaḥḥāk said: in the greeting are ten good deeds, with mercy twenty, and with blessings thirty.

تَحِيَّةً is in the accusative governed by ﴿فَسَلِّمُوا﴾, because its meaning is "then greet (ḥayyū)," like your saying: "I sat in sitting" (qa‘adtu julūsan).

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 24, verse 58–61 (part 1 of 2):

﴿O you who have believed, let those whom your right hands possess and those who have not yet reached puberty among you ask permission of you at three times: before the prayer of dawn, and when you put aside your clothing at midday, and after the prayer of 'Isha'. These are three times of nakedness (awrat) for you. There is no blame upon you or upon them beyond these, as they circulate among you, some of you attending to others. Thus does Allah make clear to you the verses, and Allah is Knowing and Wise.﴾ ﴿And when the children among you reach puberty, let them ask permission as those before them asked permission. Thus does Allah make clear to you His verses, and Allah is Knowing and Wise.﴾ ﴿And women past child-bearing who have no hope of marriage—there is no blame upon them if they put aside their outer garments without displaying adornment. But to refrain is better for them. And Allah is Hearing and Knowing.﴾ ﴿There is no blame upon the blind, nor upon the lame, nor upon the sick, nor upon yourselves, for eating from your houses, or the houses of your fathers, or the houses of your mothers, or the houses of your brothers, or the houses of your sisters, or the houses of your paternal uncles, or the houses of your paternal aunts, or the houses of your maternal uncles, or the houses of your maternal aunts, or from that whose keys you possess, or from the house of your friend. There is no blame upon you whether you eat together or separately. But when you enter houses, greet one another with a greeting from Allah, blessed and good. Thus does Allah make clear to you the verses, that you may understand.﴾

"It is related that 'Umar sent a young man of the Ansar, called Mudlij, to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and he was sleeping. He knocked on the door and entered, and he awoke and sat up, and something was uncovered of him. 'Umar said: 'I wish that Allah had forbidden our sons and our women from entering upon us at these hours except with permission.' Then he went to the Messenger and found that this verse had been revealed, so he fell down in prostration." (p-٤٧٢) It is also said: it was revealed concerning Asma' bint Abi Marthad. It is said that a large male servant of hers entered upon her at a time she disliked his entering, so she came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and said: "Our servants and our boys enter upon us in states we dislike."

﴿Let them ask permission﴾ is a command, and the apparent meaning is that it is obligatory, but the majority hold it to be recommended (nadb). It is also said that it was abrogated (naskh) when the houses came to have doors; this is related from Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn al-Musayyab. The apparent meaning of ﴿those whom your right hands possess﴾ is general, covering male and female slaves; this is the view of the majority. Ibn 'Umar and others said: male slaves only, not female slaves. Al-Sulami said: female slaves only, not male slaves.

﴿Those who have not yet reached puberty among you﴾ is general to children, whether slaves or free. Al-Hasan, Abu 'Amr (in one narration), and Talha read (al-hulm) with a sukun on the lam, which is the dialect of Tamim. It is also said that ﴿among you﴾ means among the free, whether males or females. The apparent meaning of ﴿three times﴾ is three occasions of seeking permission, because when you strike something three times, nothing is understood from it except three strikes; and the saying of the Prophet (peace be upon him) supports this: "Seeking permission is three." What the majority hold is that the meaning of ﴿three times﴾ is three periods of time, and they took what follows of the mention of those times as an explanation of ﴿three times﴾. This is not necessarily fixed; rather ﴿three times﴾ remains upon its literal meaning.

﴿Before the prayer of dawn﴾, because it is the time of rising from the beds, casting off the garments worn for sleep, and donning the garments of wakefulness, and the sleeper may be uncovered.

﴿And when you put aside your clothing at midday﴾, because it is the time of putting off clothes for the midday rest (qa'ilah), since the heat of the day is at its most intense at that time. Concerning the particle min in ﴿min al-zahira﴾, Abu al-Baqa' said: it is for specification of the kind, meaning that this time is the midday; he said: or it means "because of the heat of midday." And ﴿hina﴾ is conjoined to the position of ﴿min qabli﴾.

﴿And after the prayer of 'Isha'﴾, because it is the time of stripping off the garments of wakefulness and wrapping oneself in the garments of sleep.

﴿Three times of nakedness for you﴾: each of them is called awrah because people's covering and guarding of themselves is disturbed during them. The awrah is a flaw; from it come "a'wara al-faris" (the horseman was exposed) and "a'wara al-makan" (the place was defective), and al-a'war is one whose eye is defective.

Hamza and al-Kisa'i read ﴿thalatha﴾ with the accusative (fatha). They said it is a substitute (badal) for ﴿thalathu 'awrat﴾. Al-Hawfi, al-Zamakhshari, and Abu al-Baqa' estimated it as "times of three nakedness." Ibn 'Atiyya said: it is only valid as a substitute by estimating "times of nakedness," so the qualifying noun is omitted and the qualified noun is put in its place. The rest of the seven read it in the nominative, meaning: they are ﴿three times of nakedness﴾. Al-A'mash read (awarat) with a fatha on the waw, and it has been mentioned that this is the dialect of Hudhayl ibn Mudrika and Banu Tamim; and with the nominative on ﴿thalath﴾.

Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿laysa 'alaykum﴾ may be a clause in the position of a nominative, as a description, and the meaning is: they are ﴿three times of nakedness﴾ specified for seeking permission. But if you read it in the accusative, it has no position, and it is a statement affirming the command to seek permission in those states specifically.

﴿Ba'dahunna﴾ means: after their seeking permission during them; the agent and the preposition bi-fi were omitted, so it is "after their seeking permission," then the verbal noun was omitted. It is also said: ﴿laysa 'alaykum﴾ refers to the slaves, the female slaves, and those who have not reached puberty entering ﴿upon you﴾ without permission; ﴿junah﴾ (blame) is after these three times.

﴿Tawwafuna 'alaykum﴾ means they come and go. It is the predicate of an omitted subject; its estimate is "they are ﴿tawwafuna﴾," i.e., the slaves and the children ﴿circulate upon you﴾, meaning they enter upon you in the homes morning and evening without permission except in those times. As for ﴿ba'dukum 'ala ba'd﴾, they permitted it to be a subject and predicate, but as for the genitive they estimated "a circulating party over some," which is a particular state, so it may not be omitted. Al-Zamakhshari said: it was omitted because ﴿tawwafuna﴾ indicates it, and it may be nominative by an omitted verb whose estimate is "some of you circulate." Ibn 'Atiyya said: ﴿ba'dukum﴾ is a substitute for ﴿tawwafuna﴾, which is not valid; for if he meant a substitute for ﴿tawwafuna﴾ itself, it is not permitted, since the estimate becomes "they are (some of you upon some)," and this meaning is not valid. And if you make it a substitute for the pronoun in ﴿tawwafuna﴾, it is also not valid if the pronoun is estimated as a third-person pronoun for the estimated subject "they," since the estimate becomes "they circulate (some of you upon some)," which is not valid. If you make the estimate "you circulate ﴿upon you, some of you upon some﴾," this is countered by the fact that his saying "upon you" is a substitute, indicating that they are the ones circulated upon, while "you are circulating" indicates they are circulating, so the two conflict. Ibn Abi 'Abla read (tawwafina) with the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal) from the pronoun in ('alayhim). Al-Hasan said: if a man's servant spends the night with him, there is no seeking of permission from him, nor during these three times.

﴿And when the children reach puberty﴾, i.e., from your offspring and relatives, ﴿let them ask permission﴾, i.e., at all times, for before puberty they used to ask permission during the three times.

﴿As those before them asked permission﴾, meaning the adults. It is also said: the grown-up children of a man and his relatives. This indicates that the adult son and brother are like a stranger in this matter. They spoke here about what puberty is by, which is a question mentioned in jurisprudence (fiqh). ﴿Thus﴾ refers to what was mentioned before: the seeking of permission by the slaves and those who have not reached puberty.

When Allah the Exalted commanded women to guard themselves from men and from children who have not reached puberty, during the times that are liable to uncovering their nakedness, He made an exception for ﴿the women past child-bearing﴾, who have grown old and sat aside from desire for them and from being tempted by them. So He said: ﴿And the qawa'id (women past child-bearing)﴾, which is the plural of qa'id, an adjective for females. Ibn al-Sikkit said: a woman qa'id is one who has ceased from menstruation. Ibn Qutayba said: they were so named because after old age they frequently sit. Rabi'a said: it is because they have ceased to be enjoyed, so they have despaired and no hope of husbands remains for them. It is also said: they have ceased from menstruation and pregnancy. And ﴿their garments﴾ means the outer cloak (jilbab), the robe (rida'), the veil above the headscarf (qina'), the wrap above the garments (mula'), or the headscarves (khumur), or the robe and headscarf: these are the views. It is said of a woman when she grows old: "imra'a wad'," i.e., she has set down her headscarf.

﴿Without displaying adornment﴾ means without making a display of adornment so that they may be looked at. The true meaning of tabarruj is displaying what must be concealed; or, "not intending to display themselves by setting aside (garments)"; and many an old woman shows a desire to appear beautiful.

﴿But that they refrain﴾ from setting aside their garments and cover themselves as young women do, is better for them.

﴿And Allah is Hearing﴾ of what every speaker says, ﴿Knowing﴾ of intentions. The mention of these two attributes contains a warning and a threat.

Hishām ibn ‘Abd al-Malik said: "I attained what I attained, even the caliphate, and I lacked a friend from whom I felt no shame." ﴿جَمِيعًا أوْ أشْتاتًا﴾ is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (ḥāl), meaning gathered together or dispersed. al-Ḍaḥḥāk and Qatāda said: it was revealed concerning a tribe of Kinānah who scrupled that a man should eat alone. Thus they would sit for a meal before a man who could not find anyone to eat with him until evening, and he would be compelled to eat alone. One of the poets said:
"When you prepare the provision, seek for it a companion to eat with me, for I will not eat it alone."
‘Ikrimah said: it concerns a people of the Anṣār who, when a guest came to them, would not eat except with him. It was also said: it concerns people who scrupled to eat all together, for fear that one of them might eat more than another. It was also said: ﴿أوْ صَدِيقِكُمْ﴾ refers only to when he invites you to a wedding feast. It was said: this verse is mansūkh (abrogated, i.e., its ruling has been superseded) by his saying, peace be upon him: "Verily your blood and your property are sacred to you," and by his saying, peace be upon him, in the ḥadīth of Ibn ‘Umar: "No one should milk another's livestock except with his permission," and by God's saying: ﴿Do not enter houses other than your own until you have sought permission and greeted their inhabitants﴾ [al-Nūr: 27], etc.

﴿فَإذا دَخَلْتُمْ بُيُوتًا فَسَلِّمُوا عَلى أنْفُسِكُمْ﴾. Ibn ‘Abbās and al-Nakha‘ī said: the mosques. So greet those in them; if there is no one in them, he should say: "Peace be upon the Messenger of God." It was also said: he says, "Peace be upon you" meaning the angels, then he says, "Peace be upon us and upon the righteous servants of God." Jābir, Ibn ‘Abbās, and ‘Aṭā’ said: the inhabited houses; and they said that one may enter uninhabited ones, and he says, "Peace be upon us and upon the righteous servants of God." Ibn ‘Umar said: empty houses. al-Suddī said: ﴿عَلى أنْفُسِكُمْ﴾ means upon the people of your religion. Qatāda said: upon your families in the houses of your own selves. It was said: the houses of the unbelievers, ﴿so greet one another﴾. al-Zamakhsharī said: ﴿فَإذا دَخَلْتُمْ بُيُوتًا﴾ (p-475) of these houses in order to eat, so begin with greeting their people, who are of your religion and kin.

﴿تَحِيَّةً مِن عِنْدِ اللَّهِ﴾ means: established by His command, prescribed from Him; or because greeting and salutation are a request for safety and a life for the one greeted. He described it as blessed and good, because it is a believer's supplication for a believer, by which increase and good provision from God are hoped for, end of quote. Muqātil said: (blessed) in reward. It was also said: it is blessed with reward. al-Ḍaḥḥāk said: in the greeting are ten good deeds, with mercy twenty, and with blessings thirty.

تَحِيَّةً is in the accusative governed by ﴿فَسَلِّمُوا﴾, because its meaning is "then greet (ḥayyū)," like your saying: "I sat in sitting" (qa‘adtu julūsan).

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on Surah 24, verses 62–64 (part 1 of 2):**

﴿The believers are only those who believe in Allah and His Messenger, and when they are with him on a matter of common concern, they do not leave until they have asked his permission. Indeed, those who ask your permission are the ones who believe in Allah and His Messenger. So when they ask your permission for some matter of their own, grant permission to whom you will among them, and ask Allah's forgiveness for them. Indeed, Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.﴾ ﴿Do not make the summoning of the Messenger among you like your summoning of one another. Allah already knows those among you who slip away, concealing themselves. So let those who oppose his command beware lest a trial afflict them or a painful punishment strike them.﴾ ﴿Unquestionably, to Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth. He already knows your state, and on the Day they are returned to Him, He will inform them of what they did. And Allah is Knowing of all things.﴾

When He opened the surah with His saying, ﴿A surah which We have sent down﴾ [al-Nur: 1], and mentioned various kinds of commands and prescribed limits that He had sent down to the Messenger, peace be upon him, He concluded it with what is owed to him, peace be upon him, from his community: following and obeying him, in what serves the interest of Islam, and seeking his permission if any of them has a pressing excuse, and showing him reverence in how they address him. Al-Zamakhshari said: "He, Mighty and Majestic, wanted to show them the gravity of the offence of one who leaves the Messenger of Allah ﷺ without his permission."

﴿When they are with him on a matter of common concern﴾: thus He made not leaving ﴿until they have asked his permission﴾ the third element alongside belief in Allah and belief in His Messenger ﷺ, and He made the two beliefs as though they were the cause for it and its impetus. This is together with introducing the sentence with ﹙innama﹚ ("only"), and the nominative of "the believers" is a mubtada' (subject) whose khabar (predicate) is a relative clause (mawsul) whose complement encompasses the mention of the two beliefs. Then He followed it with what adds to its emphasis and firmness, to the point that He restated it in another style, which is His saying, ﴿Indeed, those who ask your permission are the ones who believe in Allah and His Messenger﴾. He included in it another matter, namely that He made asking permission like the proof of the soundness of the two beliefs, and He alluded to the state of those before them and their slipping away, concealing themselves.

The meaning of His saying, ﴿they do not leave until they have asked his permission﴾, is: they do not leave until they have asked his permission and he grants them permission. Do you not see how He made the matter dependent, after their asking permission, on His will and His permission for whomever he deems right to grant permission to? The "common matter" (al-amr al-jami') is that for which people are gathered, and it is described as "gathering" metaphorically. This is like confronting an enemy, consulting about their affair, banding together to terrify an opponent, or whatever results in an alliance and other such things. And the matter that affects everyone, by its harm or its benefit.

In His saying, ﴿when they are with him on a matter of common concern﴾, there is an indication that it is a weighty affair for which the Messenger of Allah ﷺ must have people of opinion and strength who support him in it, assist him, and benefit from their views, knowledge, and experience in its management. So the departure of one of them in such a situation is something that burdens his heart and disturbs his judgment. Therefore He made it strict for them and restricted the matter of asking permission, even with a clear excuse and the need for it, and the arising of what concerns and affects them. This is His saying, ﴿for some matter of their own﴾. The mention of seeking forgiveness for those who ask permission is evidence that the better and more excellent course is that they do not entertain in their souls the idea of leaving, and do not ask permission for it.

It was said: it was revealed concerning the digging of the trench (al-khandaq), when some people were slipping away without permission. Therefore it is fitting that people be with their leaders and their foremost figures in religion and knowledge, supporting them and not abandoning them in any calamity, and not dispersing from them. The matter of granting permission is delegated to the Imam: if he wills he grants permission, and if he wills he does not grant it, according to what his judgment requires. End of quotation. This is a good interpretation, and the leader of an army (imam al-imara) falls under this category when people are gathered with him for the sake of a religious interest; none of them should leave the gathering except with his permission, since he may have an opinion about the presence of that one who leaves.

Makhul and al-Zuhri said: the Friday prayer is among the "common matters." So if something arises for one who is present that prevents him from attending, such as a sudden nosebleed, he should ask permission until the bad impression of him is removed.

Ibn Sirin said: they used to ask the Imam's permission while he was on the pulpit. When this became frequent, Ziyad said: "Whoever puts his hand on his nose, let him go out without permission." This was in Medina, to the extent that Suhayl ibn Abi Salih had a nosebleed on a Friday and asked the Imam's permission.

Ibn Salam said: it refers to every prayer in which there is a sermon, such as the Friday prayer, the two festivals, and the prayer for rain. Ibn Zayd said: it refers to jihad. Mujahid said: it refers to gathering in obedience to Allah.

It was said: concerning His saying, ﴿grant permission to whom you will among them﴾, what is meant is Umar ibn al-Khattab.

And al-Yamani recited ﴿amrin jami'in﴾ (as an indefinite noun, "a matter of gathering").

﴿Do not make the summoning...﴾: this is addressed to the contemporaries of the Messenger, peace be upon him. Since calling people by their names was the custom of the Bedouins, they were commanded to show reverence to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ by addressing him with the best of forms, such as: "O Messenger of Allah" and "O Prophet of Allah." Do you not see that some of the uncouth among those who had recently converted used to say: "O Muhammad"? In His saying, ﴿like your summoning of one another﴾, there is an indication of the permissibility of that among themselves, since reverence and exaltation in addressing him, peace be upon him, is commanded only for one who calls him, not for one who calls someone else. They used to say: "O Abu al-Qasim," "O Muhammad," and they were forbidden from that. It was also said: He forbade them from delaying and lagging behind when he called them. This is what al-Mubarrad and al-Qaffal chose, and it is supported by ﴿So let those who oppose his command beware﴾. This statement agrees with the context and the arrangement of the verse.

Al-Zamakhshari said: when he needs your gathering with him for a matter and calls you, do not disperse from him except with his permission, and do not equate his summoning with the summoning of one another and your returning from the gathering without the permission of the one who calls. End of quotation. This is close to what came before it. He also said: It is possible that "do not make the summoning of the Messenger" means: his supplication to his Lord should not be like the way your young ones call upon your old, or your poor upon your rich, asking him for a need, so that He may grant it or refuse it; rather, the supplications of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ are heard and answered. End of quotation.

Ibn Abbas said: it is only: "Do not consider the supplication of the Messenger against you to be like the supplication of one of you against another," meaning: his supplication against you is answered, so beware of it. Ibn Atiyya said: The wording of the verse rejects this meaning. End of quotation.

Al-Hasan and Ya'qub, in one narration, recited ﴿nabiyyikum﴾ with an open nun, a kasra on the ba', and a shadda on the ya', instead of ﴿baynakum﴾ as a locative (adverb of place); this is the reading of the majority. The author of al-Lawami' said: "It is the Prophet, peace be upon him, in apposition (badal) to 'the Messenger.' It became an apposition because their definiteness differs: the 'Messenger' is definite by the article, while 'your Prophet' is definite by being a construct with a pronoun, so it has the rank of a proper noun, and it is more definite than the one with the article. Therefore it is not valid to make it an adjective (na't) according to the well-known opinion, since an adjective must be less than or equal to what it modifies in definiteness." Then the author of al-Lawami' said: "It is also permissible for it to be an adjective, since both are definite." It seems contradictory to what he had established in choosing apposition, and it should be permissible to use an adjective, since the "Messenger" has become a proper noun by predominance, like "the House" (al-Bayt) for the Ka'bah, since whatever comes in the Qur'an and the Sunnah with the word "the Messenger" is understood only as Muhammad ﷺ. If that is the case, then both are equal in definiteness.

The meaning of ﴿yatasallalun﴾ is: they withdraw little by little from the group in secret. And "lawadhan" (clinging to one another) means: this one clings to that one, and that one to this one, in such a way that he turns with him wherever he turns, hiding from the Messenger.

Al-Hasan said: ﴿liwadhan﴾ means fleeing from jihad. It was said: concerning the digging of the trench, the hypocrites would leave without permission, while the believers asked permission when they had a need. Mujahid said: ﴿liwadhan﴾ means opposition. He also said: ﴿yatasallalun﴾ means slipping away from the row in battle. It was said: ﴿yatasallalun﴾ means (slipping away) from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, from his Book, and from his remembrance.

﴿Liwadhan﴾ is in the accusative as a verbal noun (masdar) in the position of a circumstantial phrase (hal), meaning: clinging to one another. And ﴿liwadhan﴾ is the verbal noun of "lawadha," whose middle radical is kept sound in the verb, so it remains sound in the verbal noun. If it were the verbal noun of "ladha," it would be "liyadhan," like "qama, qiyaman." Yazid ibn Qutayb recited ﴿lawadhan﴾ with a fatha on the lam. It may be the verbal noun of "ladha," but this was not accepted, since there is no kasra before the waw, so it is like "tafa, tawafan." It may also be the verbal noun of "lawadha," with the fatha on the lam due to the fatha on the waw. "Khalafa" is transitive by itself; you say: "khalaftu amra Zayd" (I opposed Zayd's command), and with "ila" you say: "khalaftu ila kadhā." So His saying ﴿'an amrihi﴾ (from His command) implies that "khalafa" carries the sense of "sadda" (turned away) and "a'rada" (turned aside), so it takes "'an." Ibn Atiyya said: its meaning is that their opposition occurs after His command, as you say: "the rain came after the wind," and "'an" is for what is beyond the thing. Abu Ubayda and al-Akhfash said: "'an" is superfluous, meaning "amrahu" (his command). The apparent meaning is that the command to beware is for obligation, and this is the view of the majority; and the pronoun in "amrihi" refers to Allah. It was also said that it refers to the Messenger. It is recited ﴿yukhallifuna﴾ with the intensive form, meaning: they leave themselves behind after His command.

"Fitnah" (trial) means killing, as also said by Ibn Abbas; or affliction, as said by Mujahid; or disbelief, as said by al-Suddi and Muqatil; or the lavishing of blessings as a gradual trap (istidraj), as said by al-Jarrah; or hardness of heart regarding the recognition of right and wrong, as said by al-Junayd; or a seal upon the hearts, as said by some of them. These statements are given as examples, not as an exhaustive list, and they refer to this world. ﴿Or a painful punishment﴾: it was said it is the punishment of the Hereafter. It was also said it is killing in this world.

﴿Unquestionably, to Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth﴾: this is like an indication of His power over them, and over the accountable person in how He deals with him through recompense, reward and punishment.

﴿He already knows your state﴾: that is, your opposition to the command of Allah and the command of His Messenger. In it is a threat and a warning. The apparent meaning is that it is addressed to the hypocrites. Al-Zamakhshari said: He introduced "qad" to emphasize His knowledge of what they are upon of opposition to the religion and of hypocrisy, and the emphasis on knowledge returns to the emphasis on the warning, because when "qad" enters upon the present tense (mudari') it has the meaning of "rubba" (perhaps, sometimes), so it agrees with "rubba" in its usage for indefiniteness, as in the verse of the poet:

*If he becomes abandoned, the courtyard deserted, perhaps there came after its departure a delegation.*

And like it is the saying of Zuhayr:

*My brother, trustworthy, wine does not ruin his wealth, but rather his gift may ruin the wealth.* End of quotation.

As for the view that "qad" when it enters upon the present tense conveys frequency, this is the saying of some grammarians, and it is not correct. Frequency is understood from the context of speech in praise, and the correct view regarding "rubba" is that it indicates the paucity of a thing or the paucity of its like. If frequency is understood, it is not from "rubba" nor from "qad"; it comes from the context of the speech, and this has been explained in the science of grammar.

The majority recited ﴿yurja'un﴾ in the passive. Ibn Yamar, Ibn Abi Ishaq and Abu Amr recited it in the active. The address shifted from the pronoun of the second person in "antum" to the pronoun of the third person in "yurja'un." It is possible that ﴿ma antum 'alayhi﴾ is a general address, and that "yurja'un" refers to the hypocrites. The apparent meaning is that "wa-yawma" is coordinated with ﴿ma antum 'alayhi﴾, so its case is that of the object (mansub mafʿul). Ibn 'Atiyya said: It is possible that the preposing and the manifest knowledge are for you, or something similar: "on the Day," so that the accusative is the accusative of an adverb of time (zarf).

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 24, verse 62–64 (part 2 of 2):

Al-habaʾ (dust particles): Abu ʿUbayda and al-Zajjaj said: it is like dust, which enters the window (kuwwa) together with the sunlight. Ibn ʿArafa said: al-habwa and al-habaʾ are fine dust. Al-Jawhari said: it is said of it, when it rises, habā yahbū habwan, and I caused it to rise, ahbaytuhu ihbaʾan. It was also said: it is the sparks flying from fire when it blazes.

Al-nathr: scattering.

Al-ʿadd (biting): the impact of the teeth on the thing bitten, with force. Its verb follows the pattern faʿila with a kasra on the ʿayn, but al-Kisaʾi related ʿadadtu with a fatha on the ʿayn of the word.

Fulan: a metaphor for the knowledge of whoever has understanding.

Al-jumla (the whole) of speech: it is the gathered whole, not the dispersed.

Al-tartil: the successive articulation of words, with a brief pause between them, from their saying: thaghrun murattal, i.e., a mouth with well-separated teeth (mufallaj al-asnan).

Al-subat: rest. From it comes the day of Saturday (yawm al-sabt), because of the custom of resting on it. It is said of the sick person when he is relieved from the fatigue of his illness: masbut. Abu Muslim said this. Al-Zamakhshari said: al-subat is death, and al-masbut is the dead, because he is cut off from life.

Maraja: Ibn ʿArafa said: it mixed. Maraja al-amr: it became mixed up and disturbed. It was also said: maraja and amraja: he let flow. Maraja is the dialect of the Hijaz, and amraja is the dialect of Najd.

Al-ʿadhb: the sweet. Al-furat: that which reaches the utmost in sweetness.

Al-milh: the salty. Al-ujaj: that which reaches the utmost in saltiness. It was also said: the bitter. It was also said: the hot.

Al-sihr (in-laws): Al-Khalil said: for the people of a woman's household only the term ṣihr is used, and for the people of a man's household only the term khitan is used, though some Arabs make them all ṣihr.

Al-siraj: the sun.

Al-hawn: gentleness and softness.

Al-ghurfa: the upper room; every high building is a ghurfa.

ʿabaʾ, from al-ʿibʾ, which is the heavy burden. It is said: ʿabaʾtu al-jaysh, with the light and the heavy form, meaning I prepared the army for fighting. It is also said: ma ʿabaʾtu bihi, i.e., I did not regard it as worthy of account, like your saying: ma ikturathtu bihi (I did not care for it).

﴿The believers are only those who believe in Allah and His Messenger, and when they are with him on a matter of common concern, they do not leave until they have asked his permission. Indeed, Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.﴾ ﴿Do not make the summoning of the Messenger among you like your summoning of one another. Allah already knows those among you who slip away, concealing themselves. So let those who oppose his command beware lest a trial afflict them or a painful punishment strike them.﴾ ﴿Unquestionably, to Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth. When He opened the surah with His saying, ﴿A surah which We have sent down﴾ [al-Nur: 1], and mentioned various kinds of commands and prescribed limits that He had sent down to the Messenger, peace be upon him, He concluded it with what is owed to him, peace be upon him, from his community: following and obeying him, in what serves the interest of Islam, and seeking his permission if any of them has a pressing excuse, and showing him reverence in how they address him. Al-Zamakhshari said: "He, Mighty and Majestic, wanted to show them the gravity of the offence of one who leaves the Messenger of Allah ﷺ without his permission."

﴿When they are with him on a matter of common concern﴾: thus He made not leaving ﴿until they have asked his permission﴾ the third element alongside belief in Allah and belief in His Messenger ﷺ, and He made the two beliefs as though they were the cause for it and its impetus. This is together with introducing the sentence with ﹙innama﹚ ("only"), and the nominative of "the believers" is a mubtada' (subject) whose khabar (predicate) is a relative clause (mawsul) whose complement encompasses the mention of the two beliefs. Then He followed it with what adds to its emphasis and firmness, to the point that He restated it in another style, which is His saying, ﴿Indeed, those who ask your permission are the ones who believe in Allah and His Messenger﴾. He included in it another matter, namely that He made asking permission like the proof of the soundness of the two beliefs, and He alluded to the state of those before them and their slipping away, concealing themselves.

The meaning of His saying, ﴿they do not leave until they have asked his permission﴾, is: they do not leave until they have asked his permission and he grants them permission. Do you not see how He made the matter dependent, after their asking permission, on His will and His permission for whomever he deems right to grant permission to? The "common matter" (al-amr al-jami') is that for which people are gathered, and it is described as "gathering" metaphorically. This is like confronting an enemy, consulting about their affair, banding together to terrify an opponent, or whatever results in an alliance and other such things. And the matter that affects everyone, by its harm or its benefit.

In His saying, ﴿when they are with him on a matter of common concern﴾, there is an indication that it is a weighty affair for which the Messenger of Allah ﷺ must have people of opinion and strength who support him in it, assist him, and benefit from their views, knowledge, and experience in its management. So the departure of one of them in such a situation is something that burdens his heart and disturbs his judgment. Therefore He made it strict for them and restricted the matter of asking permission, even with a clear excuse and the need for it, and the arising of what concerns and affects them. This is His saying, ﴿for some matter of their own﴾. The mention of seeking forgiveness for those who ask permission is evidence that the better and more excellent course is that they do not entertain in their souls the idea of leaving, and do not ask permission for it.

It was said: it was revealed concerning the digging of the trench (al-khandaq), when some people were slipping away without permission. Therefore it is fitting that people be with their leaders and their foremost figures in religion and knowledge, supporting them and not abandoning them in any calamity, and not dispersing from them. The matter of granting permission is delegated to the Imam: if he wills he grants permission, and if he wills he does not grant it, according to what his judgment requires. End of quotation. This is a good interpretation, and the leader of an army (imam al-imara) falls under this category when people are gathered with him for the sake of a religious interest; none of them should leave the gathering except with his permission, since he may have an opinion about the presence of that one who leaves.

Makhul and al-Zuhri said: the Friday prayer is among the "common matters." So if something arises for one who is present that prevents him from attending, such as a sudden nosebleed, he should ask permission until the bad impression of him is removed.

Ibn Sirin said: they used to ask the Imam's permission while he was on the pulpit. When this became frequent, Ziyad said: "Whoever puts his hand on his nose, let him go out without permission." Ibn Salam said: it refers to every prayer in which there is a sermon, such as the Friday prayer, the two festivals, and the prayer for rain. Ibn Zayd said: it refers to jihad. Mujahid said: it refers to gathering in obedience to Allah.
